## Windows Operator evidence — 2026-09-07, Stage 1 qualification remains open

### Brave second-video selection and reconnection — 2026-09-08

The operator confirmed that voice now answers, but selecting the second YouTube
video fails. The previous deterministic desktop parser accepted only the third
video. Selection now accepts observed positions 1 through 20, preserving the
historical third-video execution record. Missing or ambiguous lists still block;
completion still requires the expected video identity and advancing playback time,
with no advertisement playing. An unknown previous write is observed on explicit
resume rather than clicked again.

The six new ordinal regressions passed with the full recursive suite:
7,422 tests, no failures or skips, in 237.8 seconds. An isolated wrong-index
mutation failed the expected second-video identity assertion; the baseline and
restored copies passed and production hashes stayed unchanged. Evidence is
`.cache/windows-operator/ordinal-mutation/proof.json` and
`.cache/windows-operator/brave-setup/full-suite.tap`.

The supplied Brave extension identity was registered explicitly for the installed
native helper. Desktop operator mode is enabled; authenticated installed HUD
configuration returned HTTP 200 with `operatorEnabled: true`. The installed
parser, controller and tool description match authored source hashes, with
recoverable backups in `brave-setup/module-backup/`. This does not establish
playback success or refresh the older installer artifact identity.

Backend restart exposed a separate reconnect gap: the native host exits on pipe
closure, but the extension only reconnects on a click or browser startup. Its
asynchronous debugger cleanup can also race a new connection. Separately, no
authenticated extension incorrectly returned a successful empty tab list; the
bridge now reports `EXTENSION_DISCONNECTED` with a reconnect instruction. That
regression failed before repair and passed afterward, including reconnection.
Attended playback and restart recovery remain unverified until observed in Brave.

### PIN-unlock voice regression — 2026-09-08

The operator installed the reviewed 0.1.11 package and reported perpetual
hearing/listening with wake word unavailable after entering the PIN. Installed
ASAR identity matched the reviewed artifact. All three wake-word models existed,
their HTTP asset requests succeeded, and the eight stored provider keys decrypted;
missing models or erased credentials did not explain this incident.

The HUD issued VAD, wake-word and speech-to-speech configuration requests before
PIN verification. Those protected requests returned 401 and were cached for the
page lifetime. Successful PIN verification had no recovery callback. An isolated
Chrome reproduction using the production HUD confirmed no wake-word/S2S retry
after unlock and a subsequent click constructing voice with default tuning.

The repair shares generation-bound configuration across the app and voice widget,
refreshes all three endpoints after successful unlock, and waits for current facts
before constructing voice. Proactive speech is deliberately dropped while those
facts are pending, as while the PIN gate is closed; it must not create an early
mistuned loop. WebSocket continuation retries a pending refused handshake promptly
and ignores stale pre-unlock authentication probes. No audio thresholds changed.
Nine focused regressions passed. The real-browser before/after fixture verifies
authorized configuration reload and server-provided VAD on an immediate click;
it uses disposable PIN/HTTP facts, not the operator's microphone or credentials.
Evidence is `.cache/windows-operator/pin-voice/`. Attended speech remains a separate
gate until the corrected installed UI is exercised.

The final recursive suite passed **7,416/7,416 tests**, zero failures, skips,
cancellations or todo, in 235.1 seconds (`pin-voice/full-final.tap`). Two old
source-shape checks were updated to follow the shared loader; their original
failure is retained in `full-suite.tap`. Removing the configuration generation
guard or WebSocket probe generation check in isolated copies fails the intended
assertions; production hashes remain unchanged (`pin-voice/mutation/proof.json`).

Four installed UI files were backed up and copied with source/target SHA256
equality. The real installed 0.1.11 boot then returned 200 for all three voice
configuration routes, with wake word enabled, models present and S2S enabled.
The operator confirmed that "Hey Jarvis, what time is it?" received a spoken
answer after PIN entry without reloading. Live evidence at 2026-09-08 09:08 UTC
records wake detection and a turn with 154 incoming audio chunks and 21 outgoing
audio parts. This verifies this startup repair on this configuration, not the
separate ten-run Windows Operator qualification. Installed manifest and sanitized
HUD facts are `pin-voice/installed-files.json` and `installed-state.json`.
The startup Gmail announcement is an existing revoked/expired authorization
alert from the immune explainer. No Gmail account or token was changed; that
external prerequisite remains blocked separately.

The first clean recursive campaign run executed 7,295 tests, with 7,295 passes, zero failures and zero skips. It used selected free ports, project-local long-form TEMP/TMP, and Node v26.1.0. ## ⚠ NUMBERING COLLISION — BUG-280 is assigned twice (recorded 2026-08-21)

`main` carries a **BUG-280 for `close_window`** (merged via PR #16, commit `842d7f6`), and the
branch `fix/weather-enrichment-inert-hud-card` independently used **BUG-280 for the search
provider chain** (commit `fddc3ab`) plus BUG-281…BUG-290 for nine further tickets. None of
BUG-280…BUG-290 was ever written into this file, which is why the collision was invisible: the
registry stopped at BUG-279 while eleven ticket numbers were in use in commit subjects, code
comments and test filenames.

**Not renumbered here on purpose.** Those numbers are embedded in shipped commits, ~10 test
filenames and dozens of code comments; rewriting them is a large, purely cosmetic churn and it is
the operator's call, not a session's. What is fixed is the invisibility: the numbers below are
recorded, and the next session should grep the branch — not this file alone — before assigning.

**It happened again, live, the same day.** While this session was staging its work, a concurrent
session in the same working tree created `test/bug-291-reauth-failure-names-its-cause.test.js`
alongside a `from-gmail.js` change. Neither ticket was committed yet, so the narration guard
written here was renumbered **BUG-291 → BUG-295** rather than contest the number; 291 belongs to
the gmail re-auth ticket. **291 will therefore look skipped in this file until that session lands
its entry — that is expected, not a gap.** The general lesson, and the reason this note exists:
grepping `BUGS.md` for the highest number is not enough on a shared tree. Grep the branch, the
untracked test files, and `git status`, immediately before assigning — a number is only yours once
it is committed.

## BUG-400 — the HUD asked for a token the server no longer had: the token prompt reopened on every 401 of a PIN-only deployment and hid the PIN screen (✅ FIXED 2026-09-03, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-09-03, five mutation probes recorded in `test/bug-400-auth-gate-no-401-listener-without-a-token.test.js`. Three defects under one symptom; each fixed at its cause.

**Symptom (operator, packaged build).** "MYTHOS needs your access token … Entered once per browser." on every launch of `MYTHOS.exe`. Entering the correct token from `mythos/.env` answered *"This deployment requires both a PIN session and the bearer token … the cookie channel is reserved for the PIN session"* (409). After the token was removed from the keystore at the operator's request ("keep the PIN"), the same prompt still appeared and its exchange endpoint answered 404 — nothing typed could pass it.

**Measured from outside the app, 2026-09-03, same server:** `GET /health` → `{"authRequired":false}`; `GET /api/pin/status` → `{"configured":true}`; `GET /api/health` → 401 *"set MYTHOS_AUTH_TOKEN …"*; `POST /api/auth/session` → 404. So the missing credential was a PIN session and every surface said "token".

**Why only the .exe.** The packaged app resolves its vault to userData, which carries `Identity/pin.json`; the repo vault has none. `pinSessionRequired()` is therefore true only in the packaged build and `npm start` cannot reproduce any of this. (Combined mode — token AND PIN — was the operator's starting state, and its 409 is the H1 security fix of 2026-08-08 working as designed; the operator chose to drop the token. That cell stays a 409 by design and is pinned by the BOUND cases.)

**Defect 1 — `ui/public/js/auth/auth-gate.js`.** Subscribed to `onUnauthorized` ABOVE its `/health` probe; the `not-required` branch `return`ed out of the async IIFE only, so the subscription outlived the decision. Its own comment promised "do nothing at all, ever." Fix: subscribe only after the probe says a token is configured (holder + null-checked cleanup). No listener beats a guarded listener — nothing left to fail open.

**Defect 2 — `ui/public/js/status-banner.js`, found by GATES.md gate B.** Same store, same 401s, offered **Enter token** → `openAuthGate()`. Fixed at the STORE: `auth-state.js` gains `setTokenRequired()`; once `false`, `markUnauthorized()` cannot raise the flag, and a 401 that raced the probe is cleared. Every present or future subscriber is covered without knowing about it. Real behavioural tests (pure ESM), not source-shape.

**Defect 3 — `server/index.js` `requireToken()`.** Three deployments, two sentences: PIN-only fell to *"set MYTHOS_AUTH_TOKEN"*, naming a secret the server did not hold — the sentence that sent the operator to `.env`. Now: *"this deployment is PIN-locked. Unlock it with POST /api/pin/verify (the HUD PIN screen). No MYTHOS_AUTH_TOKEN is configured, so there is no token to enter."* Token-only and combined sentences unchanged, pinned verbatim.

**Not fixed here, recorded so it is not re-derived:** after a correct PIN the lock screen runs `teardown(); onUnlock();` with no reload, and nothing in `app.js` re-runs the one-shot boot fetches that 401'd (`/api/config/vad`, wake-word config). The token path reloads for exactly this reason. A naive reload would re-lock, because `derivePinGate` locks on `configured:true` alone and `/api/pin/status` does not report session validity. To be measured live before deciding.

**Verification:** `node --test test/bug-400-…` 14/14; neighbours `auth-gate-state`, `server-auth`, `pin-gate-state`, `pin-session` 69/69; `actions-widget-glyph`, `bug-317`, `compose-caption-clear`, `open-artifact-auth` 36/36. Probes (a)–(e) each red on exactly the predicted cases, restores hash-verified.

## BUG-401 — the VOICE widget wrote the live-S2S result into the browser-TTS row, so `live s2s` read `checking…` forever and `browser tts` showed a value that was not its own (✅ FIXED 2026-09-03, mutation-proven — the s2s row; the state-line latch is SPLIT OUT and still open)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-09-03 for the off-by-one. Three probes recorded in `test/bug-401-voice-widget-s2s-row.test.js`. The second half of the original diagnosis — the top-line state latching `unavailable` — is **not fixed** and is restated at the end of this entry so it is not lost inside a ticket marked fixed.

**Symptom, from the operator's HUD screenshot at 03:00:54.** `browser tts  enabled` and `live s2s  checking…`, while the server log recorded a completed Gemini Live turn 14 s later (`live.turn-parts turnId:1 audioParts:27`) plus a Live tool call. S2S was demonstrably ON, the row for it claimed it was still being checked, and its value was displayed under a different row's label.

**Mechanism.** `ui/public/js/widgets/kinds/voice.js` builds `rows` as `[wakeword, recognition, synthesis, s2s]`, and the `/api/config/s2s` handler assigned `rows[2].value` — `synthesis`, labelled `browser tts` — in **both** its success and its `.catch()` path. `rows[3]` was therefore never written and kept its initial `checking…`, and a browser capability read from `window.speechSynthesis` was overwritten with a server setting. Two wrong readings from one off-by-one, which is why it is not cosmetic: an operator debugging voice is told S2S is still being checked (it is running) and that browser TTS is enabled (that was never measured).

**Fix.** A new pure exported `applyS2sResult(rows, cfg)` selects the row by `key === 's2s'` and is the only writer; both call sites go through it. **A key, not a corrected index** — `rows[3]` is right today and wrong the moment a row is inserted, and an index cannot be checked by reading it (GATES.md gate D: derive the selector from a property in the code). Pure and exported so `node:test` drives it with no DOM, since `ui/public` is a no-build ESM tree with no jsdom in the repo.

**The test is deliberately NOT source-shape.** A grep for `rows[2]` would now match the explanatory *comment* the fix added, which still contains that string — the exact false-anchor failure this repo has already had. Probes: (a) reinstating the shipped assignment reds 5 of 6 cases; (b) writing `disabled` instead of `unavailable` on the unreachable path reds only the honesty case; (c) swapping the key selector for `rows[3]` leaves the four ordered cases green and reds only "addresses by key, not position" — the one assertion that can distinguish a derived selector from a corrected index.

**Class.** BUG-175 inverted — false discouragement instead of false reassurance — in the file whose own header is about BUG-175.

### STILL OPEN, split out of this ticket: the state line latches `unavailable`

`mountVoice`'s top-line state is painted from `document.querySelector('[data-voice-state]')`. When the compose bar has not mounted yet the `else` branch writes `UNAVAILABLE` and **never re-checks** — there is no observer and no retry on that path, while the success path installs a `MutationObserver`. The file's own comment acknowledges the race ("compose-bar mounts in the same boot pass as the widgets, so it may not exist yet on first paint") without closing it. Confirmed on the same screenshot: `VOICE unavailable` while the wake-word row beneath it was updating normally, so the widget was alive and only that line was stuck. Not fixed here because the fix is a real choice (poll for the pill, observe `#compose-root` for insertion, or have compose-bar publish its state to the store the way BUG-400 made `auth-state.js` do) and it should not ride inside an off-by-one fix.

**Campaign follow-up, 2026-09-07 — state-line mechanism reproduced and repaired; packaged HUD still unverified.** The entry's S2S row fix remains intact. Current `app.js` mounts widgets synchronously before `createComposeBar`, while static HTML supplies an empty `#compose-bar`. A real headless Edge page mounted the actual `mountVoice` and then actual `createComposeBar`, called `setVoiceState("listening")`, and observed `unavailable` instead of `listening` before the repair. This measures the missing-pill premise without relying on a source-shape assertion.

`widgets/kinds/voice.js` now observes the stable compose container for child creation/replacement/removal and `data-voice-state` changes. An absent pill remains `unavailable`; teardown disconnects the observer. No boot reorder, audio change or second voice-state channel was added. The same mounted-module probe now follows listening, speaking, replacement and removal, and remains unchanged after teardown. This is browser widget verification, not a claim that a complete packaged application or microphone session was tested.

`test/bug-401-voice-widget-state.test.js` plus existing S2S-row tests passed **7/7**. Isolated-copy mutation `subtree: true` to `false` preserved initial listening but failed the subsequent speaking assertion, retaining listening: the browser exercised the exact descendant-attribute behavior being repaired. Original source was never mutated. Evidence: project-local `.cache/campaign/voice-widget-before.log`, `voice-widget-after.log`, `voice-widget-mutation.log`, and `voice-widget-tests.tap`. The original fixed-row status is preserved; complete ticket closure still requires the packaged HUD oracle.

## BUG-402 — the packaged build cannot find the build engine it installed: `setup-dsh.js` writes to `MYTHOS_TOOLS_DIR`, `adapters/dsh-agent` never reads it (FIXED 2026-09-10)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-09-10 — shared DSH resolution is covered by `test/bug-402-shared-dsh-location.test.js`. A fresh packaged rebuild remains owed.

`scripts/setup-dsh.js` `dshSearchHomes()` considers four homes — `MYTHOS_DSH_INSTALL_DIR`, `MYTHOS_TOOLS_DIR/DeepSeek Harness`, `<repo>/DeepSeek Harness`, `mythos/` — and WRITES to the tools dir whenever Electron sets it. `adapters/dsh-agent/index.js` `DSH_INSTALL_ROOTS` has two: `<repo>/DeepSeek Harness` and `mythos/node_modules`, both derived from `__dirname`. In a packaged build `__dirname` is `resources/app.asar.unpacked/…`, neither exists there, and the harness is not shipped (`build.files`). Boot log: `dsh-agent.offline … Looked in: …app.asar.unpacked\DeepSeek Harness…, …app.asar.unpacked\mythos\node_modules…` and `impact: every build will fail`. The HUD banner offers **Finish setup**, which installs to the tools dir the adapter will not look in — so the offered remedy cannot work. `%APPDATA%\MYTHOS\tools\DeepSeek Harness` holds only the vendor `package.json`. Writer and reader disagree on a path. Fix: the adapter must consume the same `dshSearchHomes()` (one function, both callers) and a test must assert the two lists are the same list, not two lists that happen to agree in a dev checkout.

## BUG-403 — `primeAuthSession()` produced no log line on a boot where its token was present and its exchange would have answered 409 (DIAGNOSED 2026-09-10)

**Status:** 🔍 instrumentation shipped 2026-09-10 — `primeAuthSession()` logs `entered` before its first branch. The original cause remains unreconstructed; diagnosed, not fixed.

On the 21:30Z and 21:43Z boots of the packaged build, `%APPDATA%\MYTHOS\logs\main.log` carried no `auth.session-prime:` line at all, and a grep of the whole file finds none ever. `resolveAuthTokenForPriming()` has no loopback guard and `decryptedKeysForChild()` has no key filter; `keystore-recrypt` reported all 9 keys decrypting; the server demanded a token, so the child received one. Every non-success path of `primeAuthSession()` logs, and a 409 from the combined-mode server was certain — yet nothing was written. Either the function is not reached on the path `whenReady()` actually takes when a PIN is configured, or `log()` is not bound to the file at that moment. Check that settles it: a temporary `log('auth.session-prime: entered')` as its first line, one boot. Not investigated further because the operator's fix (BUG-400) does not depend on it.

## BUG-404 — the adb fork-server outlives MYTHOS with its cwd inside the install tree, so the tree cannot be rebuilt, updated or uninstalled until someone finds and kills it (FIXED 2026-09-10)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-09-10 — persistent children use a writable runtime cwd, covered by `test/bug-404-child-runtime.test.js`. The EBUSY packaged rebuild remains owed.

Measured while rebuilding the packaged app: three consecutive `electron-builder --win --dir` runs failed with `EBUSY: resource busy or locked, rmdir …\app.asar.unpacked\mythos` after every `MYTHOS.exe` process had been stopped. The directory could be emptied but not removed — the signature of a live process whose *current working directory* is that folder. It was `adb.exe -L tcp:5037 fork-server server` (pid 4388, started 6 s after the app, from `%APPDATA%\MYTHOS\tools\Android Platform Tools`). `android-child` spawns adb from the server child, which the Electron main process forks with `cwd: MYTHOS_DIR`; adb's daemon inherits that cwd and, by design, detaches and survives its parent. Killing it released the lock and the fourth build succeeded. The `pc-child` PowerShell (pid 17688) also survived the parent kill and held the tree first — same class, second instance.

Consequences beyond a developer rebuild: the NSIS updater replaces the install tree and will meet the same `EBUSY`; an uninstall will leave `resources\app.asar.unpacked\mythos` behind. Fix: spawn adb (and every long-lived child) with a cwd outside the install tree — `MYTHOS_TOOLS_DIR` or userData — and run `adb kill-server` in the app's before-quit path; test by asserting the spawn options' `cwd` is not under `MYTHOS_DIR`. Related: BUG-402 (the tools dir already exists for exactly this kind of thing).

## BUG-405 — a dead pid cost ninety-two seconds and four turns because the failure named the recovery tool instead of running it (✅ FIXED 2026-09-03, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-09-03. Six mutation probes recorded in `test/bug-405-dead-pid-returns-the-window-list.test.js`. Two halves: the trigger (`open_web`) and the recovery (`delegate`).

**Measured from the operator's live voice session, audit vault 2026-09-03:**

```
22:34:57  cua_bring_to_front{pid:6960}   ok     <- 6960 was real
22:35:18  open_web{browser:true, ...}    ok     <- relaunched Brave
22:35:38  open_web{browser:true, ...}    ok        6960 is now dead
22:36:27  ui_elements{pid:6960}          fail   (24ms)
22:36:58  focus_window{pid:6960}         fail   (4ms)
22:37:45  list_windows{}                 ok     <- recovery, turn 1
22:37:56  list_windows{}                 ok     <- recovery, turn 2
22:38:30  cua_bring_to_front{pid:16652}  ok     <- correct at last
```

Every Brave process on the machine carried a start time of 22:35:18 and pid 6960 no longer existed, so the two instant failures (24ms, 4ms) were **correct**. The defect is the ninety-two seconds and four turns spent re-deriving a pid the failing call already had the means to return — during which MYTHOS logged two incidents about its own confusion, one reading *"resulting in perception of hallucination by operator"*. Nothing was hallucinating.

**Cause 1 — the trigger.** `open_web(browser:true)` hands a URL to the OS default browser via `externalOpener`. If that browser is not already running this LAUNCHES it, invalidating every window pid the model holds, and the return value said nothing about it. Now returns `windowPidsMayBeStale: true` and says so in the confirmed step.

**Cause 2 — the recovery.** All three dead-pid failures in `from-pc.js` ended with "call list_windows". Correct advice, and the model obeys it — the cost is the round-trips.

**Why the fix is at the delegate seam, and what the first attempt missed.** The first version decorated those three sites. That set was chosen by *which sites happened to carry the advice sentence*, not by the reason, and the reason covers every tool that takes a pid — there are **twelve**. `ui_elements` is not one of the three, does not route through `foregroundThenRetry`, and returns PowerShell's bare text straight from `delegate()`. That is precisely why the operator's FIRST failure (22:36:27) carried no recovery advice at all while `focus_window`'s did. One guard at the seam every pid-taking tool already passes through covers all twelve, including any added later. GATES.md gate B caught this; the `ui_elements` test case is the one that fails against the three-site design.

**Regression found by an existing guard, worth recording.** Removing the per-site advice in favour of the seam's dropped the recovery step entirely whenever `list_windows` itself could not be read — `test/close-window-honesty.test.js` had guarded that sentence since `close_window`'s own incident and went red. The contract is now explicit: **the ADVICE is unconditional for a dead pid; only the LIST depends on the lookup.**

**Scope.** `from-pc.js` and `from-dashboard.js` both sat exactly at their file-size ratchet ceilings (1552 and 1418), so the logic went into a new `src/core/effectors/window-recovery.js` and both files ended at or under their ceilings — no baseline was raised. `see_and_click` failing at 22:38:31 with the CORRECT pid 16652 is NOT this bug: it read the screen fine and honestly reported the requested text was not on it.

## BUG-406 — the half-duplex gate held the operator's microphone for 40% of a conversation, and 92 seconds of that ended in a timeout rather than in actual echo (🔴 DIAGNOSED 2026-09-03, deliberately NOT fixed here)

**Status:** 🔴 measured, not fixed. **Deliberately deferred** — see the closing note.

**2026-09-10 update:** BUG-428 wires the server's numeric echo verdict into the existing ceiling decision, behind `VOICE_ECHO_VERDICT_TO_CLIENT=false` rollback. No timer tuning and no barge-in echo veto. A verdict is evidence of a transcript, not a labelled acoustic sample; a live room is still required and no operator session was run here. Also, the historical `frames zeroed` column sums cumulative counter snapshots; it cannot establish the number of distinct frames lost. Release durations remain directly measured.

**Measured from `voice.capture-suspend` releases, operator session 2026-09-03 (~11 minutes of conversation):**

| release reason | n | total held | worst single hold | frames zeroed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `own-voice-ended` (normal) | 25 | 159.4s | 11.0s | 37,918 |
| `own-voice-ceiling-near-field-energy` | 5 | 68.1s | **21.4s** | 6,810 |
| `own-voice-ceiling-no-evidence-of-echo` | 2 | 24.2s | 13.1s | 2,235 |
| `suspend-window-elapsed` | 2 | 16.0s | 8.0s | 0 |
| **total** | **34** | **267.7s** | | **46,963** |

`framesDropped` was 0 throughout — nothing was lost in transport. The audio was **zeroed**, deliberately, by the own-voice gate.

**The signal is the ceiling releases, not the total.** Holding the mic while MYTHOS is genuinely speaking is correct half-duplex behaviour, and `own-voice-ended` is that working. The 7 releases that hit a CEILING are the gate being wrong: `own-voice-ceiling-no-evidence-of-echo` is the gate stating it held for up to 13.1s and **never found the echo that would justify it**, and `own-voice-ceiling-near-field-energy` held up to 21.4s on energy that near-field is most likely the operator's own voice. Together, 92.3 seconds of a ~660-second conversation.

**Corroborating, from the same session:** three `live-turn-no-user-transcript` anomalies whose healer playbook already names this exact mechanism — *"the operator's speech reaches Gemini but is not transcribed, most often because the half-duplex gate held it past the preroll ring"* — plus one `audio-duck-suppressed` reading *"mic-hot windows keep closing with no speech — ducking is arming on playback, not on you"*.

**NO AUDIO CAPTURE IS NEEDED — that part of the original entry was wrong.** `voice.capture-suspend` already logs the gate's own inputs on every release: `peakRms`, `bleedFloor`, `learnedFloor`, `bleedPeak`, `prerollFrames`, `flushedFrames`, `flushedZeroed`. The 34 releases from this session are the corpus.

**ONE MECHANISM PROPOSED AND THEN REFUTED, recorded so it is not re-derived.** `learnedFloor` does move exactly once and then latch: `[0.035, 0.0707]` across the session, the lower value on the FIRST release only, with `bleedPeak` equal to `learnedFloor` on every later row. That looks like the floor adopting the operator's own voice as bleed and going deaf for the rest of the session — and it is NOT the cause, because **`LEARNED_FLOOR_ENABLED = false`** in `ui/public/js/voice/barge-in-policy.js`. The learned floor is dormant by design: `bleedFloor()` returns `initialFloor` (0.035) and the learned value is computed and REPORTED for telemetry while deciding nothing. That file's own Q8 note explains why it was switched off, and it names this same failure — *"0.1781 learned against a 0.069 operator peak held real barge-ins for 13.4 seconds"*. Corroborating: `bargeVetoed: 0` on every release this session, so the barge-in policy vetoed nothing at all.

So against the floor actually in force (0.035) the picture is mixed — roughly 13 of 32 releases had `peakRms` below it — and the mic-hold is **not** explained by either floor. The hold is decided elsewhere (the own-voice hold in `voice/s2s-bridge.js`, not `barge-in-policy.js`), and that is where the next session should start.

**What remains solid, and is the whole reason this ticket exists:** 267.7s held, 46,963 frames zeroed, `framesDropped: 0`, and 7 of 34 releases ending at a CEILING rather than because MYTHOS stopped speaking — including one 21.4s hold whose reason is `near-field-energy` and two totalling 24.2s whose reason literally states no echo was found. Those numbers are measurements, not inferences.
**WHY THIS IS NOT FIXED IN THE SAME PASS, recorded so it is not read as an oversight.** Loosening this gate wrongly makes MYTHOS hear its own voice and answer itself, which is a worse failure than the one being fixed, and this repo has already mis-diagnosed this area twice (`bleedPeak measured the operator`; `own voice fed Gemini's VAD`). A correct fix needs a recorded audio corpus, the two ceiling constants traced to their real justification, and a replay harness — not a constant nudged at the end of a long session. **Revisit trigger:** any session that can capture mic + speaker audio together. **Durable form:** a replay test over captured frames that asserts the gate opens within N ms of the last real speaker frame, with the near-field case as its adjacent must-keep-passing.


**Campaign evidence reconciliation, 2026-09-07 — same 34 releases reproduced; no threshold change.** Running the existing offline voice-session verifier over the last of 35 stored runs (boot marker 2026-09-02T22:05:11.764Z) reproduced this entry's table exactly: 25 normal releases held 159409ms, five near-field ceiling releases held 68124ms, two no-evidence ceiling releases held 24203ms, and two media windows held 16000ms. Total: **267736ms and 46963 zeroed frames**. The verifier scored 17/21 criteria; failures were interruption ratio, seven own-voice ceilings, self-started turns, and one ACK deadline. These are historical log findings, not regressions newly introduced by this campaign.

The contradictory corpus notes above are resolved narrowly: release telemetry is sufficient to reproduce branch counts and durations, but insufficient to establish acoustic ground truth or safe release timing. Current `s2s-bridge.js` declares `lastEchoRatio = null` because no server echo verdict reaches the client. Consequently `ceiling-no-evidence-of-echo` means the policy had no positive echo input and low peak energy; it is **not a measurement that no speaker echo occurred**. The logged records omit synchronized microphone/playback samples, per-chunk scheduled playback end and AudioContext clock/state. Those missing facts prevent distinguishing a late player end callback, suspended playback, network timing and actual room echo, or measuring excess hold from the final audible frame.

The 8000ms watchdog refreshes on each audio chunk; the separate 30000ms absolute cap bounds the preroll ring. Neither should be lowered from release totals. The adaptive learned floor remains dormant and untouched. Existing gate/player/preroll/backstop suites passed **98/98** offline. Evidence: `.cache/campaign/voice-session-replay.log`, `voice-release-audit.json`, and `voice-gate-tests.log`. Next acoustic verification needs synchronized playback-end and microphone evidence with near-field speech and own-voice controls; scalar release summaries alone cannot supply that oracle.

## BUG-407 — MYTHOS held two answers to "which browser", neither derived from the other, so a named request could not fail: it silently resolved to something else (✅ FIXED 2026-09-03, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-09-03. 9 mutation probes recorded in `test/bug-407-one-answer-to-which-browser.test.js`.

**Reported by the operator, 2026-09-03:** *"If I ask you to open YouTube on a browser, it opens on Brave."*

Two independent code paths answered that request, and neither read the other:

| route | how it chose | could it be named? |
|---|---|---|
| `open_web({browser:true})` | `shell.openExternal` → the **OS default** | **no — there was no parameter** |
| `browser_launch_debug()` | `BROWSER_SEARCH_ORDER`, **brave-first** (BUG-130) | yes |

**Measured on the operator's machine:** `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\Associations\UrlAssociations\https\UserChoice` reads `ProgId = BraveHTML`, whose `HKCR\BraveHTML\shell\open\command` is `"…\Brave-Browser\Application\brave.exe" --single-argument %1`. So Brave really is the Windows default, both routes agreed, and **the disagreement was latent rather than live**. Set Chrome as the default and one spoken sentence routes to Chrome down one path and Brave down the other.

**The part that was already biting.** A named request had nowhere to go. `open_web`'s own tool description had to admit it: *"that is always the OS DEFAULT browser and cannot be pointed at a named one (BUG-398 E3: the operator asked for Chrome three times and got Brave every time)."* A request that cannot be expressed does not fail — it silently resolves to something else. The only route that *could* honour a name was `browser_launch_debug`, which offers a signed-out debug profile (BUG-408), not the window the operator is logged into.

**Fix.**
1. `src/core/effectors/browser-target.js` (new) owns the question: name normalisation, executable discovery, the executable→name map **derived from `BROWSER_SUBPATHS`** rather than typed again, the OS-default read, and the http/https rule for a URL bound for a browser process.
2. `open_web` gains **`browserName`**. When present, MYTHOS resolves that browser's executable and hands it the URL directly — Chromium reuses a running instance, so it opens a tab in the operator's **real, logged-in** window, with no debug port and no Electron hop (it therefore works on a plain `npm start`, where the default route cannot). Unnamed is unchanged: `shell.openExternal`.
3. An **unnamed** debug launch now prefers the OS default when MYTHOS can drive it, falling back to `BROWSER_SEARCH_ORDER`. BUG-130's brave-first order is demoted from "the default" to "the fallback", which is what it always was.
4. `browserSource` (`requested` / `os-default` / `search-order` / `browser-executable-env`) rides out on the launch result, so an unnamed launch never leaves the operator to discover which browser it picked or why it was not theirs.

**Security at the new edge.** The named route hands a model-composed string to a browser **process**, where `file:///…` is a local-file read primitive. `externalUrl()` parses with WHATWG `URL` and admits only http/https, the same rule `electron/main.js` already applies before `shell.openExternal`, and the parsed `href` is passed as the single positional argv element with no shell — so it can never be read as a Chromium flag. A probe confirmed `file:`, `javascript:`, `data:`, `ms-msdt:` and `search-ms:` are all refused **without spawning anything**.

**One thing the probes corrected.** The first version of the scheme test asserted that `https:/\evil.example` is refused, on the strength of this codebase's own comment naming it as the shape a `startsWith` check lets past. Measured: WHATWG treats a backslash as a slash for special schemes, so it parses to `https://evil.example/` and is **accepted** — correctly, because that is what a browser would resolve it to. The rule being enforced is the scheme, never the host. The test now pins the normalisation instead of a refusal that does not happen.

**Deliberately NOT done.** `shell.openExternal` was not taught a browser name. It cannot be: it hands the URL to the OS handler for the scheme, which is by definition the default. Adding a name there would mean re-implementing browser discovery inside the Electron main process, a second copy of exactly the fact this ticket exists to de-duplicate.

**Also collapsed here.** The URL-shape rule (`URL_SHAPED` / bare-domain) had two copies for one turn of this fix — `from-dashboard.js` now imports it from `open-external-route.js`, with a source-shape guard against a third appearing.

**Scope.** `from-dashboard.js` sat exactly at its ratchet ceiling (1418), so the `browser:true` branch moved into `src/core/effectors/open-external-route.js` and the file ended at 1410. No baseline was raised.

## BUG-408 — the debug browser is a different, signed-out identity and nothing MYTHOS said told the operator that (✅ FIXED 2026-09-03, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-09-03. 4 mutation probes recorded in `test/bug-408-debug-profile-identity.test.js`.

**Reported by the operator, 2026-09-03:** *"It's sometimes open on Brave where I think it's a debug Brave window."*

They were right, and nothing gave them a way to know it. `browser_launch_debug` runs with `--user-data-dir=%LOCALAPPDATA%\MYTHOS\<name>-debug-profile` — a separate Chromium profile with none of their logins, history, bookmarks or extensions. Both profiles were in use minutes apart in the reported session (`chrome-debug-profile` 04:02, `brave-debug-profile` 04:05). A window that looks like their browser and is signed out of everything reads as a **broken browser**, not as a second profile.

The launch result said nothing about any of it. The only related sentence was BUG-345's ads caveat, and only for chrome/edge — a Brave launch said nothing at all.

**Fix.** Every launch now reports two machine-readable facts (`separateProfile: true`, `signedIn: false`) and states in its spoken caveat that this is MYTHOS's own `<browser>` profile, naming the directory, for **every** browser. The ads caveat keeps its exact previous scope; `test/adblock-caveat.test.js` was rewritten deliberately so its false-positive guard asserts *"Brave is never warned about ads"* rather than *"Brave has no caveat"* — the intent it was always protecting.

**DISPOSITION PINNED — the separate profile is not the bug and is not changing.** Chromium refuses `--remote-debugging-port` on a profile another instance already has open, so driving the real profile means closing the operator's browser first; and a debug port on a fully logged-in profile lets any local page drive it, which is worse than an inconvenience. The reason is written in `browser-launch-plan.js` and a test asserts the sentence is still there. Where the operator genuinely wants their real window, the route is **BUG-407's `browserName`**, which uses no debug profile at all.

## BUG-409 — `browser_switch` closed nothing: `disconnect()` cannot stop a CDP-attached browser, so the next launch raced a survivor for the debug port (✅ FIXED 2026-09-03, live-reproduced and mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-09-03. 8 mutation probes recorded in `test/bug-409-switch-actually-closes-the-browser.test.js`.

`browser_switch` called `browserAgent.disconnect()`, which for a CDP-attached browser runs playwright's `browser.close()`. The installed `playwright-core`'s own types say what that does, verbatim: *"In case this browser is obtained using browserType.launch(), closes the browser and all of its pages. In case this browser is **connected to**, clears all created contexts belonging to this browser and **disconnects from the browser server**."*

`launched` is set true only inside `launchLocal()`. `browser_launch_debug` spawns the process itself and then attaches, so **every debug browser MYTHOS starts takes the connected-to branch** and survives its own disconnect.

**Reproduced live, spawned Brave on port 9223:**

```
after 3s                 : pid 13152 alive, port owner 13152
after browser.close()    : pid 13152 ALIVE, port owner 13152   <- the bug
after CDP Browser.close  : pid 13152 gone,  port owner (none)
```

**And the CDP close alone is NOT the fix.** Measured across 10 trials:

| profile | browser | `Browser.close` | survivor |
|---|---|---|---|
| warm | chrome ×3 | resolved | none |
| warm | brave ×3 | resolved | none |
| **cold** | **chrome ×2** | **resolved** | **`chrome.exe` still running** |
| cold | brave ×2 | resolved | none |

A first-run Chrome sits on `chrome://intro/default-browser` — its own make-me-default flow — and that outlives `Browser.close` **while the command reports success**. A resolved close is not a closed browser.

**Fix.** `adapters/browser-agent/browser-process.js` (new) closes and then **proves** it: ask over CDP → poll the profile-scoped process list → escalate to `taskkill /T /F` on the pids that list returned → report which step worked (`cdp` / `kill` / `none` / `unknown` / `not-ours` / `refused`). `browserAgent.closeLaunchedBrowser()` wires it up and is deliberately **separate from `disconnect()`**, which is also called on shutdown and by `connect()` itself — terminating from there would kill the session the caller is re-establishing. `browser_switch` now **refuses to launch** when the close fails, instead of launching onto a held port.

**The authorisation is structural, not a check.** Nothing in that module accepts a pid from a caller. Every pid it can kill was produced by asking Windows which top-level process carries a `--user-data-dir` under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\MYTHOS\*-debug-profile`, and `isMythosDebugProfile()` refuses anything else — **including the empty string, whose `-like '**'` filter would otherwise match every process on the machine**. The operator's real browser keeps its profile elsewhere, so it cannot be named by the query, let alone killed by it.

**A hole found in this fix before it shipped, recorded because it would have rebuilt the bug through the fix for the bug.** The first draft sent the close and then polled for survivors, so an **empty** survivor list meant "closed" — including when it was empty because nothing was ever there. That has a live caller: the operator can start their own Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port` on their real profile, MYTHOS attaches to it, and `browser_switch` would then have reported a clean close of a browser it never touched and launched a second one onto a port the first still held. It now looks **first**, so "nothing of ours is running here" is its own answer (`not-ours`).

## BUG-410 — the attached browser was recorded from the REQUEST, not from what answered, so MYTHOS drove an invisible window under the visible one's name (✅ FIXED 2026-09-03, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-09-03. 4 mutation probes recorded in `test/bug-410-attached-browser-is-observed-not-requested.test.js`.

**Reported by the operator, 2026-09-03:** *"Only once it was able to open YouTube on Brave, but it cannot navigate to the video by looking at it."*

`browser_launch_debug` ended with:

```js
// This is the only trustworthy source — over CDP, Brave reports a plain
// `Chrome/<version>` product string, so a version probe cannot tell them apart.
attachedBrowser = want || 'chrome';
```

The first half of that comment is **true and still is** — measured 2026-09-03, a Brave holding the debug port answered `Browser.getVersion` with product `Chrome/152.0.7977.65`. The second half was not: `want` is not a trustworthy source, it is **the request**. It was merely the only answer anyone had looked for.

**Why it mattered.** Because of BUG-409, a browser MYTHOS launched survived its own disconnect and kept the port, so a switch spawned a second **visible** window while the CDP session stayed attached to the first — and this line labelled the session with the name of the window the operator was looking at. Navigation and clicks went to the invisible window; `see_and_click` read the visible one, which never changed.

**Fix.** The oracle is the **process listening on the port** — its executable path names it outright (measured: port 9224 → OwningProcess 21708 → `chrome.exe`). `attachedBrowser` is now set from that. A disagreement with the browser just launched is a **loud failure** naming both facts ("Launched chrome, but the debug port is held by brave…"), never a silent relabel. Where the port owner cannot be read (not Windows, PowerShell blocked) the result carries `browserIdentity: 'assumed'` rather than `'verified'` — the same distinction BUG-106 draws between knowing and vouching.

**A probe that reddened nothing, and what it found instead.** "Put `attachedBrowser = want || 'chrome'` back but keep the mismatch guard" was expected to go red and did not: every test at the time passed a `want` equal to the browser chosen, so both expressions agreed. The mutation was not useless — it named an uncovered path. On an **unnamed** launch `want` is null, so `want || 'chrome'` reports chrome for a Brave the OS default or the search order picked: the same wrong-label defect from the other direction. A test for that case now exists, and the probe reds it.

## BUG-411 — `browser_launch_debug` decided whether to spawn by reading its own connection state, so an OFFLINE adapter with a live browser spawned a rival onto a held port (✅ FIXED 2026-09-03, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-09-03. 4 mutation probes recorded in `test/bug-411-launch-adopts-instead-of-spawning.test.js`.

**Reported by the operator, 2026-09-03:** *"Sometimes it is able to open, sometimes it is not able to open, sometimes open two, three chromes at the same time."*

The tool branched on `browserAgent.getStatus().state` and nothing else — ONLINE, CONNECTING, otherwise **spawn**. But OFFLINE is a statement about *this process's connection*, not about the machine. A browser can be running and holding port 9222 with the adapter OFFLINE: the poller gave up (the operator's own log, `browser-agent.giving-up` at 22:21:45 after seven failures), the connection dropped (`disconnected unexpectedly`, twice that session), or a previous `browser_switch` left one alive because `disconnect()` never closed it (BUG-409).

**And this is why the outcome felt random.** Two browsers were deliberately spawned onto one port, twice, with different endings:

| port | result |
|---|---|
| 9223 | chrome bound it, then **brave took it** — both processes alive |
| 9224 | chrome bound it, **brave exited** — one listener, chrome |

So "sometimes it opens, sometimes it does not, sometimes there are three" is **one race with at least two observable endings**, not several separate faults.

**Fix.** Look before spawning: try to adopt whatever is already on the port. It costs nothing when nothing is there — a refused connect fails in well under a poll interval, which is the measurement BUG-140 already relies on when it polls this same call. On adoption, the identity comes from BUG-410's port-owner oracle: a **named** request that does not match refuses (and says to close that window, which is the only true remedy for a window MYTHOS did not open); an unnamed request adopts and reports `portOwner`, `unknown` included.

**`attachedBrowser` stays null for an adopted browser, deliberately.** Its contract since BUG-106 is "a browser MYTHOS launched and can therefore vouch for **and close**" — and that value is what authorises `browser_switch`'s close. Setting it on adoption would let MYTHOS try to close a window it never opened. A mutation probe pins it.

**Not fixed here, and not this bug.** `buildBrowserLaunchArgs` still carries no URL, so navigation remains a separate CDP step after the launch. That is by design (the launch tool takes no URL) and it is the reason a launch and a navigate can end up in different browsers when the port is contested — which is what BUG-410's oracle now catches rather than what this change removes.

## BUG-412 — the BUG-410 fix left the same defect at three sites in the files it had just edited, and made a neighbouring comment false on the way past (✅ FIXED 2026-09-03, mutation-proven; one part deliberately not fixed)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-09-03. 7 mutation probes recorded in `test/bug-412-one-predicate-for-which-browser-answered.test.js`. **Found by running the scope gates against BUG-407..411's own commit, after it was pushed** — gate B: derive the set from the reason, not from the diff.

The reason BUG-410 gave was *"an identity taken from the request instead of from what answered"*. That is not a property of one branch. The fix touched one.

### 1. `requireOnline()` carried BUG-410 verbatim, twenty lines above BUG-410's fix

```js
attachedBrowser = status.mode === 'launched' ? 'chrome' : null;
```

`launchLocal` tries playwright channel `'chrome'` and **falls back to `'msedge'`**. On a machine without Chrome it launches **Edge**, and this labelled it chrome.

**And the comment justifying the literal was made false by BUG-407, in the same commit.** It read: *"via launchLocal's chrome-first/edge-fallback — the same default path browser_launch_debug uses for an unnamed request, so it earns the same 'chrome' label."* That parity was real until BUG-407 taught the unnamed path to read the OS default and verify it against the port owner. So the fix broke the argument for the neighbouring line and left the line standing — defect class 11, with class 10 riding on it.

**Fix:** `launchLocal` now records the channel it actually got and reports it through `getStatus()`. The label is read from the launch instead of re-derived by its caller. An unnameable channel stays `null` — unknown stays unknown.

### 2. The already-ONLINE branch skipped its own guard

```js
if (want && attachedBrowser && attachedBrowser !== want) { ...refuse... }
return ok({ alreadyOnline: true, browser: attachedBrowser || 'unknown' });
```

The guard is **skipped whenever `attachedBrowser` is null**, so a request naming brave got `ok({ browser: 'unknown' })`. The adopt path added in BUG-411 refuses exactly that case. Same predicate, opposite answers, in one function.

**Fix:** one predicate, `namedRequestRefusal`, with each caller passing what it knows. `attached` (BUG-106's value — non-null means MYTHOS launched it) selects the remedy, because `browser_switch` can close our own browser and nothing can safely close someone else's. `browser-process.js` refuses that close, so offering `browser_switch` for a foreign window would be a dead end.

### 3. The CONNECTING branch — DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED

It never compares `want` at all. A `want` check was added here and **reverted**: the identity of a connect still in flight is not unknown, it is *not yet decidable*, and refusing turned a poller race into a hard failure of `browser_switch` — two tests in `bug-107` went red, correctly. The **action** stays guarded one step later, because `checkBrowserTarget()` refuses a named `browser_navigate` while `attachedBrowser` is null, with an accurate message. What remains is a narration cost: "ready", then a refusal on the next call.

**Revisit trigger:** an Audit row showing a `browser_launch_debug` success on the CONNECTING branch followed by a `checkBrowserTarget` refusal in the same turn. **Durable form:** the join returning the uncertainty in its result rather than a bare `ok`. Pinned by a test so it cannot drift silently.

### Two probes that reddened nothing, and what they found

- **(e)** Deleting `launchedChannel = 'msedge'` from the fallback reddened **nothing**. `bug-106`'s test stubs `ensureOnline`/`getStatus`, so it asserted the *consumer* while nothing asserted the *producer* — the fix's own new field could be deleted from the branch that needed it most with the suite green. Closed with a derived source-shape test that extracts the channels `launchLocal` asks playwright for and the channels it records, and compares the two sequences: it catches a deleted assignment *and* the worse shape, recording `'chrome'` on the msedge branch.
- **(g)** Replacing the delegation body with `return null` also reddened **nothing** — the test "asserting" the delegation compared two exports and a `typeof`, neither of which the mutation touches. Closed by stubbing the adapter and checking the value actually comes back through.

Two vacuous guards out of seven probes, in a change written specifically about vacuous guards.

### Also in this pass

- `identifyBrowserOnPort` moved from `from-browser.js` into `adapters/browser-agent/browser-process.js`, beside `processOnPort` — the two halves of one answer were a file apart. The effector delegates.
- A duplicate `supportedBrowserList()` was defined in `from-browser.js` *and* exported from `browser-target.js`. Removed; the effector imports it.
- `from-browser.js` ended at **1609**, inside the 1610 ceiling this PR had already tightened it to. No baseline was raised.

### Deliberately not fixed, filed with the check that settles each

- **`main.js:1301` calls the non-closing `disconnect()` on shutdown**, and it is now the last caller that means *close*. Its sibling comment names BUG-029 exactly — *"leaves an orphan holding a browser… after MYTHOS is gone"*. Not swapped for `closeLaunchedBrowser()` because `stopRunningLoops()` is **synchronous by design** and the close is genuinely async (a PowerShell query plus a verification poll); a fire-and-forget async call there would not complete, which is the un-awaited-write class. `Start Agent OS.bat`'s orphan cleanup is the existing backstop. **Revisit trigger:** a debug browser found alive after a clean MYTHOS exit. **Durable form:** an awaited async shutdown step, or a synchronous kill by the recorded pid.
- **`launchLocal` cannot launch Brave and never consults the OS default.** Playwright's `channel:` accepts its own channel names, and Brave is not one — reaching it needs `executablePath`, whose precedence against `channel` is a vendor-resolution question (class 13) that has not been read. So the lazy bring-up in `requireOnline()` can still start Chrome or Edge on a machine whose default is Brave. In BUG-407's set by its own reason; a capability gap rather than a wrong answer, and the label is now honest either way. **Revisit trigger:** an operator report of the lazy path opening the wrong browser. **Durable form:** `launchLocal` taking a resolved executable from `browser-target.js`, so all three launch routes share one resolver.

## BUG-413 — the attach harness read the machine’s auth token when the caller explicitly passed none, so its own “no token” test could not fail on a machine that had one (✅ FIXED 2026-09-09, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ fixed 2026-09-09. Found while auditing why the pre-commit hook was red on the operator’s machine and green everywhere else.

**THE BUG.** `scripts/verify-lib.js` resolved its token as `opts.token || process.env.MYTHOS_AUTH_TOKEN || ""`. An explicit `token: ""` means *the caller is deliberately supplying no token*, but `||` cannot tell that from *the caller said nothing* — empty string is falsy — so it fell through to the environment. This machine carries a User-scope `MYTHOS_AUTH_TOKEN` (set for the phone node), so `attachMythos({ port, token: "" })` attached successfully and `verify-lib-attach.test.js`’s “fails loudly when the server wants a token and none was given” never saw its rejection.

**WHY NOT HYPOTHETICAL.** Measured 2026-09-09: the full suite was red on this machine with exactly this one subtest failing (`Missing expected rejection`), so the pre-commit hook blocked every commit here while CI and other machines stayed green. It is defect class 3 — the fixture was friendlier than production — and class 14: the test was structurally incapable of observing the contract it was written to protect, on any machine that had the variable set.

**THE FIX.** `opts.token !== undefined ? String(opts.token) : (process.env.MYTHOS_AUTH_TOKEN || "")`. An omitted token still consults the environment; an explicit one, including the empty string, wins. The test no longer depends on the host: it now *sets* `MYTHOS_AUTH_TOKEN` deliberately before asserting the rejection, and a second test pins the adjacent case — an omitted token must still fall back to the environment — so the guard has known bounds in both directions.

**PROOF.** Probe run 2026-09-09 with `MYTHOS_AUTH_TOKEN` set in the shell: restoring the `||` fallback made test (a) fail with `Missing expected rejection` while (b) stayed green; the mutation was confirmed applied by `git diff` and `grep` before the run, and the file was restored from a full-path backup afterwards. Baseline 23/23 before and after.

**SCOPE.** `parseHarnessTarget` has the same `||` shape for its own flag/env merge and was deliberately left alone: there an empty `--token` flag and an absent one mean the same thing to a CLI user, and no test claims otherwise. Only `attachMythos`, which has a caller-supplied options object and a test asserting the distinction, was changed.

## BUG-414 — the real-browser route never had an oracle: 33 of 33 opens told the operator "I cannot confirm the page rendered" (FIXED 2026-09-09)

**Status:** FIXED 2026-09-09. Five mutation probes, all landed, all fired, no survivors; source restored by byte copy with a matching hash. Not yet exercised against a real browser with pc-child running -- see the remaining evidence below. LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-09-09 against the operator's running Brave.

**THE FILED CAUSE WAS WRONG, AND THAT IS THE FIRST HALF OF THIS ENTRY.** This ticket was opened as a tool-SELECTION defect -- "the voice model reaches for the HUD card tool when the operator asks to open a website" -- off a 97:4 ratio of `open_web` to `browser_navigate`, and proposed renaming `open_web` to `show_hud_card`. Measuring the premise before writing code (gate A) disproved it, and the rename would have made things worse.

Two counting errors produced the 97:4. The Audit ledger writes TWO row shapes per call -- a request row carrying `args`, and an outcome row carrying decision/outcome/reason and no args -- so counting rows counts most calls twice and invents a large bucket of typeless calls that do not exist. And nothing asked what the calls were FOR. Splitting request rows only, 2026-08-18 to 09-08:

| population | rows | what they are |
|---|---|---|
| `open_web` with `browser:true` | 33 | the real-browser route, correctly chosen |
| `open_web` as a HUD card | 75 | 32 search, 30 youtube, 6 weather, 4 flights, 2 web, 1 image |

Exactly ONE card-only row is website-shaped, and it is `type:"youtube"` with a watch URL -- that type used correctly. The model is not confusing the two surfaces. Renaming would have moved the word "open" away from the only code path that has been opening the operator browser.

**WHAT THE SAME ROWS DO SAY.** Of those 33 real-browser opens, ZERO are verified: 27 returned ok+unverified, 3 failed, 3 recorded no outcome row at all. Every successful one told the operator, in substance, that it could not confirm the page rendered. That is the complaint. "It did not even open" is what an unverifiable open feels like from outside, whether or not it worked.

**AND IT IS A SIBLING-PATH GAP, NOT A NEW CLASS.** `from-dashboard.js` HUD branch was given a real render ack by BUG-273 B3 and returns `verifiedOk` when the dashboard answers -- 32 of the 75 above. The `browser:true` branch returned straight out of the hand-off and asked nothing at all. That file own comment predicted the shape: *"BUG-272 T2 only ever fixed the browser:true branch; this is the dashboard one."* The two halves keep being fixed alternately. This is the other half.

**THE FIX.** `open-external-route.js` gains `settleExternalOpen`, which reads the browser own top-level window title back through pc-child `list_windows` after the hand-off -- the same move `from-computer.js` `open_folder` makes against Explorer, bounded poll and all. Three looks, 250ms apart, first match wins, so the whole oracle fits inside the 1500ms ack deadline `open_web` is measured against (BUG-295 counted 44 breaches in one session, and `live-tool-adapter.js` argues `open_web` out of SLOW_TOOLS on the grounds that it is not slow).

The title token is DERIVED from the hostname, never a site table: strip `www`, drop the public-suffix label, keep labels of three or more characters that start with a letter, take the longest. `news.google.com` gives `google`, `open.bigmodel.cn` gives `bigmodel`, `google.co.uk` cannot contribute `co`, and an IP address yields nothing so the oracle is skipped rather than guessed at. The window search is scoped to the browser OWN process, derived from `BROWSER_SUBPATHS` -- `from-pc` `findWindowByTitle` searches every window, and a Notepad document called `youtube-notes.txt` would satisfy it.

**WHAT IT PROVES, AND WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT.** It proves the page is ON SCREEN. It does not prove THIS CALL put it there: if the operator already had that site focused, it verifies without having caused anything. Kept on purpose and pinned by a test, because the question the operator asks is "is it open", not "did you cause it", and a window title cannot honestly answer the second. Three things it cannot see, all stated in code rather than discovered later: a cold browser start (which outlasts the poll, so absence is reported as AMBIGUOUS and never as "nothing opened"), which TAB (a Chromium window is titled by its active tab), and a browser MYTHOS cannot name (Firefox as the OS default skips the oracle entirely).

**WHAT DID NOT CHANGE, deliberately.** Every path still returns `ok:true` -- the hand-off did succeed and the oracle can only sharpen the reason attached to it. `confirmedStep` still rides on every unverified branch (BUG-273 B2), so the model keeps permission to say the browser was handed the URL. And wherever the oracle cannot run -- no usable token, an unnameable browser, pc-child offline -- the pre-fix reason string comes back byte for byte, asserted by three tests so a silent rewording cannot pass for a working guard.

**Remaining evidence.** No live attended run: this checkout has no pc-child session and no configured Brave, so the poll timing (three looks at 250ms) is reasoned from Chromium instance reuse rather than measured. What a healthy result looks like afterwards: an `open_web(browser:true)` audit row carrying `unverified:false` and an `evidence.oracle` of `window-title`. A bad one: `browser has N windows open and none of them is titled for X` recurring on sites that clearly did open, which would mean the token rule is too strict, or `I could not see a <browser> window` recurring, which would mean the poll budget is too short for this machine.

**LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-09-09 — this is the run the entry above said it did not have.** Real pc-child, real Brave (the operator's own window, pid 12400), real handoff, no injected deps anywhere:

```
list_windows before      -> brave x1, title "MicroMundo Triage Board - Brave"
titleTokenForUrl(...)    -> "youtube"
performExternalOpen      -> { opened: true, via: named-browser, browser: brave }  (10ms)
settleExternalOpen       -> unverified: false                                      (893ms, 3 polls)
  evidence.oracle        -> window-title
  evidence.observed      -> "YouTube - Brave (brave, pid 12400)"
  evidence.expected      -> "youtube"
```

The title flipped from the operator's open tab to YouTube inside three polls and the oracle read it back off the browser's own window. Before this change that same call returned `unverified` with "whether the page actually rendered in the browser" -- which is what all 33 real-browser opens in the vault said.

**What this run did NOT cover.** The unnamed OS-default route. `performExternalOpen` needs Electron's `shell.openExternal` and refuses honestly under bare node ("the MYTHOS desktop shell is not running"), so the run used `browserName:"brave"`, which reaches the identical `settleExternalOpen` call with the identical oracle. The handoff mechanism differs; the verification does not. The default route still wants one attended pass inside the shell.

## BUG-415 — the launcher never asked which browser the operator uses, so it started Chrome on a Brave machine (FIXED 2026-09-09)

**Status:** FIXED 2026-09-09. Four mutation probes on the fix plus two on the guard it obsoleted; all landed, all fired, no survivors. Not launched against a real browser -- see the remaining evidence. LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-09-09: Brave really launches. The run also found a defect this fix created -- see below.

**Measured on this machine before touching anything.**

```
osDefaultBrowser()              -> { name: brave, progId: BraveHTML, drivable: true }
resolveLaunchTarget(null)       -> { name: brave, source: os-default }
findBrowserExecutable(brave)    -> ...\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\Application\brave.exe
findBrowserExecutable(chrome)   -> ...\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe
findBrowserExecutable(edge)     -> null      <- Edge is NOT installed here
```

So `resolveLaunchTarget` has answered "brave" correctly since BUG-407, and `launchLocal` is the one launch site in the codebase that never asks it: it tried playwright channel `chrome`, fell back to `msedge`, and stopped. On this machine that silently starts Chrome -- a browser the operator does not use -- and on a machine with neither it fails outright while Brave sits installed and reachable. `browser-target.js` own header states the rule this broke: *"when a change derives the same fact twice by different means, point both at the same input."* Three sites answer "which browser"; two read the resolver, and this was the third.

**The fix.** `planLocalLaunch` (pure, exported, testable with no Playwright and no browser installed) builds the ordered attempt list: the resolver answer first, then `BROWSER_SEARCH_ORDER` deduplicated behind it. The tail is kept on purpose -- the resolver returns the best answer, not the only viable one, and a UserChoice entry can outlive an uninstall. Playwright has channels for chrome and msedge and none for brave, so a browser with no channel is launched by `executablePath`; a candidate with neither is dropped rather than burning a real launch timeout.

**The profile now follows the browser, which is a defect the fix itself would otherwise have created.** `debugProfileDir(name)` takes a name precisely so switching browsers does not hand Brave the directory Chrome wrote, and the caller passes a hardcoded `chrome-debug-profile` path. Every resulting directory is still shaped `MYTHOS/<name>-debug-profile`, which is what authorises `browser-process.js` to close it -- asserted, because a launch into a directory that guard rejects would produce a browser MYTHOS started and cannot stop.

**DECIDED: the profile stays EMPTY.** The ticket asked whether to attach to the operator real profile instead. No. This launcher drives with CDP, so pointing it at their logged-in session puts an automated agent inside it, and `browser-process.js` close path is structurally authorised only for a debug-profile directory -- a real profile could never be closed by us. The other half of that decision is shipped too: `browser_launch_debug` description now SAYS the window will be signed out, and names `open_web(browser:true)` as the route to the real logged-in window. A signed-out window is correct behaviour and reads as a fault unless the model can say so first.

**IT BROKE A GUARD, AND THE GUARD WAS RIGHT.** `bug-412` asserted that every `channel: 'x'` literal in `launchLocal` had a matching `launchedChannel = 'x'` literal in the same order. With the ladder derived, the body holds zero channel literals and assigns from a variable, so that guard went from strong to structurally blind in one commit -- the false-green class. It was NOT relaxed. It was re-pointed at the invariant it always meant: every attempt name must be recoverable from that attempt own launch options, through the same two resolvers the rest of the system uses. That is strictly stronger than the regex, since it catches a plan that asks for msedge and calls it chrome, which textual order-matching could not. The half the derived test cannot see -- that the identity comes from the attempt that succeeded rather than a literal -- is kept as a narrow source-shape check. Both halves were mutation-proven after the rewrite.

**Remaining evidence.** No live launch. Whether Playwright can start Brave by `executablePath` into a fresh profile is unproven on this checkout, and it is the one thing these tests structurally cannot cover (they exist because every browser is installed on a dev machine, so a test against the real filesystem can only ever observe one outcome). What a healthy attended run looks like: `browser_launch_debug` with no browser named opens BRAVE, signed out, and `browser_navigate` afterwards reports `browser: "brave"`. A bad one: a Playwright error naming brave.exe, which would mean the executablePath form needs channel-style arguments this plan does not pass.

**LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-09-09.** The open question was whether Playwright can start Brave by `executablePath` into a fresh profile. It can:

```
planLocalLaunch (live, no injected deps)
  1. brave   source=os-default   executablePath=...\BraveSoftware\...\brave.exe
  2. chrome  source=search-order channel=chrome
  3. edge    source=search-order channel=msedge
launchLocal -> true in 1147ms, launchedChannel = brave
processes started: 7 x brave.exe under MYTHOS/brave-debug-profile, 0 x chrome.exe
closeLaunchedBrowser -> { closed: true, method: context-close, survivors: [] }
```

The old ladder would have started Chrome here, since Chrome is installed and Edge is not. Note what this run does NOT distinguish, because the machine cannot: Brave is also first in `BROWSER_SEARCH_ORDER`, so a live run on THIS machine cannot separate "the resolver was consulted" from "the fallback order happened to agree". The unit test does that, with a fixture resolving to edge.

**AND THE FIX CREATED A DEFECT, FOUND BY THE SAME RUN.** The launch log said `"browserPid":null` and `.browser-agent.pid` was never written, with seven brave.exe processes plainly running. `findChromePidByUserDataDir` filtered on `$_.Name -eq 'chrome.exe' -or 'msedge.exe'`. That file has exactly one consumer -- `Start Agent OS.bat`'s orphan reap -- so BUG-415 disarmed it for the default browser: an automation Brave surviving a dirty shutdown would keep playing audio invisibly, which is the symptom BUG-029 exists to prevent.

The repair is a deletion, not another list. `browser-process.js`'s `processesForProfile` already ran that query, with the same `--type=` filter and quote escaping, has never filtered on process name, and guards harder -- `isMythosDebugProfile` refuses anything but `.../MYTHOS/<x>-debug-profile`, so no wildcard reaches the `-like` and the query cannot be aimed at the operator's real profile. This was the third copy of the query and the only broken one. A browser-name check survives only to IDENTIFY a row, derived from `BROWSER_SUBPATHS` via `executableIndex()`, whose own comment predicted this exact defect: *"a hand-written second copy of the same mapping would not be [free], and would fail in the fail-open direction."* Nothing matching returns null rather than a guess, because `--type=` does not exclude the crashpad handler and a wrong pid would make the reap report success while the orphan lived.

Tests in `test/live-2026-09-09-brave-reached-two-blind-spots.test.js`; four mutation probes, all landed, all fired. One is worth reading: the probe that restored a hand-rolled query was NOT caught by the behavioural tests -- an injected PowerShell stand-in answers with Brave rows whatever script it is handed -- and was caught by the query-shape test and the not-a-debug-profile refusal instead.

## BUG-416 — the bridge issued a new browser identity on every reconnect, so a desktop task could never be resumed (FIXED 2026-09-09)

**Status:** FIXED 2026-09-09. Six mutation probes across three files, all landed, all fired, no survivors; all three restored by byte copy with matching hashes. Not exercised against a live backend restart with the extension attached -- see the remaining evidence. LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-09-09 end to end through the real compiled C# host over a real named pipe.

**The defect, traced through source rather than reproduced** (the desktop operator is not set up on this checkout, and the original entry said so). `hello` minted `randomUUID()` on every connection. The controller persists its target -- `save(id, { target })` in `src/core/desktop/controller.js` -- and on resume calls `browser_video_list` with the browserId inside it. After a backend restart the bridge looks that id up among live clients, does not find it, and answers BROWSER_REQUIRED, "Choose an observed connected browser". `observe()` retries three times and blocks with that reason. So the reconnection shipped in `8afc989` restores the PIPE and can never restore the TASK -- and it names the wrong cause, telling the operator to choose a browser that is already connected.

**The fix, as the operator chose it.** The extension persists an instance id in `chrome.storage.local` and sends it in `hello` behind a protocol bump to 2. The bridge requires a UUID-shaped id, adopts it as the `browserId`, and refuses a second live client claiming the same one. The refusal closes the NEWCOMER, never the running session, which is what makes it safe for the reconnect race -- the extension retries on its own backoff after the stale client is reaped -- while a genuine clone simply never connects and is announced on the bus rather than being mysterious. Protocol 1 is refused outright: the extension ships from this repo with the bridge, so there is no third-party client to preserve, and an old extension silently falling back to random identities would rebuild this bug behind a version number.

**THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THIS ENTRY: the same class bit the fix itself.** The first pass had the extension persisting an id and the bridge requiring one, with every unit test green -- and it could not have worked in production for one line. `electron/native-browser-host.cs` does not FORWARD the hello frame; it rebuilds it from an allowlist of four fields, deliberately, because the frame arrives from a browser extension and everything unnamed is dropped at the trust boundary. `instanceId` was not on that list. In production the host would have stripped it and the bridge would have refused every real connection as identity-invalid, forever, in a silent reconnect loop. Nothing in the unit suite could see it, because those tests inject into the bridge directly and never traverse the host. Only `browser-extension-electron-entry.test.js`, which spawns the real compiled exe, went red. The host now validates the id at the edge with `Guid.TryParseExact(instanceId, "D", ...)` and passes it through, and a test pins the two validators to the same shape -- if they ever disagree, a frame that passes one is refused by the other and the symptom is again a silent loop.

**A third thing the fix required, and would have failed silently without.** `chrome.storage.local` is gated behind the `storage` permission in MV3. Without it `chrome.storage` is `undefined`, the `try`/`catch` in `ensureInstanceId` falls through, and a FRESH id is minted on every connection -- the original bug wearing the fix’s clothes, passing every test that injects a working storage. The permission is added and a test asserts the manifest declares it, because this is one manifest edit away from reverting invisibly.

**The rigs were tightened in the same change, or the guard would be untested again.** Every controller rig returned a fixed `browserId` of `b` or `brave` and never checked the one it was handed, so resume tests passed AROUND the bridge -- the friendly-fixture class, and exactly what the original entry predicted. The reconnect fixture now carries a real in-memory `chrome.storage.local` (a forgetful stub would let a fresh-UUID implementation pass) and a `crypto.randomUUID`, and it awaits properly: `connect()` resolves the persisted identity before opening a port, so no port exists synchronously and firing the retry timer now does asynchronous work.

**Remaining evidence.** No live backend restart with the extension attached; that needs the attended Brave setup this checkout does not have. What a healthy run looks like: kill the backend mid-task, restart, and the extension reconnects with the SAME `browserId` it had before, so a persisted target resolves and the task resumes instead of answering BROWSER_REQUIRED. A bad one: `browser.extension.identity-invalid` or `browser.extension.protocol-mismatch` repeating on the bus, which would mean the extension needs reloading after this update -- expected exactly once, since protocol 1 is refused.

**LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-09-09, through the configuration that made the first pass unworkable.** The host was compiled fresh from the current `.cs` and every frame travelled extension-side stdin -> compiled host -> named pipe -> real bridge. Eight checks, all green:

```
connect  protocol 2, instanceId 97b8e15b-...  -> bridge ONLINE
         browserId == the extension's own instanceId (not a fresh one)
         welcome frame back: { type: welcome, browserId: 97b8e15b-..., protocol: 2 }
         browserName "brave" survived the host's four-field rebuild
kill + reconnect, SAME id                     -> detached, then connected, SAME browserId
duplicate live id                             -> browser.extension.collision, first client untouched
protocol 1                                    -> refused AT THE HOST: "Invalid extension handshake"
instanceId "not-a-uuid"                       -> refused AT THE HOST, same message
```

That is the claim the ticket makes -- identity survives a reconnect, so a task keyed on `browserId` can resume -- demonstrated on the wire rather than in a fixture.

**A second thing the run found: the host config advertised the wrong protocol.** `start()` wrote `{ protocol: 1, ... }` into `browser-extension-host.json` while a hello had to carry 2. Nothing reads that field today (the C# host takes only `pipeName` and `allowedExtensionIds`), which is exactly why it would have survived indefinitely and misled the first person to add a reader. It is derived from `PROTOCOL` now, pinned by a test that reads the constant out of the source rather than restating the number.

**STILL NOT COVERED:** no real Brave with the extension attached, and the desktop operator was disabled (`DESKTOP_OPERATOR_ENABLED:"false"`) throughout the 2026-09-09 live session, so this path has still never carried a real browser.

**A claim filed here earlier the same day was WRONG and is withdrawn.** This entry said the installed native host predated the fix and would refuse every hello. Measured 2026-09-10 00:10Z against the running install (`MYTHOS.exe` 0.1.12, rebuilt that morning): the packaged host binary contains the `instanceId` literal, the unpacked extension manifest declares `"storage"`, and the unpacked app source carries `settleExternalOpen`, `planLocalLaunch`, `ACCOUNT_STATUSES`, `BYO_PREMIUM`, the Anthropic provider, the BUG-417 engine change AND the `processesForProfile` pidfile repair committed only an hour before. **The installed app is current.** The prerequisite is therefore not a rebuild — it is switching the desktop operator on. Expect exactly one `browser.extension.protocol-mismatch` when an old extension first reconnects, and none after it reloads.

## BUG-417 — an ordinal addressed the Nth VISIBLE card while the tool promised result 1 through 20 (FIXED 2026-09-09)

**Status:** FIXED 2026-09-09. Seven mutation probes across the engine and the controller, all landed, all fired, no survivors. Not run against a live YouTube page -- see the remaining evidence. LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-09-09 on a real YouTube search page -- with a measured margin of zero, see BUG-421.

**The defect.** `snapshot()` ranked a card only if `visible(card)` AND `refs.has(el)`, and `refs` is filled by the targets loop above it, which also requires `visible()`. The item list was therefore viewport-only and `ordinal` indexed into it.
