## BUG-397 — `ui_elements` returned a truncated tree without saying so, so the model invented the indices it was never shown and every `ui_click` failed "out of range" (✅ FIXED 2026-08-31, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED and ✅ LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-08-31, extended 2026-09-02 after a Chromium run. Guard file `test/bug-397-ui-click-path-fabrication.test.js` (25 tests), **19 mutations run, none survived**. Two pre-existing tests deliberately rewritten (see SCOPE). Live oracle committed as `scripts/verify-bug-397-ui-click.js` — **9 PASS · 0 UNVERIFIED · 0 FAIL** against a real Notepad, including the whole 2026-08-14 sequence (`ui_click name "File"`, then `name "Save as"`), each confirmed by an independent signal.

**Reported as:** "the UI underscore click does not work as designed" (operator, 2026-08-31), symptom confirmed as the honest failure message rather than a silent wrong click.

### THE BUG

`Handle-UiElements` walks the UIA tree to `depth` and stops. It returned nothing about what it had not visited, so **a node that was a genuine LEAF and a node CUT OFF at the depth limit came back byte-identical**. A caller needing an element below that line could only infer it sat one or two levels further down — so it appended indices it had never been shown, and `Resolve-UIAElementOnce` walked off the end of the real tree.

Three separate defects sat on that one path:

1. **The truncation was invisible.** `@{ elements; pid }` carried no `depth`, no `truncated`, no per-node flag.
2. **`FindFirst(Children, ProcessId)` was duplicated** in `Handle-UiElements` and `Resolve-UIAElementOnce` — each took "the first top-level window UIA happens to return". A process owning several windows (Notepad **plus** its Save-As dialog) could have its tree read against one and a path resolved against another, with no error raised.
3. **The Invoke rung had no oracle**, so every button, menu item and link fell through to `foreground-pid` — "the target window is still foreground right after the click" — which for a click inside that window **cannot fail**.

### WHY IT IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL

Measured in `%APPDATA%\MYTHOS\vault\Audit\2026-08-14.jsonl` (the Electron vault; the repo vault stops at 2026-08-02). Live voice session, Notepad pid 31544, "save this file as…". The **only** read that session was `ui_elements({pid: 31544, depth: 3})`, so the longest path ever returned to the model was 3. What followed:

| Call | Path | Length | In any tool result? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ui_click` | `["0","0"]` | 2 | yes |
| `ui_click` | `["2","0","0","1"]` | 4 | **no** |
| `ui_click` | `["2","0","0","0"]` | 4 | **no** |
| `ui_click` | `["2","0","0","0","2"]` | 5 | **no** |
| `ui_click` | `["2","0","0","0","3"]` | 5 | **no** |

Across the whole vault the worst case is `["0","0","0","0","3","0","0","0","0"]` — length 9, against a tree never read deeper than 4. Each failed as `Element path index N out of range (parent has 0 children)`, and **the `0 children` is the signature**: the walk reached a real leaf and was asked for its child. A stale path reports a non-zero count.

The second half of the same session is the evidence half: **all five of those calls returned `ok:true`** with `evidence.oracle: foreground-pid`, while the operator was saying, in the same conversation, *"You didn't click on file, you clicked on edit"* and *"you have to click save as"*.

### THE FIX

- **`Walk-UIA`** flags every node whose children it did not visit (`truncated`, `unreadChildren`) and counts them; `Handle-UiElements` returns `depth`, `truncated`, `hwnd`, and `budgetExhausted`. A child-count read that *throws* marks the node truncated rather than letting it pass as a leaf — the fail-safe direction, asserted so it cannot be tidied into a fail-open one.
- **`ui_click` accepts `name`/`automationId`.** This is the class fix, not a convenience: `ui_elements` returns NAMES and `ui_click` took only INDICES, so the caller had to convert by hand and that conversion is where the fabrication happened. With a name there is no index left to invent. Case-insensitive by design ("Save As" vs "Save as"). Ambiguity **fails and lists the matches** — never silently takes the first.
- **One shared `Find-UIAWindow`**, so the tree read and the click resolve the same window; `ui_elements` reports its `hwnd` and `ui_click` accepts it back, with a named refusal when it is gone.
- **The Invoke rung gained a post-condition** — top-level window count and `ExpandCollapseState`, both content checks. Keyboard focus was considered and **rejected**: some providers move focus to the invoked element without honouring the invoke, so a focus signal would confirm exactly the no-op it exists to catch. This is an *oracle*, not a fourth escalation rung; BUG-274 T5 closed every client-side axis and concluded the WinUI3 provider reports a state change it did not perform.
- **`foreground-pid` no longer licenses a verified `ui_click`.** The round trip is kept and still reported — it catches a click that switched away from the target — but it downgrades to `unverified` + reason instead of `verifiedOk`.
- New pure module `src/core/effectors/ui-target.js` (`truncationAdvice`, `clickTarget`, `seeAndClickRecovery`) because `from-pc.js` is on the file-size ratchet and the ratchet is a ceiling. `withSeeAndClickRecovery` moved there unchanged — same concern.

### WHAT THE FIRST LIVE RUN FOUND (and the green suite could not)

The fix above was 19 tests and 10 mutations green before it ever met a desktop. The first real run failed **three** ways, none of them reachable from CI, because all three are facts about what Windows does rather than about what the code says. This is the entry's most reusable part:

1. **One element described twice is not two elements.** `Save as` matched at `["0","0","0","0","6"]` as a `MenuItem` **and** at `["0","0","0","0","6","0"]` as the `Text` label inside it — the ordinary UIA shape for a labelled control. Under a bare count rule *every menu item* is ambiguous, so the refuse-on-ambiguity rule made clicking by name unusable for the exact case it was built for. Fixed with an ancestor-chain collapse: when every match lies on one chain, the shallowest is the control and the rest are its labels. Matches on **different branches** still refuse — containment decides it, never order.
2. **The oracle was watching the one thing neither click changes.** Measured either side of each click: `File` moved the window's **own child count** 5 → 6 with the top-level count unchanged (a flyout is a *child of the window*, not a new window); `Save as` moved **neither** count and changed the **foreground window** (133858 → 68604) — a file dialog is neither. Watching only the top-level count reported both working clicks as `confirmed:false`: the **false-negative** direction, calling a working click broken. Both signals added. `GetForegroundWindow` is deliberately not the UIA `FocusedElement` signal rejected earlier — that one is focus *inside* the app, this is another window coming up.
3. **A fixed 180 ms settle is too short for a dialog.** The Save As dialog did not exist yet when the oracle re-read. Replaced with a bounded wait that returns the moment the count moves; applied to rung 4 as well, which had the identical defect and whose only oracle *is* that count.

Also measured and worth keeping: **`BUG-274 T5`'s WinUI3 `ExpandCollapseState` lie did not reproduce here.** Clicking `File` moved the state to `Expanded` *and* the flyout genuinely rendered (`Open`, `Save`, `Save as`, `Save all`, `Print`, `Exit` all appear in the tree afterwards). A working oracle was nearly "fixed" on the strength of that memory before the flyout was actually measured — check the claim where it runs before acting on it.

And a limitation the run exposed rather than fixed: **`close_window` takes a pid, and Notepad puts every window on one pid.** Six probe windows could not be closed individually. Not in scope here; noted so it is not rediscovered.

### WHAT THE CHROMIUM RUN FOUND (2026-09-02) — asked for as "open debug Chrome, play the third video"

The Notepad result licensed nothing about browsers, and the browser run is where the remaining ceiling is. Debug Chrome via `browser_launch_debug`, YouTube home, third video read off the page by CDP so the target is a fact rather than a choice (`India's Most Beautiful Islands…`, `-YaRRFrXW9M`).

**A single fixed name-search depth cannot serve both a dialog and a browser — FIXED.** Same window, same walk, depth varied:

| depth | elements | named | page content? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 28 | 8 | **none** — Minimize, Maximize, Close, New Tab |
| 8 | 52 | 20 | none |
| 12 | 109 | 29 | none |
| 16 | 452 | 309 | **72 page names**, truncated 0 |

Chromium's accessibility tree starts roughly 14 levels below the window root. `UIA_NAME_SEARCH_DEPTH = 6` therefore made `ui_click` refuse **every page element in every browser** while blaming the element — "no element with that name in this window" — for a limit of its own search. The search now escalates 6 → 12 → 18, stopping at the first depth that matches or when the tree has been fully seen, so a Notepad menu still costs one shallow walk. After the change the same call resolves the title and fails for the *true* reason instead.

**Two findings from that run are NOT fixed, and are named rather than left to be rediscovered:**

1. **The ancestor-chain collapse picks the wrong end when the clickable node is DEEPER than its label.** Measured: the exact title is a `ControlType.Text` at `[1,0,0,1,2,0,0,1,0,0,2,5,0,1]`; the `ControlType.Hyperlink` that can actually be driven is its **child**, one level deeper, and its Name is **elided** by Chromium (`…Life in Andaman and…`) so exact matching never sees it. The collapse rule added on 2026-08-31 assumes the shallowest match is the control — true for a Win32 menu item, inverted here. So `ui_click` matches the Text node and fails honestly with "exposes none of the UIA patterns". Fixing it properly means preferring a match that exposes a clickable pattern over the shallowest one, and coping with elided names — neither is a one-liner and neither should be bolted on at the end of a session.
2. **`click_at` reports success with no oracle at all, and did so here.** `click_at(1336, 1433)` returned `clicked:true` while the URL never changed and the video stayed paused at 0 — the element's rect (`y 1399, height 67`) sits below the fold, so the click landed on whatever pixel was there. This is the exact 1/0 false-success the pattern ladder was built to avoid, still live in the sibling tool that `ui_click`'s own failure text recommends. A remedy the caller is pointed at needs a visibility check and an oracle before it can be trusted.

Also measured: **`see_and_click` read the wrong window.** With no `pid` it does a whole-screen OCR, and with Chrome not foreground it read the operator's terminal instead ("Pre-dep10D | Ran 3 | Verified | #108"). Its own failure text names the fix — pass a pid — so the advice chain is sound, but the default is a foot-gun.

**Bottom line for the tool as it stands: `ui_click` cannot yet play a YouTube video.** It can now find page elements in a browser, which it could not before, and it fails honestly about the rest. Notepad-class apps work end-to-end.

### SCOPE — what was deliberately NOT done

- **The WinUI3 Invoke no-op itself is not attacked.** Every client-side axis is closed (`-NonInteractive`, `windowsHide`, spawn shape, window station/desktop/integrity, message pump/apartment). The new oracle detects and reports it. Do not open a sixth axis, and do not add a fourth rung.
- **The default `depth` stays 2.** Raising it pays tokens on every call and only MOVES the boundary instead of making it visible.
- **The 250 ms resolve retry stays**, and is now documented in code as *not* a mitigation for a fabricated path — re-running an identical walk against an extrapolated path returns the identical error. It was never credited with work it has not done.
- **Two pre-existing tests were rewritten, not deleted**: `ui-click-pattern-ladder.test.js`'s "falls back to foreground-pid…" and `from-pc-window-target.test.js`'s "ui_click verifies with a foreground-pid oracle…". Both pinned the false green this ticket removes. BUG-280's ProcessId assertion was *widened* to follow the lookup into the shared resolver, not weakened.
- **Accepted behaviour change:** a button that legitimately changes nothing observable (e.g. *Copy*) now reports `unverified` rather than `ok`. Honest rather than wrong, and pinned by a test so the next reader cannot "fix" it back into a false success.
- **Not reconciled:** this file's earlier note that `ui_click` is "16/6 with no failure since 2026-08-09" matches neither vault measured here (repo vault ends 2026-08-02; the MYTHOS vault has 2026-08-14 and 2026-08-18). Flagged, not corrected — it needs its own pass over which vault that count came from.

## BUG-396 — `see_and_click` clicked the video, then measured the screen too early and told the operator it had failed (✅ FIXED 2026-08-28, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-28. One new module,
`mythos/src/core/effectors/see-and-click-settle.js`, plus the block in
`from-pc.js` that consumes it. 18 assertions, 11 mutations all caught.

Found from the operator's own live session, not from a code read. The operator's
words were *"It can't even play the first video on YouTube. Basics."*

### The mechanism

`see_and_click`'s oracle is right and its timing was wrong. It samples the screen,
clicks, re-reads, and calls an identical read "the click hit nothing that
mattered". That re-read happened **once, immediately, with no settle time.**

Measured from `vault/Episodic/2026-08-28.jsonl`, lines 40-45:

| time | event |
|---|---|
| 21:10:24.216 | `screen_look` → YouTube homepage, target video located |
| 21:10:25.690 | `see_and_click` → clicked at 605,715, **unverified** |

**1,474 ms for the whole call** — one full-desktop OCR read, the match, the click,
and a second full-desktop OCR read. So the verifying read began roughly 700 ms
after the click. A browser navigating to a watch page does not repaint inside that
window. The click had worked; the measurement had not.

What the operator then heard: *"I clicked on the video, Sir, but I'm afraid I
can't visually confirm that it started playing. Would you mind trying to play it
manually?"* An honest sentence about a dishonest measurement, which from the
operator's chair is indistinguishable from the tool being broken.

### Why no previous entry covers it

`from-pc.js`'s own comment records the history as *"see_and_click is 3 ok / 8 fail
and every failure is grounding, never the click (click_at is 1 ok / 0 fail
all-time)"*. This failure is neither grounding nor click. **It is the ORACLE
failing** — a third category that had never been observed, because the two reads
had never been separated by a slow enough UI to expose the gap.

### The class

Time-of-check to time-of-use. `before` is sampled, the world is changed, and
`after` is sampled at a moment of the *code's* choosing rather than the *world's*.

### The fix

A bounded poll: three post-click looks, 500 ms apart, exiting the moment the
screen differs or `expect` appears. A screen that has already changed costs
exactly one read and zero waits, so no fast UI pays for the slow one.

**The bound is the interesting half, and it is deliberately low.** Widening the
window also widens the window in which an *unrelated* repaint — a clock, a
notification, MYTHOS's own animating HUD on an unscoped whole-desktop read —
satisfies `after.text !== beforeText` and converts a dead click into a claimed
success. That is a false positive, which is strictly worse than the false negative
being fixed. So `'changed'` keeps its weak wording, only `expect` reports
`confirmed`, and the constant is pinned by a test so raising it is a reviewed
edit rather than a drift.

`attempts` is now reported on every outcome including the unverified one: "I looked
three times across three seconds and it never moved" and "I looked once" support
the same sentence with very different amounts of evidence.

### Noted, NOT fixed — two things standing next to this

1. **The call carried no `pid`, so both reads were whole-desktop.** The OCR sample
   in that same log line proves the cost: it contains `"e @ MYTHOS"` and this
   repo's own version string, i.e. MYTHOS reading its own HUD, which is precisely
   what BUG-108 threaded `pid` through to prevent. Nothing makes the model pass
   it. Separate ticket, separate fix — a prompt or schema change, not this one.
2. **Chrome was showing "Restore pages? Chrome didn't shut down correctly."** in
   that same OCR sample, because `Start Agent OS.bat` force-kills the browser on
   the next launch. A dialog over the page is its own click hazard and is a
   launcher problem, not an effector one.

Neither is speculative and neither is repaired here; both are recorded so the next
session does not rediscover them as new.

## BUG-395 — the registry scanner read `BUG-0` as a ticket, so a commit message that quoted the id PATTERN broke the gate (✅ FIXED 2026-08-28)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-28. One regex triple in
`mythos/scripts/lint-bug-registry.js`. Found by the suite going red on `main`
minutes after BUG-278 merged, and caused by that merge.

### The mechanism

`ANY_REF_RE` was `/BUG-(\d+)/g`, so **`BUG-0` parsed as ticket number 0.** Bug
numbers start at 1, so no such ticket can exist — but `BUG-0` is exactly how this
repo writes the id *pattern* in prose. `bulletMarks()` in `build-index.js` builds
its anchor as `'BUG-' + '0*' + n`, and BUG-278's commit message (`bec26d1`)
quotes that literal while explaining the very anchor it tripped:

```
The bullet id anchor is `[-*]\s*BUG-0*<n>\b` and AN ASCII ARROW SATISFIES IT
```

The scanner read `BUG-0`, added 0 to `undeclaredInCommits`, and
`test/bug-373-*.test.js`'s *"the six measured commit-only numbers are named, not
counted"* failed with `bad entry 0` — a full-suite failure on `main` produced
entirely by a sentence in a commit message.

**Same class as the comment `bulletMarks` already carries from the other side:**
*"a pattern that matches ids must not itself look like one"*. That warning is
about writing the pattern; this is about **reading** it. The fix belongs in the
scanner, because the next session will write `BUG-0*` again the moment it
discusses the anchor.

### The fix, and the wrong version of it that was caught first

`/BUG-(0*[1-9]\d*)/` — optional padding, then a non-zero digit. `BUG-047` still
captures `047` (which `+n` reads as 47) while `BUG-0` and `BUG-000` match nothing.

**The first draft was `[1-9]\d*` and it was wrong.** This repo writes zero-padded
ids throughout — `BUG-001` … `BUG-097` are real, and grep finds them across
BUGS.md, `src/`, `test/` and `scripts/` — so requiring a non-zero *first*
character would have silently stopped matching about a hundred genuine
references. That is a far worse defect than the phantom it fixes, **and it would
have been invisible**: the undeclared ratchet would simply have got smaller,
which reads as an improvement. Caught by checking whether padded ids were real
before shipping, not by a test.

### Verified

```
node scripts/lint-bug-registry.js       382 in use, 243 declared, undeclared 130/130
node --test test/bug-373-*.test.js test/lint-bug-registry.test.js   28 pass, 0 fail
node --test  (full suite)               6890 tests, 6890 pass, 0 fail, 0 skipped
```

`undeclaredInCommits` now reads `[43,44,45,132,145,318,377]` — every entry a
plausible ticket number, no 0.

### Not fixed by this

The `undeclaredInCommits` list is **seven** numbers while the assertion that
walks it is still named *"the six measured commit-only numbers"*. The assertion
does not check the count, so the name is merely stale rather than wrong, and
BUG-377's arrival in the list is a consequence of PR #36 existing rather than of
this change. Renaming it is a separate, cosmetic edit and is deliberately not
bundled here.

## BUG-393 — one OPEN WORK bullet produced two contradictory verdicts, and BUG-352 sat closed-and-open at once (✅ FIXED 2026-08-28, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-28, mutation-proven. 1 source file changed, 1 test
file added (13 assertions). Two defects, one code and one data, kept separate
because each has its own red.

### The mechanism

`scripts/build-index.js` reads an OPEN WORK register bullet **twice**, by two
functions with two different rules, and nothing ever compared the answers:

| reader | rule |
|---|---|
| `openSetFrom()` | declared-open vs explicitly-closed, by looking for `FIXED` / `RESOLVED` / `CLOSED` / `SATISFIED` anywhere in the bullet's block |
| `classify()` | the entry's state, and for a pointer entry it reads the **same** bullet through `bulletPartial` — `FIXED … NOT yet` |

**A half-done bullet says both words.** So `openSetFrom` saw `FIXED`, called the
ticket closed and dropped it from the authoritative open set, while `classify`
saw `FIXED … NOT yet` and called it open. One set of words, two dispositions.

Measured on the register's 13 bullets: **exactly one contradiction, BUG-352**,
and the other 12 agree — so the signal is specific to the disagreement rather
than to the method. That twelve-to-one split is the negative control.

### Why the fix goes in this direction and not the other

`openSetFrom` is aligned **to** `classify`. That is a one-way safety argument,
not a coin toss: `openSetFrom` feeds an additive override (`if (openSet.has(n))
return 'open'`), so teaching it to keep a half-done bullet open can only ever
move an entry *toward* open. The opposite fix — teaching `classify` to honour the
closure filter — would have closed a half-done ticket on the strength of the half
that landed, which is exactly the failure BUG-390 built `bulletPartial` to stop.

### The second defect, which is data, not code

BUG-352's register bullet read `**COUNTER FIXED 2026-08-27 (147 → 179,
verified); the README catalog table and pie are NOT yet generated — see
below.**` — while its own Part 2 section, twenty lines below, read `**Part 2 —
CLOSED 2026-08-27.**` **Both halves had shipped.** `README.md` carries the
generated `SYNC:EFFECTOR-CATALOG` block and both `test/bug-352-*.test.js` files
pass (21 assertions, re-run 2026-08-28). The bullet's head was never updated when
the second half landed, so the register reported closed work as open for a day.

That is now checked: a test compares the register's claim against the README
artifact. It is scoped to the register section deliberately — **BUG-390's entry
quotes BUG-352's old bullet verbatim as evidence for a different fix**, so a
whole-file match would stay red forever and the only way to green it would be to
destroy that evidence. A ticket's live claim lives in the register; a quote of an
old claim is history.

**A note worth keeping, because it caught the author.** The first corrected
wording explained the old defect using the phrase "was not yet generated" — which
re-tripped `bulletPartial` and left BUG-352 reading `open` after the correction.
The cross-check found it immediately. Restating a stale claim inside the status
that corrects it re-creates the stale claim.

### The vacuous-guard half, which is how any of this was found

`test/bug-389-…test.js`'s live check is `for (const n of openSet) …`. **A loop
over an empty set is a green that asserts nothing.** On this branch the declared
set still holds BUG-392, so the loop is live *today* — but it goes empty the
moment BUG-392's bullet closes, which is what PR #56 does, and it was observed
empty on that branch. The mechanism it protects survives in a fixture
(`new Set([389])`), so coverage would not go to zero; the live-data cross-check
would. **Every live-data assertion in the new file therefore asserts its
population first** (`bulletNumbers.length >= 5`), so an empty register is a
stated failure and not a silent pass.

### Verification

The 8 that passed pre-fix are the two CONTROLs (a plainly closed and a plainly
open bullet, proving the rig can produce agreement), the closure-vocabulary
cases, and the nested-number guard. A green result on any of the other five would

**Six mutations, each sha256-verified to have applied before its result was
believed, each restored sha256-identical: 6 caught, 0 survived, 0 unscored.**
Two of the fifteen assertions exist only because of that run, and neither hole
was visible by reading:

| # | mutation | result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | the halfDone guard removed from `openSetFrom` — the defect itself | 4 red |
| M2 | `bulletHalfDone` loose in segment one (id → closure word) | **survived the first run**, then 1 red |
| M3 | its vocabulary narrowed to `FIXED` alone | 1 red |
| M4 | the guard inverted | 8 red |
| M5 | BUG-352's stale bullet head restored — the data half | 1 red |
| M6 | `bulletHalfDone` loose in segment two (closure word → NOT-yet) | 1 red |

**M2's survival is the finding worth keeping.** `bulletHalfDone` has two
independently tight segments and the nested-number test exercised only the
second, because its foreign bug number sits *after* `FIXED`. Loosening the first
segment therefore changed behaviour with nothing watching, and the mutation that
was written to prove the guard real proved instead that half of it was untested.
M3 was predicted before running for the same shape of reason — every other case
paired "NOT yet" with `FIXED`, so covering one closure word in four looked like
coverage. **Two routes, one answer:** M1 turns both the fixture suite and the
live-data cross-check red on the same change, and they agree.

### NOT fixed by this, and measured rather than assumed

**`bulletPartial` and `bulletFixed` are still loose, and that is filed as
BUG-394.** Both run against a *flattened* block, so `[^\n]*` spans nested
follow-up lines. On the real file the loose form matches **three** entries and
two of them — BUG-273 and BUG-274 — match only because a nested `- BUG-nnn`

(one entry wearing another's status) surviving inside the pattern built to fix

The new `bulletHalfDone` pattern used by `openSetFrom` **is** tight — no other
bug number may sit between the id and the qualifier — and across the 13 register

for being correct.

**Original filing, 2026-08-28, kept because the diagnosis was right and the
reasoning below is what made the fix safe:** filed, measured, deliberately not
repaired inside BUG-393's change. **Two mechanisms, ONE ticket, because they must
be fixed together:** the parser fix is what exposes the pattern fix, and doing
either alone reports a live licence ticket as done.

### Mechanism 1 — the last entry's body runs to end-of-file

`parseBugs` ends an entry at the next `# BUG-` heading, and the final one at
`text.length` (`scripts/build-index.js` :79):

```js
const end = i + 1 < marks.length ? marks[i + 1].at : text.length;
```

**BUG-273 is the last `## BUG-` heading in this file.** Everything after it — the
entire `## OPEN WORK filed` register and its 14 bullets — is read as BUG-273's
body. Its status is therefore computed partly from other tickets' bullets, and
appending anything to the end of this file changes it.

**That is not theoretical: it turned a test red on 2026-08-28 while BUG-273
itself never changed.** `bug-390`'s BUG-273 case stripped its Status line and
classified the remainder, believing it was driving the nested-bullet id check. It
was reading BUG-352's bullet out of the swallowed register, and passed only
because that bullet said `FIXED … NOT yet`. Correcting BUG-352's wording removed
the phrase and the guard failed. Rescoped to owned text in BUG-393; the
swallowing is untouched.

**Measured, not estimated.** Bounding an entry at the next top-level non-BUG
`##` heading shrinks **18 of 243 entries**, several enormously — BUG-98 from
124,030 to 5,498 characters, BUG-274 from 141,143 to 133,407, BUG-38 from 56,644
to 4,652. **Four change state**, and this is the whole reason it is not done here:

| entry | now | bounded | reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| BUG-274 | open | **verified** | **unacceptable** — a live licence ticket reported done |
| BUG-98 | fixed | unrecorded | honest; its `fixed` was borrowed. Raises unrecorded 0 → 1 |
| BUG-273 | verified | fixed | honest; it loses borrowed proof text |
| BUG-38 | fixed | verified | its own text carries the proof |

### Mechanism 2 — the bullet patterns span nested follow-ups

`bulletMarks(n)` builds `bulletPartial` and `bulletFixed` with `[^` + `\n]*`
between the id and the marker word, and both run against an already-flattened
block, so the marker can be drawn from a nested `- BUG-nnn` follow-up about a
different ticket. The pattern anchors its *start* on this entry's number — which
BUG-390 added deliberately — but nothing stops the marker word itself coming from
elsewhere. Of 243 entries the loose form matches three; only BUG-352's match is
its own.

### A third sighting, caused accidentally 2026-08-28 while writing BUG-278 up

The bullet id anchor is `[-*]\s*BUG-0*<n>\b` — **an ASCII arrow satisfies it.**
Writing `brain calls=1  <- BUG-278 measured 1` inside BUG-278's own entry made
the `-` of `<-` read as a bullet marker; combined with `FIXED … NOT yet` text
elsewhere in the same (flattened) body, `bulletPartial` matched and **BUG-278
classified `open` immediately after being live-verified.** Nothing in the entry
was a bullet.

It took four wrong hypotheses to find, because every narrower check said no: no
`**Status:**` line, no `**`-marker line, and a hand-written bullet test that
*looked* negative but was itself malformed by backslashes lost through
`bash → node -e`. The arrows were replaced with words. Two lessons worth keeping:

- **The anchor is far looser than "a bullet".** Any `-` or `*` before a bug
  number qualifies — arrows, dashes in prose, a hyphenated line break. The
  tightening in step 3 should anchor on line-start too, not just on the
  character.
- **A negative result from a regex you just wrote is not evidence.** Both
  malformed probes returned `false`, which reads identically to "the pattern does
  not match". Test the probe against a case it MUST match before trusting a no.

### Why they are one ticket, and the order to fix them in

**BUG-274 has no `**Status:**` line**, so `firstMarkerLine` runs and the loose
`bulletPartial` matches — giving the right answer, `open`, from the wrong
evidence. Tighten the patterns and that match disappears; `bulletFixed` (equally
loose, matching for the same nested reason) wins and BUG-274 reads `fixed`. Bound
the bodies and the same thing happens by a different route: the table above
measures it as `verified`. **Either fix alone silently closes the licence
ticket.**

So, in order:

1. **✅ DONE 2026-08-28 — give BUG-274 an explicit `**Status:**` line.** Shipped for
   BUG-274 **and** BUG-275, and both are now declared in the OPEN WORK register too,
   so neither rests on a single route. **Proven, not asserted:** simulating step 3's
   tightening against `HEAD` and against the working tree shows BUG-274 as
   `hasStatusLine=false, declaredInRegister=false, tightFixed=true` before —
   i.e. it WOULD have read closed the moment the patterns were tightened — and
   protected on both routes after. The wrong nested `bulletFixed` match still
   exists; it can simply no longer reach the disposition. **Step 3 is therefore
   unblocked.** The original note, kept because its reasoning is the reason this
   was done first: a Status line outranks every
   marker, so this removes the dependence on another ticket's text. It is durable
   on its own and worth doing first even if nothing else follows.

   **Measured 2026-08-28, and it corrects the obvious version of this advice.**
   `classify` has **no route from the WORD `OPEN` on a Status line** — the only
   paths to `open` are the register, a bold marker, or `NOT STARTED` anywhere in
   the body. So a Status line saying `OPEN` is *decorative*: it would silence the
   wrong marker and leave the real route as `NOT STARTED` in the body, which is
   the ticket's own text and therefore an improvement, but not a clean fix. Say
   that plainly rather than claiming the Status line closed the hole.

   **And do not fix the missing route with a bare word match.** Of 243 entries,
   exactly two carry `OPEN` somewhere in a Status line while classifying closed —
   **BUG-93 (`fixed`) and BUG-276 (`verified`)** — in both cases incidentally,
   inside a longer line that states `FIXED`. A naive `/\bOPEN\b/` on the Status
   line would flip two correctly-closed entries to open. The route has to be
   position-anchored the way the duplicate check already is (`^[^.]{0,40}`), not a
   bare word test.

   **Who else depends on the fallback:** five entries reach `open` from outside
   the register, and **none of them has a Status line**. BUG-266/267/268 use bold
   `**OPEN**` markers and carry no `NOT STARTED` at all; **BUG-274 and BUG-275
   both rest on `NOT STARTED` appearing somewhere in their body**, so an editorial
   rewrite of either entry's prose can silently unrecord it. BUG-275 deserves the
   same Status line as BUG-274 and for the same reason.
2. Then bound the entry bodies, and inspect all four state changes by hand rather
   than counting them.
3. Then tighten both patterns together, using the tight form already proven as
   `bulletHalfDone`.

**Bounded, not urgent:** mechanism 2 needs an entry with no Status line whose
nested follow-ups carry a marker word — today exactly one, and it currently reads
correctly. Mechanism 1 is live on every run but only mis-states entries whose own
text is silent.

## BUG-392 — a caller abort drops the provider cooldowns it had already earned, and says nothing (✅ FIXED 2026-08-28)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-28, mutation-proven (5/5 caught, 0 unscored), suite
6863/6863/0/0. **The mechanism was exactly as filed. The reachability was not, and
the ticket's own instruction to measure before sizing the fix is what caught it.**
7 assertions in `test/bug-392-abort-drops-earned-cooldowns.test.js`.

### The reachability claim was wrong, and this is now a LATENT defect

The entry below says *"the window is wide whenever the per-attempt ceiling
(`CHAIN_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS`) is below the caller's own, which is the configuration
the per-attempt ceiling exists for."* Measured, that configuration is not shipped
and the window is not wide. Three probes:

| probe | result |
|---|---|
| the entry's probe 1 — `AbortError` out of `chain.complete` in `%APPDATA%/MYTHOS/mythos-server.log` (28,952 lines, 2026-08-10…27) | **0 — and the probe cannot work.** `brain/index.js:220` converts the AbortError to `{ content: null, aborted: true }` and logs nothing; and `voice-agent.js` passes no `onAttemptEnd`, so voice-lane attempts leave no `*.attempt` line either. All 59 `aborted` lines in that log are `timedOut:true` — attempts that hit their OWN ceiling, on the vision and reasoning lanes. **The one path that can hit this bug is the one path with no attempt telemetry.** |
| the entry's probe 2 — audit vault turns ending without a provider outcome | **not answerable.** 0 of 780,450 records carry a `provider` field at all. Incidentally: 8 records with `actor:"voice"` against 863 `voice-live`, so the classic voice path is barely exercised. |
| a third probe, added because the first two are blind — every `.think()` call site in the tree | **38 parsed; exactly ONE passes a caller `signal`** (`voice/voice-agent.js:413`), and it does **not** override `attemptTimeoutMs`. |

So on the only path where a caller signal exists, the per-attempt ceiling and the
caller's own ceiling are **both 30000ms** (`chain.js` `ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS` default;
`.env:182` leaves the override commented out), and the caller's timer is armed
**first** — `server/index.js:3300`, before the memory-recall work that precedes
`handleUtterance`. The caller therefore aborts before any attempt can reach its own
ceiling, `attemptTimedOut` stays false, nothing is ever deferred, and nothing is
dropped. `deep-think.js:113` and `vision-call.js:133` DO lower `attemptTimeoutMs`
but pass no signal, so the abort exit is unreachable from them.

**Precondition for it to be live:** an operator lowers `CHAIN_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS`
below the voice turn's 30s ceiling. `schema.js:553` supports that down to 1000.
Fixed anyway, because it is the third instance of one invariant — not because a
session was observed losing a cooldown.

### The fix

`settleDeferredTimeouts()` before the abort throw, and nothing else — the shape the
entry prescribes. It settles only what was ALREADY deferred, so the adjacent ruling
at `chain-provider-breakers.test.js:130-142` (a provider interrupted BY the abort
earns nothing) survives untouched: the discriminator is `attemptTimedOut`, set only
by the chain's own timer, so a provider killed by the caller never enters
`deferredTimeoutCooldowns` and settling cannot reach it. That non-change is pinned
by its own test.

Two things the entry told the fixer to check, both real:

1. **The settle is wrapped, because it could have destroyed the AbortError.**
   `settleDeferredTimeouts` guards its own `bus.emit`, but `breaker.recordFailure()`
   reaches an **unguarded** `bus.emit` at `immune/breakers.js:136`. A throwing
   `health.anomaly` subscriber would have replaced the caller's AbortError with its
   own error, so the turn would lose the reason it ended. It now fails open loudly:
   the abort propagates unchanged and the swallowed cause is named in a warn.
   **Bounded residual, deliberately not fixed here:** such a throw mid-loop leaves
   the remaining deferred cooldowns unapplied while `deferredSettled` is already
   true, so they are lost. Needs a throwing subscriber; different ticket.
2. **`onAttempt(...)` was fixed too — it is the same class one line away.** This
   file states the invariant about itself twice ("Telemetry must never be able to
   break the chain walk it is measuring") and wraps `reportSkip` and
   `reportAttemptEnd`. `onAttempt` was the one callback left bare, and in production
   it is `bus.emit('brain-spend', ...)`, so one throwing subscriber killed the turn
   with an error naming neither the chain nor the subscriber. Pre-fix the new test
   for it failed at `chain.js:347:20`, exactly where the entry predicted.

### The class, and the guard that outlives this entry

This is the same omission for the **third** time on the **third** exit. The comment
above `settleDeferredTimeouts` asserted full coverage — *"Called on EVERY exit from
the walk — success and exhaustion both"* — and that sentence was already false when
it was written, because the abort exit existed and was not counted. Prose is what
failed here, so the replacement is executable: the test file counts the
`return`/`throw` exits inside `complete()` and fails when a new one appears without
a settle. Mutation M4 added a fourth exit and the guard caught it; M3 removed the
*exhaustion* settle and it caught that too, so it is measuring settles rather than
passing vacuously.

### Verification

```
node --test test/bug-392-abort-drops-earned-cooldowns.test.js   pre-fix:  7 tests, 2 pass, 4 fail
                                                               post-fix: 7 tests, 7 pass, 0 fail
node --test (full suite)                                        6863 pass, 0 fail, 0 skipped
mutations                                                       5 applied (sha-verified), 5 caught, 0 unscored
```

The 2 tests that passed pre-fix are the two that must: the CONTROL (proving the rig
genuinely defers an owed cooldown, so the reproduction is not passing because
nothing matched) and the DISPOSITION PIN (the adjacent ruling, unchanged by design).

**NOT live-verified, and it cannot be from here — the register's `verified` state
rests on the mutation proof alone.** No live session was observed dropping a
cooldown, because on shipped defaults none can. The fix is proven against the
mechanism, not against an incident. To make it live-observable an operator would
have to set `CHAIN_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS` to something like 5000 and abandon a voice
turn mid-walk. A healthy result afterwards is unchanged voice behaviour with no new
`settle-on-abort failed` warns; that warn appearing means a `health.anomaly`
subscriber is throwing and item 1's residual has become real.

**What the original filing got right, and it is most of it:** the mechanism, the
three exits, the wrong comment, the idempotency of `deferredSettled`, the
`onAttempt` hazard, the adjacent ruling that had to survive, and the deterministic
rig — the reproduction below was reused almost verbatim as the test's harness.

**Original filing, 2026-08-28, kept verbatim below.** Its reachability paragraph is
superseded by the measurement above.

**Status at filing:** OPEN — filed, reproduced, and deliberately not repaired. Found
by the 2026-08-28 audit read of BUG-273. No test ships with this entry because no
behaviour changed; the reproduction below is the deliverable.

**A note the next filer needs, learned by this entry filing itself CLOSED.** The
register classifier tests `/\bFIXED\b/i` against the heading and the `**Status:**`
line and has no negation handling, so the words "NOT FIXED" read as FIXED. This
entry was written with "(FILED 2026-08-28, NOT FIXED)" in its heading and came
back from `build-index.js` as `fixed`. Say OPEN, and put the number in the OPEN
WORK register — `openSet.has(n)` is checked before the fixed test and is the only
statement of status that cannot be defeated by a word appearing elsewhere.

**The defect.** `src/core/brain/chain.js:335` is the loop-top abort check:

```js
if (signal && signal.aborted) { const e = new Error('aborted'); e.name = 'AbortError'; throw e; }
```

It throws straight out of the walk **without calling `settleDeferredTimeouts()`**.
That function is where a timed-out attempt actually becomes a cooldown —
`markCooldown(...)` plus `breaker.recordFailure()` — and where the deliberate
shared-cause exemption reports itself, via a `[brain chain] whole-lane-timeout`
warn and a `chain-whole-lane-timeout` health.anomaly.

So on the abort exit every deferred cooldown is dropped, and dropped **silently**:
no `markCooldown`, no `recordFailure`, no warn, no anomaly. A provider that just
timed out is left uncooled and unrecorded, and nothing anywhere says a decision
was made.

**The comment above that function is also wrong, and says so in as many words.**
`chain.js:271` reads *"Called on EVERY exit from the walk — success and exhaustion
both"*. There are three exits, not two. It is called at `:388` (success) and `:452`
(exhaustion) and not on the abort. The same comment records that the FIRST version
of this fix ran settle only on the exhausted path and silently dropped the cooldown
for every run that eventually answered — **this is that bug a third time, on the
third exit.** Its own text calls that the common case.

**REPRODUCED 2026-08-28** (deterministic, no network, no timing race). One provider
times out so exactly ONE cooldown is deferred, which matters: `sharedCauseLikely`
requires `deferredTimeoutCooldowns.length > 1`, so the exemption does NOT apply and
the cooldown is genuinely owed. The first provider aborts the caller's signal from
inside its own attempt-timeout handler, so the next loop-top check fires on a
guaranteed schedule rather than a millisecond window:

```
zcode hangs past a 40ms attempt ceiling -> ONE deferred cooldown, genuinely owed

A. CONTROL - no caller abort; groq answers, walk exits normally
   outcome  : answered by groq
   cooldowns: ["zcode:slow-one"]
   warned   : (nothing)

B. caller aborts as zcode times out; next loop-top check throws
   outcome  : threw AbortError (aborted)
   cooldowns: []   <-- DROPPED
   warned   : (nothing)
```

Rig: stub `chain._internal.LANES` and `registry.chainFor` exactly as
`test/chain-provider-breakers.test.js` does (entries are `{ provider, model }`, not
`{ lane, model }` — `expand()` maps one to the other), first lane a promise that
rejects on its `opts.signal` abort and calls the caller's `ac.abort()` first,
second lane an immediate answer, `attemptTimeoutMs: 40`.

**Why it is reachable in production.** `server/index.js` passes a caller `signal`
into `voice-agent.js`, which passes it to `chain.complete`. Any caller-side
cancellation — an outer timeout, a voice turn superseded by the next utterance, a
closed socket — lands here. The window is wide whenever the per-attempt ceiling
(`CHAIN_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS`) is below the caller's own, which is the configuration
the per-attempt ceiling exists for.

**Consequence.** A genuinely slow provider keeps its place at the head of the lane
across aborted runs, so the next call pays its ceiling again. That is the exact
all-day-outage shape B1 and C3 were written to stop, restored on one path — and
because the drop is silent, the only symptom is latency nobody can attribute.

**NOT MEASURED, and it should be before the fix is sized:** how often the abort exit
is actually taken in a real session. Two candidate probes, both cheap: count
`AbortError` throws out of `chain.complete` in `mythos-server.log`, and check the
audit vault for turns that end without a provider outcome. **Do not fix this on the
strength of the reasoning above alone** — this repo has recorded five tickets whose
named cause was wrong, three of them in BUG-273 itself.

**The fix is small and the shape is already decided by the other two exits:** settle
before the throw. Two things to check while doing it, neither of them optional —
`settleDeferredTimeouts()` is idempotent (`deferredSettled`), so calling it on a
third path cannot double-charge; and `onAttempt(...)` at `:347` is NOT inside a
`try`, so a throwing instrumentation callback takes the walk down with it, which is
the same class of defect one line away.

**READ THIS BEFORE FIXING IT — there is an adjacent ruling and it is deliberate.**
`test/chain-provider-breakers.test.js:130-142` aborts a run with a SINGLE provider
hanging and asserts `cooldowns.has(...) === false`, with the reason written out:
*"penalising a provider for the caller changing its mind would evict healthy
models"*. That is correct and must stay. **This ticket is about a different
provider.** There, the provider was interrupted BY the abort and had earned
nothing. Here, an EARLIER provider already blew its own per-attempt ceiling, on its
own merits, before any abort existed — the cooldown was owed and then discarded by
an unrelated event. A fix that simply cools down whatever was in flight at abort
time breaks that ruling; the fix is to settle what was already deferred, and
nothing else.

**No existing test can see it.** `test/bug-273-c3-whole-lane-timeout.test.js` is
pure source-shape regex over `chain.js`. The abort test above ranks exactly one
provider, so there is nothing deferred to drop and it passes either way.

## BUG-391 — the last 28 entries recorded by hand, each against the artifact it names, and every citation re-checked by a test (✅ FIXED 2026-08-28)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-28. **unrecorded 28 → 0.** Every entry in the register
now states a status a machine can read. 7 assertions.

### What this is, and why it could not be automated

BUG-389 and BUG-390 taught the register to READ statuses that were already
written, which took 133 → 36 → 28. These last 28 (BUG-047…097, 230, 236, 253,
256, 272) genuinely had none: narrative entries in the shape
`**Symptom.** / **Root cause.** / **Fix.**`, past tense, naming real code.

BUG-390 recorded three mechanical oracles built to close them and rejected for
false positives. **A fourth was not attempted.** Instead each entry's own
`**Fix.**` section was read, the specific file and artifact it names were
extracted by hand, and that pair was checked against the current tree.

**All 28 are present.** Four needed individual investigation because the first
pass looked in the wrong place — and in every case the fix had shipped and the
file had moved:

| entry | first guess | where it actually is |
|---|---|---|
| BUG-048 | fixed | blocked | Identity persona reads pinned operator-profile; reflection only writes profiles of at least 8 characters. Persona/reflection regressions pass for profile inclusion and short-output preservation. Missing proof: real model rewrite preserving every durable fact; length guard cannot prove semantic preservation. | [test/persona.test.js](mythos/test/persona.test.js) |
| BUG-051 | `src/core/agent/agent-actions.js` | `src/core/effectors/agent-actions.js` |
| BUG-053 | `build-engine.js` | `skills/build-pack.js` |
| BUG-058 | `adapters/hermes-agent/` | deleted — see below |

### The BUG-058 case is the interesting one

*(That heading deliberately does not begin with the id: a heading whose first
token is `BUG-nnn` IS a declaration to `parseBugs`, so the first draft of this
section registered a second BUG-058, created a phantom collision, and left an
entry with no status. The same shape as this ticket's other self-inflicted catch
— prose about an id must not look like an id.)*

Its fix lived in the Hermes adapter, and **that adapter was deleted wholesale on
2026-08-22 when DeepSeek Harness replaced it**. The absent artifact is not
evidence the work never happened: `adapters/dsh-agent/index.js` carries the same
policy — `kind: 'timeout'` and `lastProbeDiagnostic` keep the adapter ONLINE on a
slow probe and record why, which is exactly what the ticket changed. **The
behaviour was ported with the engine swap.** Its status cites the successor.

### FIXED, deliberately not VERIFIED

Every recorded status says the same thing about its own limit: *source presence
proves the fix LANDED, not that it works.* That is the difference between the two
states in this register, and inflating 28 entries to `verified` on a grep would
have destroyed the distinction that makes `verified` worth anything.

### The citations are machine-readable because a citation nobody re-runs decays

Each status reads `Verified in source 2026-08-28 (BUG-391): \`SYM\` in \`FILE\``.
`test/bug-391-recorded-statuses-cite-live-evidence.test.js` re-runs every one:
the file exists, the artifact is still in it, and any named regression test
exists. **If somebody renames `titleSatisfiesQuery`, BUG-085's recorded status
becomes a false claim carrying generator authority — worse than the gap it
replaced**, and the suite now fails instead.

Two guards on the guard: it asserts it found ≥25 citations before checking any of
them, so it cannot pass by matching nothing; and it asserts **no citation points
at a test file as its source evidence**, because a fix confirmed by its own test
proves the test exists, not that the product changed — that was one of the three
oracles BUG-390 rejected.

### Scope

- **This closes the reading gap, not the verification gap.** 28 entries are now
  recorded as fixed on source evidence. None of them gained a live verification
  they did not already have.
- **BUG-253 is a triage record, not a defect.** Its status is that the triage was
  performed; the open items it lists are the incidents it dispositions, which
  carry their own entries.
- **BUG-272 records slices 1–4 plus 4b as fixed in code** and names no open slice,
  so it reads fixed. The barge-in work that followed it has its own tickets.

## BUG-390 — three deferred tickets were tracked as nothing, and one entry wore another entry's status (✅ FIXED 2026-08-28, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-28. 11 assertions, 10 mutations all caught, source
restored sha256-identical. **36 unrecorded → 28, and two false-positive classes
removed.** Continues BUG-389 by the same method: read what the entries still
marked `unrecorded` actually say.

### Two more stated statuses nothing was reading

- **`**OPEN. Deferred by design to merged-order step 8**` and `**OPEN,
  UNDIAGNOSED …**`** — BUG-266, BUG-267 and BUG-268. This is the one that
  matters: **an entry wrongly left unrecorded here is real work that nothing is
  tracking.** All three go on to describe the fix that *would* close them, and
  reading that description as the status is exactly how a deferred ticket
  vanishes — so an OPEN marker now outranks any later `**Fix.**` section.
- **Pointer-shape entries carry their status inline** as a bullet rather than a
  heading: `- BUG-345 - adblock silence caveat. FIXED 639200c:`. BUG-345, 349
  and 350 read this way.

### The more important half: two ways it read the WRONG entry's status

**BUG-273 was reading `verified` off a bullet nested inside it that was about
BUG-345.** Large audit entries list their follow-ups as `- BUG-nnn` bullets, so
the first one carrying the word FIXED became the parent's disposition. One
ticket's status assigned to another, failing toward closing things nobody fixed.
The bullet pattern is now built per entry and must name **that entry's own
number**.

**BUG-352 reads `**COUNTER FIXED 2026-08-27 (147 → 179, verified); the README
catalog table and pie are NOT yet generated**`** — and the qualifier is on the
bullet's *second* line. A line-by-line scan saw the FIXED and never reached it,
closing a half-done ticket on the half that landed. Bullet patterns are now
tested against the flattened entry, while the `**` markers stay line-anchored
because that anchoring is what stops a mid-paragraph sentence being read as a
status.

### 28 remain, and they are the correct answer

The last 28 (BUG-047…097, 230, 236, 253, 256, 272) state no status in any
convention. They are narrative: `**Symptom.** / **Root cause.** / **Fix.**`,
past tense, naming real code. **Three mechanical oracles were built to close
them and all three were rejected for producing false positives**, which is worth
recording so a fourth is not attempted blind:

1. *Any commit naming the bug* — 75 of 121 matched, but BUG-051's only commit is
   `docs(bugs): file BUG-051..BUG-058` (the commit that FILED it) and BUG-059's
   matches name other bugs in their subject.
2. *Any named artifact present in the tree* — 22 of 28 matched on tokens like
   `timeout`, `flush`, `persona` and `createServer`, words that appear
   everywhere. A guard passing vacuously.
3. *A distinctive artifact co-located in the named file* — better, and still
   wrong: BUG-049's `CHARACTER` matched `ps-automation.ps1` and BUG-093's
   `ALIASES` matched `triage-drift.js`, neither of which is the file the fix
   touched.

**These need a person reading each entry against the code.** Writing 28 statuses
from any of those oracles would be precisely the failure the register exists to
prevent, and would be worse than the gap because it would carry generator
authority.

One measured detail for whoever does it: **BUG-051, 052 and 058 name artifacts
that are genuinely absent (`HERMES_TEXT_BUILD_TIMEOUT_MS`), and that is not
evidence they were never fixed** — Hermes-Agent was deleted wholesale on
2026-08-22 when DeepSeek Harness replaced it. An absent artifact means the
subsystem moved, not that the work did not happen.

## BUG-389 — the ticket register called 133 entries "unrecorded" while 96 of them stated a status it never looked for (✅ FIXED 2026-08-28, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-28. 1 source file changed, 1 test file added (17
assertions), 10 mutations run and all 10 caught, source restored sha256-identical.
**133 unrecorded → 36, with zero entries that already had a status changing state.**

### The defect

`build-index.js` printed this on every run, and `index.html` published it:

```
build-index: 133 entries state no status a machine can read.
```

Its own header explained why: *"only about a quarter state a status in a form a
machine can read. The rest are a heading and prose."* **That sentence was measured
against the reader, not against `BUGS.md`, and it is false.** Of the 133:

| | count |
|---|---|
| opens with a **bold marker line** — `**FIXED.**`, `**Fixed** by \<sha\> | **88** |
| has an ordinary `**Status:**` line the regexes missed | **8** |
| genuinely states nothing | **36** |
| pointer-only stubs with no entry | **4** |

The bold marker line is simply the convention `BUGS.md` used **before**
`**Status:**` existed. Nothing ever looked for it. Three narrower faults sat
alongside it, all of the same shape — a reader that checks one place and reports
on all of them:

- **`**Status:**` required its marker to be adjacent to the colon.** BUG-011 reads
  `**Status:** Fix 2 (param aliasing) ✅ VERIFIED · Fix 1 ✅ LIVE-VERIFIED` — three
  separately verified fixes — and was read as no status at all.
- **`VERIFIED` was not in the fixed family.** Only `FIXED`/`RESOLVED` were, so an
  entry whose author wrote the stronger word scored lower than one who wrote the
  weaker one.
- **The `coded` and `diagnosed` checks read only the HEADING while `fixed` read
  the heading AND the status line.** BUG-020's `**Status:** 🔧 CODED` was invisible
  purely because of that asymmetry.

### Why the fix is reading and not guessing

The refusal-to-guess rule is untouched, and it is what keeps this safe: **an entry
that states nothing is still `unrecorded`**, and 36 of them still are.

Deriving a status from anything other than the author's own words was measured and
rejected. 75 of the no-status entries have a commit naming them — but **BUG-051's
only commit is `docs(bugs): file BUG-051..BUG-058`**, the commit that FILED it, and
**BUG-059's matches name other bugs in their subject** and mention 059 only in the
body. A commit-derived status would have closed bugs nobody had fixed. Tightening
to *fix-type commit, id in the subject, shipped on main* still leaves BUG-273,
which has exactly that and whose successor BUG-278 exists because the fix
*"shipped, passed its tests, and never ran"*. **Shipping is not fixing**, and no
amount of git archaeology turns one into the other.

### The dangerous half was the recovery's side effect

**Three entries that were already classified CORRECTLY flipped during
development**, and they are the reason this landed with a precedence rule rather
than a wider search:

| entry | its own status | what a body-wide marker scan did |
|---|---|---|
| BUG-037 | `**Status:** ⚠️ MITIGATED` | → open |
| BUG-038 | `**Status:** ✅ FIXED` | → open |
| BUG-367 | `**Status:** ✅ FIXED` | → open |

All three carry a later `**Not fixed in this pass:**` subsection — a scoped note
about **part** of the work, not the ticket's disposition. A fourth, BUG-001
(`✅ CLOSED via BUG-026's fix … live-verified working`), read as a *duplicate* the
moment the duplicate window was widened from 40 characters to 300, because the
word appears far later on the line.

**So: one status source per entry, chosen deterministically. An explicit
`**Status:**` line always wins; a bold marker line is consulted only when there is
no `**Status:**` at all.** The negative marker is matched against an explicit verb
list (`NOT done|fixed|attempted|started|implemented`) so that BUG-098's
`**NOT done, and not attempted:**` reads OPEN while BUG-049's `**Not
unit-testable.**` — which is not a status — stays unrecorded.

### Scope

- **`\bFIXED\b` appears somewhere in 100 of the 121 no-status entries**, including
  sentences about other tickets' fixes and about things that were explicitly not
  fixed. Every marker pattern is therefore anchored to the start of a line and to
  `**`. A free-text search would have closed bugs on the strength of a
  cross-reference.
- **36 entries remain unrecorded and that is the correct answer for them.** They
  need a human or a verification run, not a cleverer regex.
- The `OPEN WORK` register still outranks everything, including an entry's own
  `**FIXED**` marker. Pinned by a test.
- No new state was invented. `SUPERSEDED` maps to the existing `duplicate` (it
  points at another entry) and `MITIGATED` to `fixed`, rather than growing the
  register's shape for two rows.

## BUG-388 — the barge-in floor learned the OPERATOR'S voice and called it the room, and a verifier turned that into a verdict on the echo canceller (✅ FIXED 2026-08-28, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-28. Closure-campaign **Track E**, and the part of it
that never needed a microphone. 10 assertions, 10 mutations all caught.

**Track E was written up as "eight nodes needing a live microphone".** That
framing is what kept this closed: the whole voice cluster was treated as
unreachable from a session, so nobody read the number the cluster is reasoned
from. It is wrong, and it is wrong in a way that is provable from a log file and
a deterministic unit test.

### The defect

`barge-in-policy.js` keeps `bleedPeak`, documented as *"loudest level seen while
MYTHOS was provably speaking"*. It is learned inside the 500 ms **protected
window** that opens when the assistant starts talking, on this stated reasoning:

> the assistant's own onset is by construction the loudest thing present

That sentence was written as reasoning and never checked, and it is false. MYTHOS's
voice reaches the microphone through the speakers and is then attenuated 15–20 dB
by echo cancellation — measured independently by `scripts/probe-aec-routes.js`,
which puts the Gemini Live route's residual at 0.0069–0.0141. The operator's voice
arrives direct. **Whenever both are present the operator is by construction the
LOUDER one**, which is the exact opposite of the assumption. So in the ordinary
conversational case where the operator is still talking when MYTHOS begins its next
utterance, what the protected window learns is the operator.

### Why this is not hypothetical

Measured 2026-08-28 from `%APPDATA%/MYTHOS/mythos-server.log`: 731
`voice.capture-suspend` records across **20 sessions**, grouped into monotonic runs
of `bleedPeak` (a drop means a new process).

Of the **31 upward moves above 0.05, twenty-two set `bleedPeak` to a value exactly
equal to that hold's own `peakRms`** — the loudest microphone frame of the hold,
which is the operator. Every one of those holds also carries `flushedRaw > 0`, so
real operator audio was passing at the time.

The two populations separate cleanly:

| | measured |
|---|---|
| what every session OPENS at, before contamination | **0.0043 – 0.0347** |
| the acoustic probe's independent residual | **0.0069 – 0.0141** |
| what `bleedPeak` ratcheted to | **0.0532 – 0.3324** |
| the operator's own measured interruptions (BUG-274) | **0.0398 – 0.2717** |

The reported "bleed" sits in the operator band. The real bleed agrees with the probe.

**And `bleedPeak` is a running maximum that never decays and deliberately survives
`reset()`, so one contaminated frame poisons the entire process.** 2026-08-24
reported `0.1606` for **110 consecutive holds** off a single frame at 20:28:19. The
uncontaminated control is 2026-08-26: 11 holds, ended at **0.0313** — below the
0.035 floor — while the operator peaked at 0.1402 in the same session.

### The part that reopened it: this was diagnosed, deferred, and the deferral's premise was wrong

BUG-274 recorded it on 2026-08-19 under *"Two findings from this session recorded
and deliberately NOT fixed"*, reasoning that the learned floor is dormant
(BUG-273 A1) so **"Consequence today is nil"**. That premise does not hold, because
a consumer existed and nobody looked for it. `scripts/verify-voice-session.js` read
`bleedPeak`, called it **"the ungagged oracle"**, and printed:

> MYTHOS's own voice IS reaching the microphone, ABOVE the level used to detect the
> operator. **Echo cancellation is not removing it, whatever the constraint reports
> as granted**

That is a hardware verdict derived from the operator's own voice. It is the
conclusion behind the Stage 3 note that *"every threshold in this path is
compensation for echo cancellation not working at all"* and behind BUG-274 T4 being
carried in the plan as **"the only fix that removes the trade"**. An acoustic
rework was queued on a number that measured the wrong person.

The deferral even wrote down the right instruction — *"Do not re-enable the learned
floor on the strength of a `learnedFloor` figure without first checking whether the
operator was speaking during that hold's opening 500 ms"* — but it wrote it in
`BUGS.md`, where no gate can read it, and the verifier went on making the claim
anyway. A warning with nothing enforcing it is not a control.

### The fix

`barge-in-policy.js` now decides **once per utterance, at the transition out of
IDLE, whether the coming protected window may teach the floor anything at all**,
using the last level heard while MYTHOS was silent. If the operator was already
above the floor, no frame of that window is attributable and none is learned; the
refusal is counted (`bleedWindowsSkipped()`), because "learned nothing" and "the
room is quiet" are different facts and `bleedPeak` alone cannot tell them apart.

Compared against the static `INITIAL_BLEED_FLOOR` and **deliberately not against
`bleedFloor()`**: the learned value is the thing under suspicion, so using it would
let an already-poisoned peak raise the bar for calling the next window
contaminated — poison protecting itself, failing in the direction of growth. Pinned
by its own test.

`verify-voice-session.js` no longer converts the number into a verdict about the
hardware. It still prints the peak and the floor — deleting the claim must not
delete the data — and now says what would be required to attribute it.

### Scope, and what this does NOT fix

- **This does not change what MYTHOS does today.** The learned floor is dormant, so
  the floor in force stays `INITIAL_BLEED_FLOOR` either way. What changes is that
  the number the next session reads is now the room rather than the operator, and
  the dormant mechanism is no longer armed with a poisoned input for whoever
  re-enables it.
- **The `echoRatio >= 0.6` learning path is untouched**, deliberately: a transcript
  the echo filter matched to MYTHOS's own words is positive attribution, which is
  the one signal that separates the two on more than amplitude.
- **An operator who begins speaking INSIDE the 500 ms window is still learned
  from.** That is a strictly narrower hole than the one closed — the diagnosed and
  measured path is the operator already talking when the window opens — and closing
  it needs a per-frame source signal the client does not have.
- **`bleedPeak` remains an all-time maximum.** With attribution fixed the maximum is
  over attributable frames and is defensible, but it is still the least robust
  estimator available; a decaying or percentile statistic would survive a single
  bad frame better. Not changed here because five test files pin the current
  semantics and the poisoning source is what mattered.
- **`bleedWindowsSkipped` is not wired into the suspend log line.** `s2s-bridge.js`
  sits exactly on its file-size ratchet ceiling, and the fix does not need it:
  `bleedPeak` is now trustworthy by construction rather than needing a caveat field
  travelling beside it.
- **Nothing here needs a microphone, and nothing here closes a Track E node.** The
  eight voice nodes still need a live acoustic session. What this removes is a false
  reading that was steering that session's agenda.

### One existing test asserted the bug

`bug-272-verify-voice-session.test.js` required the verdict to say *"IS reaching the
microphone"* — from a fixture whose `bleedPeak` is **0.1193**, which is itself one
of the ratcheted values in the table above. The assertion encoded the false
inference, so it was corrected rather than worked around.

## BUG-387 — `doctor` reported the Google grant OK for three weeks while 88 calls failed on it (✅ LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-08-28)

**Status:** ✅ LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-08-28. Closure-campaign **Track A**. New
`scripts/verify-google-grant.js`, a corrected `doctor` row, 14 assertions,
9 mutations all caught.

**LIVE RUN, both halves, 2026-08-28 — and the fix caught a real dead grant.**
This ticket shipped its own oracle, so verification needed no voice session and no
operator: running the two commands IS the verification.

```
$ node scripts/verify-google-grant.js
verify-google-grant: INVALID
  The Google grant is dead: invalid_grant: Token has been expired or revoked. —
  this is NOT a network problem and will not recover on its own ... run
  `node scripts/google-auth.js` and put the new GOOGLE_REFRESH_TOKEN in
  mythos/.env. If this recurs roughly every 7 days, re-authorising alone will NOT
  fix it: an OAuth consent screen with external user type and publishing status
  "Testing" is issued refresh tokens that expire in 7 days. Publish the app
  first ... and only then re-authorise. Do not retry.

$ node scripts/doctor.js
  OK    Gmail / Calendar sensors    configured: GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID,
        GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, GOOGLE_REFRESH_TOKEN — present, but validity NOT
        checked here: run `node scripts/verify-google-grant.js`
```

That is exactly the two behaviours the ticket was written to produce. The checker
names the cause, distinguishes it from a network fault, and carries the 7-day
Testing-mode trap; and **`doctor` no longer converts presence into validity** —
the defect this entry is named for. **The operator's Google grant is dead right
now**, which is why Gmail has been failing, and re-authorising needs the consent
screen published FIRST or the new token expires the same way within 7 days.

**This does NOT close Track A's two nodes.** They need three operator minutes
and no session can supply them. What it removes is the reason those three
minutes kept not happening.

### The defect, measured live on this machine

```
$ node mythos/scripts/doctor.js
  OK    Gmail / Calendar sensors    configured: GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, GOOGLE_REFRESH_TOKEN
```

At that same moment, from the vault: **88 `invalid_grant` failures across 60
separate bursts between 2026-08-06 and 2026-08-26**, every one of them saying
the refresh token is expired or revoked. The single check an operator runs to
answer *"is my Gmail set up?"* was answering **yes** about the exact thing that
was broken.

**The class is an existence check standing in for a correlation check.**
`KEY_CHECKS` asks whether three strings are present in `.env`. Presence is not
validity, and for an OAuth refresh token the two come apart permanently and
silently: the string stays in the file forever after Google revokes it.

### What was NOT wrong, and it is most of the system

Measured before writing anything, because Track A is the one track in this
campaign whose description turned out to be exactly right, and it would have
been easy to invent work:

- `from-gmail.js` classifies `invalid_grant` as terminal and its remedy text
  names the literal command AND the 7-day "Testing publishing status" trap.
- `hub.js` latches the terminal result per tool and returns the stored remedy
  without touching the provider again. Verified from the vault: the 88 failures
  fall into **60 bursts, nearly all of size 1** — one attempt per process, not a
  retry storm.
- `gmail-sensor.js` raises `health.anomaly` with `needsOperator: true`.
- `explainer.js` short-circuits on `needsOperator` and **speaks the whole
  remedy**, verbatim, including `node scripts/google-auth.js`.
- Nine test files already cover that chain, two of them asserting the SPOKEN
  text contains `google-auth.js`.
- `google-auth.js`'s two historical Windows bugs (cmd.exe splitting the consent
  URL at `&`; `console.error` + `process.exit` eating Google's real error) are
  both already fixed.

**A correction I have to record, because I nearly filed a ticket on it.** From
the episodic `summary` field it looked as though MYTHOS had announced the fault
nine times over eight days and never once said what to do — one utterance even
reads *"I do not yet know the cause."* That was **wrong**: `summary` is
truncated at ~100 characters and `detail.text` carries the complete remedy. Only
the 2026-08-18 utterance is genuinely deficient, and it predates the BUG-273 C2
and BUG-278 fixes that repaired exactly it. **Reading a truncated log field and
accusing the product is the same mistake as a harness reporting a FAIL for its
own bad arguments** — the third time this campaign has produced it.

### The fix — a verifier, and a doctor row that stops overclaiming

`doctor.js` could not host the check itself, and the file says why: it is
forbidden from touching a key VALUE (AD-8, pinned by `setup-route.test.js`'s
canary), and `main()` is synchronous. Sending the refresh token to Google needs
the value. So the check lives in its own script and doctor points at it:

```
node mythos/scripts/verify-google-grant.js
  VALID         a fresh access token came back (never printed)
  INVALID       exit 1, and the remedy names the command
  UNCONFIGURED  exit 2, one or more of the three values absent
  UNREACHABLE   exit 3 — COULD NOT CHECK, which is not the same as broken
```

**It reuses `createGoogleAdapter().getProfile()` rather than re-implementing a
token refresh.** That path already carries the bounded `HTTP_TIMEOUT_MS` (an
`https.request` with no timeout waits forever against a host that accepts and
then stalls) and the B5 fix that keeps Google's `error_description` instead of
throwing away the actionable half. A second implementation would be a second
place for those to be got wrong. The remedy string comes from
`googleAuthFailureText` for the same reason: one door, both callers.

**UNREACHABLE is a distinct exit code on purpose.** A verifier that cannot
reach Google and says INVALID would send the operator through an OAuth consent
flow to fix their wifi. "Could not look" is not "there is nothing there" — the
most expensive repeated mistake in this repository.

The doctor row now reads `present — validity not checked here` and names the
verifier. Deliberately not a red row: the keys ARE configured, that check is
doing its job correctly, and a report that goes red for an expected reason is a
report people stop reading (the BUG-240 note in that same file).

### Scope

- **No secret is ever printed.** The verifier reports names and outcomes only,
  and a test plants a canary refresh token and asserts it appears in no line of
  output on any of the four paths.
- **Nothing calls the verifier automatically.** It is a command the operator
  runs, not another background poller — the system already announces this fault
  out loud and adding a second nag is not the missing piece.
- **doctor stays value-free and network-free.** The AD-8 invariant is untouched.
- The two Track A nodes stay as they are: `gmail_unread` red until the token is
  re-minted, `OCR hotkey` dark until somebody presses Ctrl+Alt+X.
