## BUG-376 — the capability-map gate blocked every commit from any checkout without the live vault (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27. 1 test rewritten, 1 added, mutation-proven.
Self-inflicted by BUG-370 the day before, and found by running the generator
on a machine that could actually reach the vault.

**Symptom.** `node scripts/build-capability-map.js --check` exited **1** from a
worktree with **zero real problems** — `mapping problems: 0`, `stale-vital
problems: 0`. The pre-commit hook runs that check, so it blocked every commit
from that checkout regardless of what the commit contained.

**Mechanism.** BUG-370 made the vault-derived `untriaged` vital preserve its
last reading when the live vault is unreachable, and stamp `stale: true` on it.
That is honest when the previous value was itself written by a vault-less
machine — which was true for the first day, so the committed island and every
local run agreed and nothing showed.

Then a machine WITH the vault wrote a fresh reading (`value: 0, stale: false`).
From that moment every other checkout wanted to add the flag back:

```
committed  : {"value":0,...,"measuredAt":"2026-08-27","stale":false}
would write : {"value":0,...,"measuredAt":"2026-08-27","stale":true,
               "staleReason":"the live vault is not reachable from this checkout"}
```

The value, the label and the stamp all matched. Only the annotation differed —
and the island comparison is a whole-object diff, so `--check` called it stale.

**The hole was in the seam between two of my own guards.** `checkVitals()`
deliberately exempts the vault vital, precisely so a gate cannot depend on
having the vault. But the separate `changed` comparison that decides "the
island is stale — run --write" does NOT use `checkVitals`; it diffs the
serialised island. One guard exempted the field and the other did not, so the
exemption was worth nothing. Both were written in the same change, an hour
apart.

**Fix.** `mythos/scripts/build-capability-map.js`. A machine that cannot
measure does not get to rewrite the field — not even to annotate it. The
preserved entry passes through **verbatim**. The value and its `measuredAt`
stamp are the honest signal on their own: the reader can see how old the
reading is without a flag, and no checkout can downgrade another checkout's
measurement. With nothing added, the diff has nothing to disagree about and
the whole class disappears rather than being special-cased.

**Attack pass (Stage 3):**

- *What else matches this?* Any future vault-derived vital would inherit the
  same rule by using the same branch. `checkVitals`'s exemption list is the
  one place that still needs updating by hand if one is added — noted rather
  than defended, since there is exactly one today.
- *Does this hide evidence?* It removes an annotation. The `measuredAt` date
  remains and is the stronger signal — a flag says "someone could not look",
  a date says how long ago someone could.
- *Who reads this?* The pre-commit hook on every commit, from every checkout.
  That is why a gate that can only pass on one desktop is worse than no gate.
- *Class:* this is the fourth member of the family recorded under BUG-373 —
  **a gate that measures a different artifact from the one it is judging.**
  Here the two artifacts were "the fields I said I would check" and "the bytes
  I actually diffed".
- *Deliberate non-change:* `--write` still refreshes the vital on a machine
  that CAN see the vault. Only the vault-less path is passive.

**Verification.**

```
before: build-capability-map --check -> exit 1 from a vault-less worktree
after : build-capability-map --check -> exit 0, "the map matches the code. OK."
node --test test/bug-370-capability-map-generated.test.js  20 tests, 20 pass, 0 fail
mutation: re-adding `stale: true` -> caught by both new assertions by name;
          script restored sha256-identical
```

## BUG-375 — a withheld phone tool blamed a missing handset when adb itself was unreachable (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27. 9 regression tests, 6 mutations, none survived.
Found by running the 2026-08-26 audit plan's **verification step 3**, which named
this rule specifically and had never been executed.

**Mechanism.** `tool-capability.js`'s phone rule gated on one boolean carrying two
facts:

```js
androidDevice = state === 'ONLINE' && Array.isArray(st.devices) && st.devices.length > 0;
```

so a false value meant *either* "adb is unreachable" *or* "adb is fine, no phone
plugged in" — and both produced the single reason string **"no Android device is
attached over adb"**. When the adapter is down, that sends the operator looking
for a handset for a problem no handset can fix.

Not hypothetical: BUG-374 measured `doctor.js` reporting `OK` for adb while
`ANDROID_ADB_BIN` pointed at a nonexistent path, which is exactly the state that
produces an OFFLINE adapter. The two bugs are the same defect in two reports, and
were found in the same hour.

**The audience makes it worse than a log line.** This reason is what
`live-tools.js` withholds a tool with, so it reaches the **model**, which relays
the remedy out loud. A wrong cause here becomes a wrong instruction spoken to the
operator.

**Fix.** `androidOnline` is now a separate snapshot fact, and the phone rule's
`reason` is a function of the snapshot rather than a constant — so the refusal
names the cause that was actually measured. `reason` may now be a string *or* a
function; the other four rules keep their strings, and the consumer resolves
either. Three things are pinned deliberately:

- **The two branches must produce DIFFERENT strings**, so a "fix" that appends
  the adb sentence to both branches fails.
- **Unknown is not offline.** A missing adapter, a `getStatus()` that throws, and
  an empty `state` all leave `androidOnline` true. Blaming adb on a failure to
  *ask* would put a wrong remedy in the model's mouth on the strength of an
  exception. Both the absent-adapter and the throwing-adapter paths are covered —
  they are different code paths, and a mutation proved it (below).
- **Every reason reaching a caller is a string**, checked across all five rules
  and both phone branches. The shape `reason: rule.reason` would have handed the
  model a function body.

**A mutation survived and it was a gap in the new test.** Setting
`androidOnline = false` inside the `catch` changed nothing, because the
"unreadable adapter" test passes `adapters: {}` — which skips the `try` body
entirely and never reaches the `catch`. A throwing `getStatus()` is a different
path, and it is now its own test. Second time in one session that an
absent-versus-throwing distinction hid an untested branch.

**What this does NOT fix.** `androidDevice` is still false for an unknown state,
so an unreadable-but-present adapter withholds the phone tools while reporting
the *device* reason. That is pre-existing, it is recorded by a test rather than
changed, and altering it inside a fix about wording would be a behaviour change
smuggled in under a message change.

**Files:** `mythos/src/core/voice/tool-capability.js`.
**Test:** `mythos/test/bug-375-phone-refusal-names-the-cause.test.js` (9 tests).

## BUG-374 — BUG-360's outage was still reproducible through the documented override, and the guard against it was a tautology (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27. 7 new tests, 2 existing ones repaired, 6
mutations, none survived. Found by running the 2026-08-26 audit plan's
**verification step 4**, which had never been executed.

**Symptom.** With `ANDROID_ADB_BIN` pointing at a path that does not exist,
`node scripts/doctor.js` printed:

```
  OK    Android platform-tools (adb)   <repo>/Android Platform Tools/platform-tools/adb.exe
```

while the runtime spawned the nonexistent path and android-child went OFFLINE
with all 14 `phone_*` tools withheld. That is BUG-360's outage, verbatim,
reachable after BUG-360 was closed — through the override the setup script itself
tells operators to set.

**Mechanism.** The runtime resolves adb in two rungs. The first is the explicit
override, taken **verbatim** — `adapters/android-child/index.js`:
`if (requested && requested !== DEFAULT_ADB_BIN) return requested`. The second is
`findInstalledAdb()`, which searches install locations and **never reads
`ANDROID_ADB_BIN` at all**. doctor's row asked only the second. Measured
2026-08-27:

| `ANDROID_ADB_BIN` | doctor asks `findInstalledAdb()` | runtime uses |
|---|---|---|
| unset | repo copy → **OK** | repo copy |
| `<nonexistent-dir>/adb.exe` | repo copy → **OK** | the bogus path → ENOENT → **OFFLINE** |

BUG-360's fix moved doctor from `resolveAdbPath()` (the write target) to
`findInstalledAdb()` (the fallback rung). Correct, and one rung short.

**THE GUARD WAS A TAUTOLOGY, which is why a closed bug stayed reproducible.**
`test/android-adb-resolution.test.js` asserted:

```js
assert.equal(row.ok, Boolean(setupAndroid.findInstalledAdb()), 'doctor and the
  runtime resolver must give the same verdict …');
```

while the row *was* `ok: Boolean(android.findInstalledAdb())`. The same
expression on both sides — it passes for every possible input, under a comment
claiming it pinned doctor and the adapter together. **Two resolvers cannot be
compared by asking one of them twice.** It now compares doctor's resolution
against the **adapter's**, for the input `src/main.js` actually passes, across
both the override and no-override cases.

**Fix.** doctor resolves through `resolveAdbBin(null, process.env)` — the same
order the runtime uses — then asks whether that resolution is *usable*, which is
a separate question that nothing was asking. `resolveAdbBin` returns an explicit
override without checking it exists (correctly: an override is an instruction,
not a guess), so doctor is the only place left to check.

Reachability is answered with the **filesystem, never a spawn** — a PATH scan for
the bare-command case, `statSync` for an absolute path. doctor's closing line
promises it reports what is *configured* and points at the `verify-*.js`
harnesses for real calls, and a report that executes adb would break that
contract. Pinned behaviourally: an existing but non-runnable file reports OK.

The hint also changes when the override is set, because BUG-360's hint is a
recorded example of one that loops forever: it said "run `setup-android.js
--install`", which re-downloaded into an already-populated directory and left the
override untouched. With the override wrong, `--install` cannot help, and the
hint now says so outright.

**A mutation survived, and it was a real gap in the new test.** Making
`whichOnPath()` always miss changed nothing, because the bare-`adb` branch is
**unreachable from the environment** on any machine with a repo-local adb — and
the first version of that test had an `if (row.detail.includes('platform-tools'))
return;` escape hatch, so it fired and asserted nothing. The branch is now driven
through exported `adbReachable`/`whichOnPath` seams with a controlled `PATH`,
the same remedy already applied to `wakewordModelsDir` and `localAdbPath`. A
guard with a conditional return reports the machine's state, not the code's.

**Also repaired: a source-shape window that failed for the wrong reason.** The
neighbouring guard matched `id:'adb'` plus at most 400 characters; this entry's
comment pushed the row past 400, so it failed claiming doctor.js no longer had an
adb row. Re-anchored to the next row rather than to a character budget. The
invariant it protects got stronger, so it was rewritten rather than deleted.

**What this does NOT fix.** The adapter keeps its own `resolveAdbBin`, a second
implementation of the same two rungs; it agrees with `setup-android.js`'s today
and is now pinned by test to keep agreeing, but it is still duplication rather
than one resolver. And reachability is a file question, not an execution one — an
adb that exists and cannot run still reports OK here, deliberately. Whether the
binary actually answers is `verify-*.js`'s job.

**Files:** `mythos/scripts/doctor.js` (658 → 739).
**Tests:** `mythos/test/bug-374-doctor-adb-override.test.js` (7),
`mythos/test/android-adb-resolution.test.js` (2 assertions repaired).

## BUG-373 — a bug number MENTIONED in a commit message counted as CLAIMING it, so one sentence blocked every commit from a checkout (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27. 10 new regression tests, mutations run, 0
survived. Second instance of one class — the first was markdown, fixed the
same day this one was filed.

**How it bit.** Two sessions were handed BUG-371 by `--next` within one
minute. Both answers were correct: the tool reads the refs and the working
tree at the instant it is asked, and neither entry existed yet. **The window
is between ASKING and WRITING**, not between committing and pushing, and no
amount of reading can close it — for most of that window the number exists
only in someone's intent. `--next` is an observation, not a lock.

The second session renumbered to 372. Its commit body still read
`...gemini,kokoro,edge,piper (BUG-371)`, so 371 was in-use-and-undeclared in
that tree, the ratchet went 136 → 137, and **every commit from that checkout
was blocked** — not only ones citing a number.

**The trap underneath.** `git commit --amend` runs the pre-commit hook while
`HEAD` is still the OLD commit. Proved in a throwaway repo rather than
reasoned:

```
hook echoes `git log HEAD -1 --format=%s`

git commit --amend -m "renamed: cites BUG-372"
  HOOK SEES HEAD SUBJECT: first: cites BUG-371      <- the OLD body

git reset --soft HEAD~1 ; git commit -m "replacement"
  HOOK SEES HEAD SUBJECT: renamed: cites BUG-372    <- HEAD already moved
```

So the amend that removes the citation is blocked by the citation it is
removing, with a message that already looks corrected. **A gate that reads
`HEAD` cannot be satisfied by rewriting `HEAD`.** The escape is
`git reset --soft HEAD~1` then a fresh commit.

**Class.** `isDoc` already exists in this script because a markdown file that
discusses BUG-999 is talking ABOUT the number, not claiming it — that fix
landed after a plan document explaining the BUG-999 fixture blocked a commit
whose only sin was explaining the gate. Commit messages are documentation too
and never got the same treatment. Same invariant, second instance, so the fix
goes at the class rather than the instance.

**The cost, measured rather than estimated — and the estimate was wrong.**
This change was argued against on the grounds that "~20 legacy bugs exist only
in commit messages, and the ratchet is the only thing pointing at them". That
claim was stated twice before anyone measured it. Measured:

```
undeclared in CODE         : 130
undeclared in COMMITS only :   6   -> 43, 44, 45, 132, 145, 318
of BUG-323..342 commit-only:   0
```

Six, not twenty, and **none** of the BUG-323..342 block the argument named —
every one of those appears in code as well. So the ratchet loses sight of six
numbers, and the new listing names all six, which is strictly more actionable
than the aggregate that hid them.

**Fix.** `mythos/scripts/lint-bug-registry.js`. The undeclared ratchet reads
code only. Commit messages keep counting toward the MAXIMUM — the same
asymmetry `isDoc` uses, because over-reporting the maximum can only make the
next free number larger, and that is the safe direction. New
`--undeclared-in-commits` names what the ratchet no longer counts, plus a
one-line mention in the normal report so the set cannot grow unnoticed.
`UNDECLARED_BASELINE` 136 → 130.

**The gate caught its own author, twice while building this.** First, adding the
test file put `BUG-373` in the source with no entry, so the ratchet read 131
against the new baseline of 130. Then, with that written, it read 131 again for
a different reason: the same test file cites the fixture number 999 to explain
that markdown was the FIRST instance of this class, and that number carries a
deliberately narrow adjudication listing exactly which files may mention it. A
`.js` file counts as code by design — BUG-164 and BUG-364 are real defects whose
only trace is a test file — so the adjudication went stale and 999 became live,
exactly as its comment promises a new file should make it. Widened to four files
with the reason recorded, rather than rewording the mention to slip past a
scanner that is correctly designed to see it.

**The older note, kept:** Adding the test file
put `BUG-373` in the source with no entry, so the ratchet read 131 against the
new baseline of 130 and blocked the commit. Fixed by writing this entry, which
is the intended remedy rather than a workaround.

**Attack pass (Stage 3):**

- *What else matches this?* Any prose channel the scan reads. Markdown and
  commit messages are both now excluded from the ratchet; the remaining inputs
  are code and config, which is where a number in use actually hides.
- *Does this hide evidence?* That was the risk, and it is why the listing
  exists. Nothing is dropped — six numbers moved from a count to a name.
- *Who reads this?* The pre-commit hook, and both sessions working this repo.
  The listing is never an exit code.
- *Is the constant correct?* The baseline is measured, not chosen: 130 is the
  code-only count on 2026-08-27, and a sibling test fails if it drifts more
  than 10 above reality so it cannot quietly stop biting.
- *Deliberate non-changes:* commit messages still feed the maximum. The
  cross-branch duplicate gap is NOT fixed — two branches can each hold a clean
  registry while their union is broken, which is exactly how both sessions
  were handed 371. It has never blocked anything and it was caught by two
  humans in under a minute; recorded, not built.

**Related, recorded, not fixed: the gate measures a different artifact from
the one being committed.** Three faces found the same day:

1. The hook validates the WORKTREE; git commits the INDEX. A stale `git add`
   from an interrupted attempt shipped a duplicate declaration past every
   check, with no concurrency involved.
2. The ratchet reads `HEAD`; `--amend` replaces `HEAD` (above).
3. Declarations are scanned in one tree; numbers are claimed across refs.

The practice that covers (1) is a PAIR and neither half suffices:
`git commit -- <pathspec>` so a stale index cannot ship, AND
`git status --porcelain` empty afterwards, because a file dirty on disk but
outside the pathspec is validated by the hook and never committed — the green
run then describes a tree absent from history. Both verified in throwaway
repos.

**Verification.**

```
node --test test/bug-373-commit-prose-is-not-allocation.test.js
  before fix: tests 10, pass 1, fail 9
  after fix:  tests 10, pass 10, fail 0
node scripts/lint-bug-registry.js --undeclared-in-commits
  6 numbers named: BUG-43, BUG-44, BUG-45, BUG-132, BUG-145, BUG-318
```

## BUG-371 — the commit gate named the failing FILE and threw away the failing ASSERTION, so a blocked commit taught nothing (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27. 8 new regression tests, 5 mutations, 0
survived. Verified end-to-end against the real TAP of the run that exposed it,
not only against the fixture.

**Found by two sessions on the same day, independently.** One had its commit
blocked and had to `sed` into raw TAP by line number to recover the numbers.
The other took a single unreproducible red in a 6460-test run and could
conclude nothing at all from it, because the assertion text was already gone by
the time it was printed.

**The gate had already learned this lesson once, and half-learned it.** It used
to print `tail -40` of raw TAP — the last few PASSING tests plus the summary —
so a blocked commit gave you a number and nothing else. Cause 3 of
`precommit-hook-environment.test.js` fixed that by grepping for `not ok`.

**The anchor was the bug.** Node's TAP nests subtests under their describe
block and INDENTS them, so `^not ok` matches only the top-level roll-up. On the
real failure that started this:

```
=== what the gate printed ===
not ok 1252 - lint-bug-registry — the numbers it reports

=== what was four levels down, indented, and discarded ===
    not ok 1 - next-free skips the fixture, and is not 1000
      error: |-
        the real maximum in use
        369 !== 367
```

The discarded half is the entire diagnosis. `369 !== 367` says *stale constant*
at a glance; without it the obvious next move is to go hunting for a bug in the
linter, which is the wrong file.

**Why no test caught it.** The cause-3 test asserts that the hook SOURCE
contains the string `not ok`. That is true of the broken anchor too, so it
passed throughout — a shape guard that cannot distinguish a working filter from
a broken one. The same vacuous-guard shape recorded elsewhere in this file.

**Fix.** `.githooks/pre-commit`. Both patterns anchored `^[[:space:]]*` rather
than `^`, and an `awk` that carries each failure's `error:` body with it,
bounded at 80 lines. The `-qE` guard that decides whether to report at all
carries the same anchor deliberately: if it ever disagrees with the filter, a
run whose only failures are nested reports "the suite died without a summary"
and falls back to `tail -40` — the exact output this block exists to replace.

Measured on the real TAP, before and after:

```
before: 1 line   — the describe-block name, which names the file and no more
after:  6 lines  — the nested assertion, its message, and 369 !== 367
```

**The test runs the hook, it does not restate it.** The pipeline is sliced from
between `REPORT-FILTER:START` / `REPORT-FILTER:END` sentinels in the hook and
executed with `out` supplied through the environment. A copy of the command in
the test would be a test of the copy.

**Two defects in the test, caught during its own development, both recorded in
the file because both generalise:**

1. The first extractor grepped for one line containing both `grep -E` and
   `not ok`. Fixing the defect made the pipeline three lines, the extractor
   silently matched nothing, and every assertion would have passed vacuously.
   Test 1 exists to watch for exactly that and caught it on the first run.
2. The first `runFilter` stripped the `printf ... |` prefix and fed the fixture
   on stdin. The strip silently failed to match, so every command ran against
   an empty `$out` and three assertions went red for a reason unrelated to the
   defect. Running the real line cannot half-work.

**Attack pass (Stage 3):**

- *Does this hide evidence?* That was the whole defect. The fix is entirely
  about surfacing evidence the gate was already holding.
- *What else matches this?* The `error:` body is now printed whenever it
  appears, independently of which `not ok` preceded it. Mutation P1 confirmed
  this: reverting the anchor drops the assertion lines but the numbers still
  print. Slightly odd output under a broken anchor, never silent — the correct
  trade for a diagnostic.
- *What is standing next to it?* The `-qE` guard, which would have drifted out
  of step. Asserted.
- *Is the output still bounded?* Yes — `head -80`, raised from 40 because each
  failure now costs several lines. An unbounded dump of a 6000-test suite is
  how this block came to print `tail -40` originally.
- *Deliberate non-change:* the else-branch `tail -40` fallback stays. A suite
  that dies without a summary emits no `not ok` at all, and an empty failure
  list there would be worse than the tail.

**Verification.**

```
node --test test/bug-371-hook-hides-nested-failures.test.js
  before fix: tests 6, pass 4, fail 2
  after fix:  tests 8, pass 8, fail 0
mutations: 5 applied, 5 caught, 0 survived; hook restored sha256-identical
end-to-end: the real suite369 TAP through the shipped filter, 1 line -> 6
```

**Not closed by this.** The unreproducible `verify-lib-attach` red that
prompted it is still unexplained: 22/22 in isolation, 36 concurrent runs by a
second session with zero failures, and four clean full suites. One occurrence,
no assertion text, nothing to work with. What this fixes is that the NEXT one
will carry its evidence.

## BUG-370 — the capability map was hand-typed, so the surface the closure campaign is measured against could not be wrong out loud (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27. 19 new regression tests, 10 mutations, 0
survived. Rendering verified in a real browser, not inferred from the source.

**Why this is filed as a defect and not just campaign work.** The map is the
acceptance surface: "everything green" means green on that map. It was 73
hand-typed nodes, and hand-typed numbers in this repository have gone stale
four separate times with a script eventually written to stop each one. This
was the last big one left.

**What was measured wrong, on 2026-08-27, before anything was changed.**

| claim on the map | reality |
|---|---|
| 6333 tests | 6436 at the time, 6441 now |
| 74 withheld from voice | 64 |
| a node named `Hermes engine` | Hermes-Agent was deleted in the W6 swap on 2026-08-22 |
| `open a file` — "no working path", status fail | `open_file` has existed in `from-computer.js` since 2026-08-21, with a sandbox guard and a read-back oracle |
| 179 registered | correct, and the only header number that was |

**And the one that mattered most.** The map named 144 of 179 registered
tools. Thirty-five had no node at all: every widget, persona, mission,
pipeline, kanban, OKF, installer, clipboard, security-scan, HUD-navigation,
artifact and local-info verb. A tool with no node cannot be shown broken,
working or dark — it is invisible, and on a map invisible reads as fine. The
campaign would have declared "everything green" over a fifth of the tool
surface it had never looked at.

**Also corrected: the campaign plan's own figures were wrong.** The plan
opens "44 capability nodes — 9 fail, 19 warn, 8 dark, ~18 ok". Measured, the
map held **73 nodes — 28 ok, 25 warn, 13 fail, 7 dark**. Every number in that
sentence was wrong, including the total. Corrected in the plan in the same
change.

**Fix.**

`MYTHOS-CAPABILITY-MAP.html` now carries a
`<script type="application/json" id="map-data">` island; the renderer reads
`CORE`/`CLUSTERS`/`NODES` out of it and the header renders every number from
it. No number in the header markup is typed by hand, and a test fails if one
reappears.

New `mythos/scripts/build-capability-map.js` (`--check` / `--write` /
`--json`), wired into the pre-commit hook. It reads only the repository — the
registered tool list, live-tools' allowlist, and the suite numbers
`sync-test-count.js` already committed to ROADMAP.md — so it costs about a
second, runs on a worktree and would run on CI. It deliberately does NOT
measure the suite itself: two generators measuring the same thing are two
numbers that can disagree.

The node-to-tool mapping is names only and is checked in **both** directions,
the shape that caught README drift in BUG-352: a tool named by a node but not
registered fails, and a registered tool named by no node fails. The second
direction is the one that would have caught `open_file` on the day it landed.

**A fifth status, `unknown`, distinct from `dark`.** The 18 newly-mapped
nodes are not dark. `dark` asserts a measured fact — a call count of zero was
read from the vault. Nothing has measured these, and colouring them dark
would launder "I did not look" into "there is nothing there". They render in
their own colour, labelled *not yet measured*.

**The vault is not always reachable, and the generator must not pretend.**
Per-tool call counts and the incident backlog live in the operator's live
vault. A worktree and a CI runner cannot see it — measured here,
`resolveVaultRoot()` falls back to the stale in-repo twin and reports **zero**
incidents. Writing that zero turns "I could not look" into "there is nothing
wrong", which is the most expensive mistake this repository keeps making. So
a vault-derived vital is preserved with its own stamp, flagged stale, and
rendered dim as `last read 2026-08-26`. It is never overwritten with a
confident zero, and it is exempt from `--check` — a gate that can only pass
on one desktop is a gate that gets switched off.

**Attack pass (Stage 3), recorded in the script's header and next to each
check:**

- *What else matches this?* A prose check ("the string Hermes must not
  appear") was considered and deliberately NOT added: it would fire on an
  honest historical note, and a gate that fires on correct content gets
  switched off. The structural check — the node's tools must exist — is what
  ships. The name was fixed by hand.
- *Does this hide evidence?* The stale-vault path is the danger, and it is
  handled above: preserved and flagged, never zeroed.
- *Who reads this?* The map is the campaign's acceptance surface and now the
  pre-commit hook. Rendering was verified in a browser — 91 nodes, five
  legend chips, the panel opening on an `unknown` node — because a green
  suite has never been able to tell this repository that a page renders.
- *What is standing next to it?* The first draft wrote the resolved vault
  path into `staleReason`, which would have committed the operator's
  directory layout into a tracked file. AD-7 violation, caught before commit;
  a test now asserts the map holds no absolute path.
- *Is this constant correct?* The suite figures are read from ROADMAP.md
  rather than re-measured, and a missing block throws instead of defaulting.
- *Deliberate non-changes:* the prose name check (above); per-node ok/fail
  counts stay curated, because only the live vault can refresh them.

**Verification.**

```
node --test test/bug-370-capability-map-generated.test.js   19 tests, 19 pass, 0 fail
node scripts/build-capability-map.js --check                exit 0
  91 nodes, 179 registered, 115 reachable by voice, 64 withheld
  (42 curated with a recorded reason, 22 danger-tier)
  ok 28 · warn 25 · fail 13 · dark 7 · unknown 18
mutations: 10 applied, 10 caught, 0 survived (7 in the script, 3 in the map data)
browser: header renders "generated 2026-08-27 / 179 registered / 115 reachable
  by voice / 91 nodes"; untriaged renders dim, "last read 2026-08-26"
```

**Not closed by this.** No map node turned green. This change makes the
instrument honest; it does not fix a single capability. The 13 fail and 7
dark nodes are still fail and dark, and there are now 18 more that nobody has
measured at all.

## BUG-369 — a `tolerant` sync slot was skipped by `--write` as well as `--check`, so the README tests badge froze 297 behind (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27. 5 new regression tests, 5 mutations, 0 survived.
Not live-verified and does not need to be: the defect is entirely inside a
documentation generator, and both modes are exercised deterministically
in-suite against a temp file.

**Symptom.** `README.md` disagreed with itself. Every strict slot read 6436;
the shields.io tests badge — the first number a visitor sees — read
`tests-6139%20pass`. Measured 2026-08-27 while building the capability-map
generator, which was about to consume those numbers as truth.

**Mechanism.** The badge slot carries `tolerant: true`, and that tolerance is
correct: it guards the PASS count, and pass legitimately varies BY MACHINE.
Fixture-gated tests `t.skip()` honestly on a fresh clone or a CI runner and
run as passes on a provisioned one, so strict equality made `--check`
unsatisfiable on the operator's machine and CI at the same time (that is the
defect the tolerance was added to fix, 2026-08-16, and it stays fixed).

But `applySlots` implemented "do not FAIL on a mismatch" as "do not LOOK at
this slot at all":

```js
if (slot.tolerant) {
  byFile.set(slot.file, content);   // <- unmodified content
  continue;                         // <- returns BEFORE the write path
}
```

The branch sat above the code that computes staleness and above the code that
writes, so no `--write` had moved that badge since the tolerance landed, and
nothing could ever move it again. The number was not merely stale; it was
structurally unable to catch up.

**Class.** Same shape as the delivery-vs-correctness guards tabulated in the
closure campaign: a check weakened to stop a false failure stopped doing its
job entirely. The remedy is the same one — narrow the weakening to exactly the
question that was wrong (should this FAIL?) and leave the rest of the
mechanism intact (should this be RECORDED?).

**Fix.** `mythos/scripts/sync-test-count.js`. Staleness is computed before the
tolerant branch; tolerance now suppresses only `staleCount++` and the stale
report. `--write` updates the slot and announces it as
`tolerant slot 6139 -> 6436 (written; not counted stale)` — a generator that
rewrites a tracked file silently is how a wrong number becomes an unnoticed
one. `--check` behaviour is unchanged, and a test locks that.

`applySlots`/`readmeSlots` are now exported and `applySlots` takes an
injectable slot list, so both branches can be driven against a temp README
instead of the repo's own.

**Attack pass (Stage 3), recorded in the test file's header comment:**

- *What else matches this?* One slot is tolerant, and a test asserts that. A
  second one appearing later must be a deliberate decision, not an inherited
  ruling — mutation M4 marks another slot tolerant and that test fails.
- *Does this hide evidence?* It did: the write was silent-by-omission. It now
  prints what it changed and from what.
- *Who reads this?* The badge is the README's most-read number and CI's
  `--check` reads the same slot table. Both paths are covered.
- *What is standing next to it?* All slots for one file share a `byFile`
  accumulator; the old branch seeded it with unmodified content. Mutation M5
  writes the tolerant edit straight to disk instead, and the strict slot then
  clobbers it — caught.
- *Deliberate non-change:* the tolerance itself. `--check` must not fail on a
  machine whose honest skips lower the pass count. Locked by test 2.

**Verification.**

```
node --test test/bug-369-tolerant-slot-never-written.test.js
  before fix: tests 5, pass 3, fail 2
  after fix:  tests 5, pass 5, fail 0
mutations: 5 applied, 5 caught by their intended test, 0 survived
```

## BUG-367 — `attachMythos` had two failure messages for one contract, so a test asserting the hint passed or failed on a race (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27, mutation-proven)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27. 1 new regression test, 1 mutation run. Not
live-verified and does not need to be: the defect is entirely in the wording of
a rejection, and both paths are exercised deterministically in-suite.

**Symptom, as it presented:** `test/verify-lib-attach.test.js` failed the
pre-commit hook with `fails = 1` while passing 21/21 in isolation and passing
in full runs minutes either side. It read exactly like flakiness, and it cost
two sessions a blocked commit — `not ok 607` in one tree and `not ok 609` in
another, hours apart. The index differs because the trees have different test
counts; the file is the same file.

**Why "flaky" was the wrong verdict.** This repo's `CLAUDE.md` documents
wandering Windows failures as fork exhaustion from concurrent node processes,
and that was the first hypothesis. It is wrong here, and the diagnostic
property is what rules it out: **fork exhaustion wanders, and this landed on
the same file twice for two independent sessions**, once with zero orphan
`node.exe` on the machine. A failure that keeps choosing the same file is not a
random casualty.

**Mechanism.** `attachMythos()` (`scripts/verify-lib.js`) rejects down two
paths, and they did not say the same thing:

    req.on('error')    →  "attach failed: <msg>. Is MYTHOS running on port N?"
    req.on('timeout')  →  "attach failed: /health timed out after Nms on port N"

The test asserted `/Is MYTHOS running on port 1\?/` against port 1 — privileged
and unbound, so normally an instant `ECONNREFUSED` down the *error* path. Under
full-suite load the connect attempt instead reaches the 2000ms deadline and
takes the *timeout* path, whose message never carried the hint. The test was
racing two of its own subject's failure modes and only one of them satisfied it.

**Fix, and why it is in the source rather than the test.** Loosening the
assertion to accept either wording would have made the test pass while leaving
two contracts in place. The hint is as true of a hang as of a refusal, and it is
the sentence that tells a harness user what to do, so the timeout path now
carries it too. One contract, no race, and the original assertion stays strict.

**Regression test:** a second case in the same file drives the timeout path
deterministically — a server that accepts the connection and never answers
*cannot* take the error path — and asserts both that it still says it timed out
and that it names the port with the hint. Mutation: removing the appended hint
fails it with "the timeout path must carry the same hint as the refused path";
restore verified by sha256, not by `git checkout --`.

**Verified:** `node --test test/verify-lib-attach.test.js` → 22 pass, 0 fail
(21 before). Nothing else reads the timeout string —
`grep -rn "health timed out"` finds only the definition and this fix's own
comment — and the change is additive, so a matcher on `/timed out/` still holds.

**Not fixed by this, deliberately:** the underlying scheduling sensitivity is
untouched. A connect to an unbound port can still lose the race to a short
deadline; that is a property of the machine under load, not a defect, and the
fix makes the outcome identical either way instead of pretending the race is
gone.

## BUG-372 — `doctor.js` read the kokoro VOICE ID and called it a model, so a dead TTS rung reported "No gaps" (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27 — the REPORT half. Whether kokoro should be
installed or dropped from the default chain is an operator decision and is
untouched. 6 regression tests, 6 mutations, none survived.

**NUMBERING NOTE, because the audit plan is misleading here.** The 2026-08-26
plan files this defect under "BUG-240 — the kokoro TTS rung is dead". BUG-240 is
already taken by a different, **fixed** defect: `@huggingface/transformers`
being unreachable from `app.asar` through ESM `import()`, closed 2026-08-15.
Same engine, different mechanism, different file, different fix. Reusing 240
would have created a third real collision in BUGS.md, so this took a new number (372 — see the collision note below).
Anyone reading the plan's BUG-240 reference should read this entry instead.

**And it is 372, not 371, by 42 seconds — `--next` IS NOT A LOCK.** A concurrent
session took the number 371 for an unrelated defect (the pre-commit hook naming a
failing test file and discarding its assertion text), committing at 13:09:56;
this work landed at 13:10:38. `lint-bug-registry.js --next` had answered **371 to
both of us, and it was right both times**. Earlier commit wins, so this renumbered.

**THE WINDOW IS BETWEEN ASKING AND WRITING**, which is narrower than it first
looks and rules out the obvious fixes. It is not a fetch problem: for most of the
window the number existed only in the other session's intent, on no ref anywhere.
And it is not a reading-uncommitted-work problem — `--next` ALREADY reads
uncommitted working-tree headings. Measured both directions 2026-08-27: appending
an uncommitted `## BUG-390` heading moved `--next` from 373 to 391, and removing it
moved it back. An entry claiming that as the gap would send the next person to
build something that already exists, which is why it is recorded here as measured
rather than as reasoned.

**The real gap is that the gate's duplicate check has never been cross-branch.**
It compares declarations within ONE working tree, so two branches can each hold a
perfectly clean registry while their union is broken — which is exactly what
happened, and why nothing failed until a human noticed. The gate did not
malfunction; its scope simply stopped at the tree, and nothing said so. Verified
feasible by the other session: `git show <ref>:BUGS.md` across every local
and remote ref, parsing `^## BUG-(\d+)`, resolves today and correctly reports that
this branch declares 368 while another tree does not; four refs carry no BUGS.md
and need a try/catch. Not built here — it is that script's owner's call, and a new
gate feature is a scope change rather than a loose end.

Renumbered by AMENDING rather than by a follow-up commit, deliberately: the linter
counts numbers cited in commit MESSAGES as in use, so a follow-up would have left
371 permanently claimed by two unrelated defects — which is precisely what BUG-280
and BUG-360 already are, and what the paragraph above claims this entry avoided.

**Symptom.** `node scripts/doctor.js` ended with *"No gaps. Every tracked key,
model and binary is present."* on a machine where `mythos/models/` contains only
`piper` and `whisper`, while `VOICE_TTS_CHAIN` was
`gemini,kokoro,edge,piper`.

**Mechanism.** The voice section printed the kokoro **voice id** (`af_heart`) and
nothing ever asked about the kokoro **model**. A voice id is a string in `.env`:
it is present whether or not any weights exist, so it can never be a gap.
Reading it as evidence of an installed engine is the same half-truth that made
this report print `OK  Android platform-tools (adb)` and "No gaps" through the
whole of BUG-360 while all 14 `phone_*` tools were dead.

**THE COST IS NOT ZERO, and the plan got this wrong.** The plan says "Rung 2
resolves unavailable on every fallback", which reads as free. It is not.
`isAvailable()` calls `KokoroTTS.from_pretrained()`, so **the probe IS the
download**: on a cold machine the first fallback to rung 2 races an ~80MB+
HuggingFace fetch against `LOAD_TIMEOUT_MS` (15s) before falling through to
edge. Measured 2026-08-27 against a deliberately bogus model id, so nothing
large was fetched: the probe took **4,066ms** to fail — a live network
round-trip — and the result is sticky for the process (second call 0ms). So a
missing kokoro model costs up to 15s of silence on the first fallback of each
process, once, and is free thereafter.

Also measured, and it removes the plan's assumed cause: `kokoro-js` and
`@huggingface/transformers` **are** installed and declared in `package.json`.
The rung is not dead for want of a dependency. `models/kokoro` is a download
cache, not a shipped asset.

**Fix.** A `kokoro` row in `assetChecks()` that is a gap only when kokoro is
actually in the chain — a machine that has dropped the rung has nothing wrong
with it, and a report that is red for an expected reason is a report people stop
reading. Three things about it are deliberate:

- **It asks the provider where to look.** `providers/kokoro-tts.js` now exports
  `modelCacheDir(env)`, the one place that decision is made, and doctor calls
  it. Recomputing the path in doctor would be BUG-360 with a different noun:
  green about a directory nothing loads from. Pinned by test — the mutation that
  hardcodes the path in doctor is caught by name.
- **It searches for weights, not for a directory.** `@huggingface/transformers`
  writes to `<cacheDir>/models--<org>--<repo>/…`, so a top-level listing misses a
  complete model, and a bare `existsSync()` goes green on an **aborted** download
  — precisely the state a 15s probe timeout leaves behind. Both directions are
  pinned.
- **It does NOT route through `src/core/setup/model-paths.js`**, though that is
  the shared model resolver and wakeword/`piper-child` use it. It searches extra
  roots, so adopting it would change which weights the provider LOADS — a
  behaviour change to a live voice path, which is a different decision from
  making the report honest. Recorded as a choice rather than left as an oversight.

The hint names two remedies that both work (drop the rung, or let the first
fallback populate the cache) and names no script. BUG-360's hint pointed at an
`--install` that unpacked into an already-populated directory while the runtime
resolved elsewhere, so following it looped forever; a test now fails if this hint
names a `scripts/*.js` that does not exist.

**What this does NOT fix.** kokoro still resolves unavailable on this machine,
and the first fallback still pays for it. `doctor.js` reports that honestly now;
it does not change it. The wider question the plan raised — every capability
doctor reports resolving through the same helper the runtime consumer uses — is
enforced here for kokoro and for adb, and is **not** enforced globally.

**Files:** `mythos/scripts/doctor.js` (575 → 658),
`mythos/providers/kokoro-tts.js` (114 → 137).
**Test:** `mythos/test/bug-372-doctor-kokoro-model.test.js` (6 tests).

## BUG-368 — `index_project` indexed a Python virtualenv instead of MYTHOS, and reported success (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27. Shares BUG-362's root cause and its test file; 13 tests, 10 mutations, none survived.

Found while fixing BUG-362, by checking the sibling tool before inventing a
skip-list policy — the house-convention question turned out to be the bug.

**Measured on the MAIN CHECKOUT** (the location matters — see the worktree note
in BUG-362), walking `mythos/`:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| files indexed | 2,000 (cap hit) | 1,381 (complete) |
| `truncated` | true | **false** |
| from `.venv` | **1,879 (94%)** | 0 |
| from `src/` | **0** | 202 |
| from `test/` | **0** | 660 |
| `from-pc.js` indexed | **no** | yes |

So `search_code` over this project was searching a Python virtualenv and had
indexed **none** of MYTHOS's own source. It reported `ok: true` throughout.

**Mechanism.** `from-code-search.js` had a `SKIP_DIRS` list and `search_files`
had none — two sibling file walkers, two sets of rules, neither aware of the
other. `.venv` was on neither. `from-code-search`'s budget is 2,000 **matched
files** and `mythos/.venv/Lib/site-packages` is full of `.py`, which `CODE_EXT`
accepts, so the virtualenv filled the budget before the walk reached `src/`.

**Fix.** The list moved to `src/core/effectors/file-walk.js` and both walkers
share it; `.venv`, `venv` and `__pycache__` were added. `env` was deliberately
NOT added — unlike the others it is a plausible name for a real source
directory, and a skip-list that swallows project content fails in the direction
nobody checks.

**Correction to my own first measurement.** I initially reported "8 files from
`src/`". That was wrong: the counter tested for `\src\` while relative paths
*begin* with `src\`, so the 8 were `.venv` paths containing a `src` component.
The true before-figure is **zero**.

**What this does NOT fix.** `index_project` still reports success on a
2,000-file truncation without saying what it dropped — it asks "did indexing
complete", never "did it index the right thing". That is the same
delivery-versus-correctness shape as BUG-362 and is not addressed here.

## BUG-362 — `search_files` spent its whole scan budget inside dependency trees and reported "found nothing" instead of "gave up" (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27. 13 regression tests, 10 mutations, none survived.

**THE REMEDY THIS TICKET PROPOSED DOES NOT WORK**, which is the most useful
thing in this entry. The original diagnosis suggested skipping
`node_modules`/`.git` "the way any file search is expected to". Measured against
the real effector on the main checkout:

| pattern | depth-first (before) | + skip node_modules/.git | breadth-first |
|---|---|---|---|
| `package.json` | 0 | **0** | 50 |
| `ROADMAP.md` | 0 | **0** | 1 |
| `from-pc.js` | 0 | **0** | 1 |
| `doctor.js` | 0 | **0** | 1 |
| `lanes.default.js` | 0 | **0** | 1 |

The skip-list changes nothing, because `.venv` is 5,202 entries within depth 6
and exhausts the 5,000-entry budget on its own, before `node_modules` is
reached. The ticket also understated the blast radius: it reported
`package.json`, but **every** file in the project returned zero.

**BREADTH-FIRST IS THE CORRECTNESS MECHANISM; THE SKIP-LIST IS AN
OPTIMISATION.** Confusing the two is how this comes back. Breadth-first tests
every entry at the current depth before ANY recursion, so a shallow match cannot
be starved by a deep sibling whatever that sibling is called — a property, not a
list anyone has to keep current. The skip-list only improves result *quality*
(`package.json` goes from 50 dependency hits to 1). Both are stated as such in
`file-walk.js`, so nobody adds a directory believing it fixes a starvation bug.

**Honest truncation.** `entries: [], truncated: true, ok: true` said nothing was
found AND that the search stopped early, and was indistinguishable from an
honest miss. A walk that gave up having found nothing now returns `ok: false`
naming the budget and the recovery. An honest miss still returns `ok: true`
with `truncated: false`, and the two are pinned apart by test. This is the same
remedy shape as BUG-365's `authoritative:false`: you cannot strengthen a
delivery check into a correctness check — carry the uncertainty where the caller
can see it.

**NONE OF THIS REPRODUCES IN A GIT WORKTREE, and a fix verified there is not
verified.** `setup-worktree.js` links `.venv` as a junction, and a Dirent for a
junction reports `isDirectory() === false` — so a worktree charges ONE entry for
it and never recurses. The budget survives, both bugs vanish, and a fix passes
for a reason unrelated to the fix. Every figure above is main-checkout, and the
regression tests build their own fixture tree rather than walking this repo, so
they cannot inherit the answer from whichever checkout runs them.

**A sandbox question asked and answered NO.** `from-code-search.js` skips
symlinks explicitly and `search_files` never did, so the obvious worry was a
junction planted inside an allowed root walking out of it. Probed with a real
junction: **contained**, before the fix as well as after. The reason is
incidental — a Dirent reports `isDirectory() === false` for a junction, so it is
never descended into. Nothing said "do not follow links"; it merely happened.
Changing `entry.isDirectory()` to `statSync(full).isDirectory()` reads like a
robustness improvement and would open a real escape, so the containment is now
pinned by a junction test and a comment instead of resting on an accident.

**A mutation "survived" and it was the harness, not the tests.** The first
attempt to mutate breadth-first back to depth-first swapped `next.push` for
`frontier.push` — which on an index-walked array is still a queue, so it
preserved breadth-first order and proved nothing. Re-run as a true immediate
recursion, it is caught by three tests. A SURVIVED result is a claim about your
harness before it is a claim about your tests.

**What this does NOT fix.** A search whose *matches* legitimately exceed 50 is
still truncated with `ok: true`; shallowest-first ordering makes that far more
useful than it was, but it is a cap, not an answer. And `search_files` still
cannot report WHICH subtree it gave up in, only that it did.

**Files:** `mythos/src/core/effectors/file-walk.js` (new),
`from-computer.js` (997 → 992), `from-code-search.js`.
**Test:** `mythos/test/bug-362-search-files-starved-by-deps.test.js` (13 tests).

## BUG-353 — the implicit ui_type/ui_click target was process-wide and never expired, so an app MYTHOS opened for its own reasons silently became the thing you dictated into (✅ FIXED 2026-08-27)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27. 17 regression tests, 17 mutations run, none survived.

**The ticket called this hypothetical. It was not.** `from-pc.js`'s own comment
described the scope limit and then guessed at a future trigger — *"a concurrent
internal `launch_app` (e.g. from-spotify.js's own auto-launch path, **if** it
ever routes through this same function)"*. It already routed through it.
`from-whatsapp.js` calls `launch_app` at three sites and `from-spotify.js` at
two, all to resolve a window they then drive by **explicit** pid. Neither module
has ever read the implicit target. They were writing to a slot only the operator
reads.

**Measured 2026-08-27** by driving the real effector with a stubbed pc-child:

```
launch_app('notepad')            -> implicit target 1111   (the operator)
launch_app('whatsapp')           -> implicit target 2222   (from-whatsapp,
                                    resolving its OWN window internally)
ui_type('dear diary')   no pid   -> typed into 2222, ok:true
```

**Why no honesty guard caught it, which is the part worth keeping.** `ui_type`
has a target cross-check: pc-child reports `typedIntoPid`, and `ui_type`
compares it to the pid it targeted. Those agreed — 2222 and 2222. **A check on
the delivered target cannot see a target that was swapped before it ran.** The
call was honest about everything except which window the operator meant.

**The second defect in the same variable: it never expired.** A pid recorded an
hour ago was still the default for the next pid-omitted call. `close_window`'s
own comment already made the argument — *"Windows recycles PIDs, so a stale
value could target an unrelated process"* — and then applied it only to closes.
A process that dies without `close_window` (crash, the operator clicks X, Task
Manager) leaves its pid behind to be recycled by something else.

**THE SCOPING KEY THE PLAN ASKED FOR DOES NOT EXIST, and building it would have
been inert.** The repair plan says *"bind it per conversation/goal with a TTL"*.
`ctx.goalId` is the only such key, and `live-tool-adapter.js:833` dispatches
every Live-voice tool call as `dispatchAction(decision, { tier, channel,
traceId })` — **no goalId at all.** On the voice path, the path that actually
says "open notepad and type this", the key would have been `null` on both sides
and matched everything. `traceId` is worse: it is per tool CALL, so `launch_app`
and the `ui_type` after it carry different ones and would never match. A
mechanism that cannot see the traffic it exists to separate is not a guard.

**THE TICKET HAD FOUR CLAUSES AND THE FOURTH HAD NO IMPLEMENTATION.** Read back
literally, BUG-353 asked for: (1) stop it being a process-wide default, (2) stop
any intervening launch retargeting typing, (3) bind per conversation/goal with a
TTL, (4) **"clear on launch"**. The first pass of this fix did 1, 2 and the TTL
half of 3, and silently skipped 4 — it only surfaced on a deliberate re-read of
the ticket text as a checklist.

Clause 4 is the one that produces a wrong-window **WRITE** rather than a stale
default. A launch ATTEMPT moves the operator intent, so the previous target stops
being what they mean whether or not the launch succeeds. Without it: Notepad is
open, the operator says "open Spotify", the launch FAILS, they dictate — and the
text went into Notepad, confidently. `launch_app` now clears the target before
delegating (INTERNAL callers exempt), so a failed launch leaves NO target and
`ui_type` falls through to its focused-window branch, which carries its own
`typedIntoTitle` cross-check. No target beats a stale one.

**So the split is made where the knowledge is.** New module
`src/core/effectors/implicit-target.js` (110 lines) owns the record, the TTL and
the expiry. The five internal call sites pass `implicitTarget.INTERNAL`, which
declares "I am resolving this window for myself and will address it by explicit
pid." Everything else — including any future caller that forgets — is bounded by
the TTL.

**TTL = 120s, and the number is argued rather than picked.** The implicit target
exists to bridge one flow: `launch_app`, then the `ui_type`/`ui_click` that acts
on what was launched. That is seconds of machine time, but the human confirm step
sits inside it (`ui_type`'s own FIX E comment records OS focus drifting during
that round trip) and `launch_app` itself polls up to 6–8s for a windowed
process. Two minutes clears a slow confirm and still expires long before a pid
can plausibly be recycled.

**Expiry is evaluated on READ, not on a timer.** A timer would have to be
`unref()`'d not to hold the process open, and an unref'd timer that never fires
is exactly how the capabilities manifest stayed wrong in BUG-366. Nothing here
needs to happen at a moment in time; it only needs to be true when asked.

**A latent bug fell out on the way.** The wrong-app branch of `launch_app`
(asked for X, a process named Y came up) cleared the target **unconditionally**.
An INTERNAL launch that resolved to the wrong app would therefore have wiped the
operator's still-valid target. It now clears only its own pid, and both halves
are pinned: a non-internal mismatch must still clear, because it set it.

**One line that looks like a hack and is not.** `from-pc.js` calls
`implicitTarget.forget()` at module load. In production that runs once at boot,
where nothing is launched to point at. It is there because the state used to be
declared *in* `from-pc.js`, so the ~20 test files that reset it by dropping
from-pc from the require cache would otherwise inherit a target from whichever
test ran before them. Making "a fresh module instance owns no target" explicit is
better than depending on where a variable happens to be declared.

**TWO MUTATIONS SURVIVED THE FIRST PASS AND BOTH WERE REAL GAPS**, not noise.
Deleting `remember()`'s pid validation changed nothing (no test asserted the
module's own contract), and deleting the module-load reset changed nothing *in
this file* — it is guarded only in the ~20 other test files that reload from-pc,
so a reader of this file would have seen an unexplained `forget()` at module scope
and deleted it. Both are now pinned locally.

Writing the first of those assertions immediately found a defect in the guard this
same change introduced: `remember(1.5)` was **accepted**, because
`typeof number && Number.isFinite && > 0` passes fractions. Now
`Number.isInteger(pid) && pid > 0`, which is both simpler and correct. Review had
not caught it; the boring loop over bad inputs did. `coercePid` in from-pc.js
shares the same fraction laxness and was deliberately left alone — it is a
caller's one-shot argument, whereas a value stored here outlives its call and is
aimed at a window later. That difference is now stated in code rather than
accidental.

**Two things were REMOVED before shipping rather than defended.** `describe()` and
the record's `name` field had a writer and no reader — nothing reads it, so delete
it rather than keep new-module surface that becomes load-bearing by accident. And
a `coercePid(r.pid)` added at the `remember` call site was reverted once
`launch_app`'s `byProcess` check (:238) was read properly: it already requires
`typeof r.pid === 'number'`, so coercing there defended a state that cannot reach
it and told the next reader a string could arrive when it cannot.

**A deliberate divergence is now pinned:** `send_key` does NOT default to the
implicit target, because with a pid `ps-automation.ps1` refuses the key when the
caret belongs to another app, which would break "press escape" aimed at whatever
the operator is looking at. That was documented in a comment and is now locked by
a test, so the next reader cannot "fix" the inconsistency with `ui_type`.

**What this does NOT fix.** A caller that omits `INTERNAL` still contaminates the
target for up to the TTL — proven deliberately as the negative control, so the
limit is measured rather than assumed. Closing it properly needs a real
per-conversation key threaded through `live-tool-adapter`, which is its own
ticket. Nothing here makes an autonomous engagement's launch distinguishable
from the operator's; the TTL is the only bound on that too.

**Files:** `mythos/src/core/effectors/implicit-target.js` (new),
`from-pc.js` (eleven sites rewired, 1552 → 1549 lines), `from-whatsapp.js`,
`from-spotify.js` (both opt their launches out).
**Test:** `mythos/test/bug-353-implicit-target-scope.test.js` (17 tests).

## BUG-365 — web search had exactly ONE working provider, so spending its free quota was a cliff onto confident wrong answers (✅ FIXED 2026-08-26, live-verified)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-26. Live-verified end to end; 18 regression tests, 12 mutations run.

**Measured 2026-08-26.** Of the chain's rungs, precisely one returned usable
results — `exa-mcp`, on a keyless free tier the vendor documents at 150
calls/day. Both DuckDuckGo rungs answered an anti-bot challenge, `jina` 401'd,
the local open-webSearch daemon returned 0 results from every engine it has, and
Wikipedia answered irrelevant articles that the chain shipped as `ok:true`.

So the operator's real ceiling was ~150 searches a day across everything MYTHOS
does — spoken questions, the build engine's research gate, autonomous goals — and
exhausting it did not degrade search, it **ended** it, in the worst available
way: by substituting plausible wrong answers for an honest failure.

**The fix adds a second keyless rung**, You.com MCP
(`https://api.you.com/mcp?profile=free`, `you-search` tool), on a quota entirely
independent of Exa's. No key, no signup, no card, nothing in `.env`. Measured on
this machine: 7 of 7 queries answered HTTP 200 with 5–20 results each. Live
chain check with `WEB_SEARCH_DISABLED_PROVIDERS=exa-mcp,exa` returned the correct
answer from `you-mcp` in 2.7s.

Two independent free quotas mean exhausting one is a step down, not a cliff.

**THE MORE IMPORTANT HALF: the SSE frame reader was wrong, and the new provider
is only what exposed it.** The existing exa-mcp reader took the FIRST `data:`
line as the JSON-RPC reply:

```js
var m = String(txt).match(/data:\s*(\{[\s\S]*?\})\s*\n/)
```

You.com sends a log notification first, so a first-frame reader turns an HTTP 200
carrying 20 results into **zero results** — indistinguishable upstream from a
dead endpoint, and exactly the plausible-empty shape that hid the other dead
rungs for weeks. The first probe written during this work did precisely that and
reported the provider broken. Both rungs now parse every frame and select the
reply by structure (`src/core/effectors/mcp-search.js`).

**A latency number is a property of the caller, not of the endpoint.** A
hand-written probe measured You.com at 1.85s against Exa at 2.8s, and "fastest
first" would have acted on that and placed You.com ahead. Both numbers were
artefacts: the probe skipped the `initialized` notification, so it timed two
round trips where the real client pays three. Re-measured *through the shipping
module*, three queries each, the order inverts — exa-mcp 1531/1634/1899ms
(median 1634) against you-mcp 2227/2621/3148ms (median 2621). exa-mcp keeps first
place; the ordering is now pinned by a test.

**Three of twelve mutations survived on the first pass, and each meant something
different** — worth recording because two of the three would have shipped as
"tested":

1. Deleting the `if (f.method) continue` notification guard broke nothing. Correct
   verdict: a notification carries `params`, never `result`/`error`, so the
   structural check already rejected it. The guard defended an unreachable state
   and was **removed**, not test-papered.
2. Deleting the `isError` check broke nothing, twice. That one was a genuine gap —
   `isError: true` is a real MCP tool-failure shape. The first replacement test was
   still vacuous, because ignoring `isError` also ends in zero results.
3. Deleting the JSON-RPC `error` branch broke nothing, for the same reason.

The pattern behind 2 and 3: **every fault path in this module produces the same
OUTCOME as a miss, and differs only in whether the cause survives.** So a test
that asserts `ok:false` proves nothing about them. Both are now pinned on the
failure trace (`you-mcp tool reported isError`, `you-mcp daily free quota
exhausted`) and on the cooldown actually arming — a fault reported as "no
results" leaves the provider looking healthy and re-paid on every later call.

**What this does NOT fix.** The scrape rungs are still dead and still cost their
timeouts when both keyless rungs are spent (BUG-361's cooldown limits how often).
The local daemon still returns 0 results from every engine. Wikipedia still ships
as `ok:true`. Google CSE and Brave remain unconfigured — CSE needs the Custom
Search API enabled on the operator's Cloud project plus a `GOOGLE_CSE_ID`, and is
a separate ~100/day pool that would take the ceiling to ~350/day across three
vendors. And **both daily caps are vendor claims, not measurements**: neither
endpoint publishes a rate-limit header, so the chain treats a sudden 429 as
normal rather than exceptional and says so in the trace.

**Files:** `src/core/effectors/mcp-search.js` (new — both MCP rungs and the shared
frame reader; `web-search.js` was at its 862-line ratchet ceiling, and moving
exa-mcp out brought it to 801), `src/core/effectors/web-search.js`,
`mythos/.env.example`.
**Test:** `test/bug-365-search-has-a-second-free-quota.test.js` (20 tests).

## ⚠ NUMBERING COLLISION — BUG-360 is assigned twice (recorded 2026-08-26)

It happened again, in the same shape the note above describes, between two sessions working on
the same day.

- **BUG-360 (a)** — the SPA dot-path 404 (commit `8f22877`, on `main` at 03:30). Its number is
  embedded in the `res.sendFile` comment at `mythos/server/index.js:1541` and in
  `mythos/test/spa-fallback-dot-path.test.js`.
- **BUG-360 (b)** — adb resolution (commit `29fb263`, at 04:28). Its number is embedded in three
  commit messages, `mythos/scripts/setup-android.js`, `mythos/adapters/android-child/index.js`,
  `mythos/scripts/doctor.js`, `mythos/scripts/parity-check.js` and two test filenames.

**(a) holds the number by this file’s own rule** — a number is yours once it is committed, and (a)
was committed an hour earlier. (b) grepped `BUGS.md` at 04:07, saw 359 as the maximum, and was
wrong because (a)’s commit had not been fetched to the local ref yet. That is exactly the failure
the note above warns about, one step further out: **grepping this file is not enough on a shared
tree, and neither is grepping the branch you are standing on. `git fetch` first.**

**Neither is renumbered**, for the same reason as BUG-280: the numbers are already in pushed
commits, four code files and three test filenames, so rewriting them is churn the operator should
authorise rather than a session deciding unilaterally. The two headings are disambiguated instead,
so the registry stops being ambiguous even though the tickets stay as they shipped.

**A second thing worth recording about (a):** it shipped inside a commit whose subject is
`test(android): make the poll-starvation guard immune to host load`. That message describes one of
the six files it touched; the SPA fix, its new test and a 78-line BUGS.md entry are not mentioned.
Root `CLAUDE.md` already records this exact shape — 262 lines of BUG-322 committed under a BUG-319
message — as a consequence of two sessions sharing one git index. Searching history by subject
will not find this fix.

## BUG-366 — the capabilities manifest was corrected only when an adapter SUCCEEDED, so a failure could stay described as still-in-progress (✅ FIXED 2026-08-26, live-verified)

**Status:** ✅ FIXED 2026-08-26. 7 regression tests, 6 mutations, none survived.

**THE AUDIT'S STATED MECHANISM WAS WRONG, AND SO WAS THE FIRST DRAFT OF THIS
FIX.** That is the most useful thing in this entry, so it goes first.

The 2026-08-26 E2E audit reported `browser-agent: CONNECTING` frozen permanently
in `vault/Identity/capabilities.md`, and blamed a coincidence of constants:
`main.js:1077` scheduling its settle re-write at a literal `10000`, exactly
`browser-agent`'s own `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS`, so the write sampled the adapter at
the instant its connect expired. Two 10000s, one race. It reads perfectly and it
survives reading the code.

**Measured, it is false.** With no debug Chrome on :9222 the connect fails with
`ECONNREFUSED` in **~15ms**, not 10s — the OS refuses immediately rather than
letting the handshake run to timeout. The two timers are three orders of
magnitude apart and never race. Measured again through the shipping adapter: 15ms
to settle, against a 10,000ms timeout.

**What actually produces a wrong manifest is three things together:**

1. The immediate boot `writeIt()` can sample the adapter inside that ~15ms
   window, because `connect()` sets `state = 'CONNECTING'` **synchronously** and
   the browser step (`main.js:942`) runs before the manifest step (`:1056`).
2. **Nothing refreshed on the `CONNECTING → OFFLINE` transition.** Only the three
   success paths called `refreshCapabilities()`. So a mid-flight sample stood.
3. The settle timer is `unref()`'d, so a process that exits before it fires never
   corrects the file at all.

**And the audit's evidence was an artefact of (3), not a live defect.**
`test/boot.test.js:17` points `MYTHOS_VAULT_ROOT` at the **repo** vault and kills
the child 200ms after ALIVE — so `mythos/vault/Identity/capabilities.md` is test
output, not system state. The packaged vault on the same machine, written by a
long-lived boot, correctly read:

```
- browser-agent: OFFLINE (CDP connect failed: browserType.connectOverCDP: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:9222
```

State *and* reason. Confirmed by mtime: packaged vault 16:25, repo vault 14:19.

**The audit's second finding — `hint: null` — is the SAME bug, not a separate
one.** `connect()` clears `hint` on entry and only sets a real one on settle, so
a status sampled mid-attempt necessarily carries `CONNECTING` with no reason
attached. Once settled, a reason always exists. One bug, two symptoms.

**The fix is (2).** Both the `else` (ok === false) and the `.catch()` branches of
the boot connect now call `refreshCapabilities()`, so the correction lands in
~15ms instead of waiting on a timer that may never fire. A status file corrected
only when things go right will always describe a broken system as still trying.

Secondary, and deliberately not sold as the cause: `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` is now
**exported** and `main.js` derives its settle delay from it plus 2s of headroom,
instead of restating the number. Two copies of one constant go stale silently
when either moves, which is true regardless of whether they ever raced.

**Why it mattered enough to fix a "stale test artefact".**
`src/core/effectors/from-memory.js:314` reads this file back to answer *"what can
you do?"*, and a dev-mode session reads the repo vault. So the wrong line was
reachable by the voice model, not merely cosmetic — it just was not reachable in
the packaged app, which is what the audit thought it had measured.

**DELIBERATELY NOT CHANGED: `boot.test.js`'s vault root.** The obvious root fix —
point it at a temp dir so it stops overwriting operator-visible state — was
considered and rejected on evidence. `mythos/vault/` is **tracked**, and **five**
test files share the `MYTHOS_VAULT_ROOT: './vault'` convention
(`boot.test.js`, `cortex-goals.test.js`, `memory.test.js`,
`phase3-run-command.test.js`, `server-auth.test.js`), one of them commenting
*"identity-only — kept"* — a recorded decision, not an oversight. And a
`mkdtempSync` vault would walk straight into this repo's documented short-`TEMP`
libuv abort, which is precisely the trap that makes a spawned server look dead.
Changing it is the operator's call, on its own ticket.

**What this does NOT fix.** The immediate write can still sample a mid-flight
adapter — that window is now ~15ms wide and self-corrects, rather than being
closed. Any adapter whose handshake genuinely takes seconds (a CDP endpoint that
accepts the socket but never answers) will still be written as `CONNECTING` once,
and will now be corrected on settle rather than at the timer. And the manifest
version discrepancy the audit noted separately (packaged vault says one version,
repo vault another, for the same gitRef) is untouched.

**Files:** `mythos/adapters/browser-agent/index.js` (export the constant),
`mythos/src/main.js` (derive the delay; refresh on the two failure paths).
**Test:** `mythos/test/bug-366-settled-adapter-reaches-manifest.test.js` (7 tests).

## BUG-360 (a) — SPA dot-path. every deep link in the HUD 404'd when the install path contained a dot-segment, while `/` kept working (✅ FIXED 2026-08-26, live-verified in-suite)

Found by accident: the full suite failed `express-5-compat.test.js`'s "the SPA fallback serves the
HUD at / and at an unknown deep path" in a git worktree under `.claude/worktrees/`, and passed on
the identical commit in the main checkout. Same HEAD, same `node_modules` junction, one variable —
where the tree sits on disk.

**Mechanism.** `server/index.js`'s SPA fallback called
`res.sendFile(path.join(__dirname, '..', 'ui', 'public', 'index.html'))` with no options.
`res.sendFile`'s `dotfiles` option defaults to `'ignore'`, and `send` applies it to **every
segment of the absolute path it is handed**, not only to the part beneath a `root`. Any segment
beginning with a dot therefore made `send` raise `NotFoundError` for a file that plainly exists;
the error middleware turned that into `{"error":"Not Found"}` with status 404. Measured directly
on express 5.2.1: the same absolute path returns 404 with the default and 200 with
`{ dotfiles: 'allow' }`.

**Why it hid.** `/` never broke. `express.static` served the root from its own `index.html`, and
static's dotfiles check runs on the **request** path relative to its root — never on the root
itself. So the HUD loaded, looked healthy, and only deep links were dead. Under the
open-source-portability rule this is a real user-facing bug, not a worktree artefact: anyone
installing under `~/.local/share/mythos`, `~/.config/…`, or any other dot-directory got the same
half-working HUD.

**The fix.** `{ dotfiles: 'allow' }` on that one `sendFile`, and the path now comes from the
existing `UI_PUBLIC_DIR` const instead of a second hand-built copy of it. No user input reaches
the path — it is `UI_PUBLIC_DIR` plus a fixed basename — so `'allow'` adds no traversal surface.
`UI_PUBLIC_DIR` also became injectable (`deps.uiPublicDir`), the same seam shape as
`routes/config.js`'s `wakewordModelsDir`, because the property could not otherwise be tested
anywhere except from a dotted checkout.

**Tests.** `test/spa-fallback-dot-path.test.js` builds a `<tmpdir>/.dotted/ui/public/index.html`,
serves from it, and asserts the deep link is a 200 `text/html` while pinning that the root still
works. A second test guards the seam itself — that production still falls back to the real
`ui/public`, and that the `sendFile` still carries `dotfiles: 'allow'` — the same
guard-the-injected-path precedent the wakeword fix set. Mutation-proved both ways: removing the
option reddens the behavioural test with the 404 body quoted in the message; typo'ing the fallback
default reddens the seam guard.

**Not covered.** Only this one `sendFile` existed in the tree; `express.static` and the gzip
handler were never affected and are unchanged. A path segment that is dotted *and* attacker-chosen
would be a different problem — there is no such path here.

## BUG-334-F — the event-loop starvation guard was a wall-clock throughput floor, so a busy host failed a correct fix (✅ FIXED 2026-08-26, live-verified under synthetic load)

Follow-up to BUG-334, whose fix (async device poll) is correct and unchanged. Only its **proof**
was wrong. `test/android-child-poll-starvation.test.js` property 1 asserted that a 10 ms
`setInterval` fired at least 15 times in 300 ms of wall clock. Observed 2026-08-25: the same tree
reported `ok 59` in a standalone `node --test` run and `not ok 59` from the pre-commit hook minutes
later, while a 1.3 GB installer was being written and scanned on the same machine. A throughput
floor measures the host at least as much as it measures the code, so the gate blocked commits for
reasons that had nothing to do with the repo.

**Replaced with a structural proof.** The property is that `refreshDevices()` hands control back
to the event loop **before** the device probe settles — a `spawnSync` body cannot do that at all,
because no window exists in which the probe is outstanding and the loop is still turning. The test
now asserts the existence of that window (the injected runner was invoked, the probe is unsettled,
and control is back in the test), that control came back within a ceiling rather than after a
floor, and that a fixed, test-chosen number of awaited loop turns all complete with the probe
still outstanding. Wall clock appears only as a 2 s ceiling — far above load jitter, far below the
10 s adb timeout this pins.

**Measured, both directions.** Under 16 CPU-saturating processes on 8 cores: the old assertion
fails (`only 3 ticks in 300ms`) and the new one passes. Under the mutation that reverts the poll to
a blocking `spawnSync` body, the new assertion fails deterministically on
`the poll started 0 device probes through the injected runner`. The new assertion is also strictly
stronger, not merely steadier: against a mutation that starts the async probe and *then* blocks
synchronously for 3 s before yielding, the old assertion passed (the block completes inside
`startAndroidChild`, before the 300 ms window opens) while the new one fails on
`the poll held the event loop for 3075ms after starting the device probe`.

**Not covered.** The test cannot detect a runner that itself blocks synchronously — nothing inside
`refreshDevices()` can defend against that, and production's runner is `runAdb`, which spawns.
Properties 2 and 3 of that file are untouched.
